title: Products and services - Introduction
heading: 2.1.3.1.2 Products and services
start_phrase: La Banque Postale Group continues to strengthen its positioning as a committed bancassurance player, offering a comprehensive range of products and services tailored to the needs of its retail customers and to business customers.
summary: Overview of La Banque Postale Group’s bancassurance model and mission-led strategy: the Group provides traditional banking plus life, personal, and property/liability insurance to retail and business customers, and fulfills a State-entrusted accessible banking mission for vulnerable groups. It integrates social, environmental, and regional targets via inclusive products, green financing, and responsible savings. In 2024 it sold the business assets of crowdfunding platforms KissKissBankBank (subsequently taken over by Ulule) and Lendopolis (acquired 100% by Lendosphere to create a European energy-transition crowdfunding leader), refocusing on core banking while maintaining sustainability partnerships. The Group states no products are market-prohibited but applies strict exclusions and risk controls: no financing of fossil fuels or infrastructure that increases air traffic (except for safety, compliance, or energy-efficiency upgrades); a Responsible Financing and Investment Charter excluding sensitive sectors and companies with serious or repeated ESG controversies; prohibitions on operating in EU-listed non-cooperative tax jurisdictions with Tax Department approval required for offers; a country exclusion list for sovereign investments over corruption, tax, or basic rights concerns; clarified defence-sector rules effective 1 July 2024 excluding all weapons/equipment banned by international conventions or EU rules and related actors; and an anti-deforestation commitment effective 1 January 2024, aligned with Caisse des Dépôts, excluding financing/investment in coffee, cocoa, rubber, palm oil, soya, cattle, and timber operators/traders without a recognized no-deforestation policy.
text:
Products and services
La  Banque  Postale  Group continues to strengthen its
positioning as a  committed bancassurance player, offering
a comprehensive range of products and services tailored
to the needs of its  retail customers and to business customers.
Its 
historical offering includes traditional banking solutions,
as 
well as diversified insurance products, such as life insurance,
personal insurance  and property and liability insurance.
La Banque Postale is also the custodian of the accessible
banking mission entrusted by the State, which guarantees
universal and  non-discriminatory  access to  essential
banking services for vulnerable groups (see 2.3.4.5.2 “Actions
implemented  to generate positive  impacts”).As part of its transformation  into a mission-led company,
the Group has taken a strategic step by integrating social,
environmental 
and regional targets into its development.
This transformation has resulted in:
•the development of inclusive banking and insurance
products to meet social  and  environmental challenges;
•the introduction of solutions promoting a just transition
and a  sustainable economy, such as green financing,
responsible savings products and offers adapted to the
projects of  individuals and companies.
In 2024, La   Banque  Postale  sold  the business assets of
KissKissBankBank (KKBB) and Lendopolis, two crowdfunding
platforms acquired in 2017. During their integration into
the Group, these companies benefited  from the strategic
support and resources of La Banque Postale to consolidate
their position and accelerate their development.
•KissKissBankBank has strengthened its role in cultural
and  social crowdfunding, supporting thousands of
projects 
led by  entrepreneurs, associations  and artists.
This dynamic enabled KKBB to become a key player in
the sector, before its takeover in Ulule, where it
continues its mission  with  an even wider community.
•Lendopolis, which speciali ses in  crowdfunding for
companies, has benefited from a structured strategy by
La  Banque  Postale to develop its offering in favour of
energy 
transition projects. Lendosphere's 100% acquisition
of Lendopolis created a European leader in crowdfunding
dedicated 
to the energy transition, while guaranteeing
its business continuity.
This strategic repositioning allows the  Group to refocus on
its core banking businesses, while promoting sustainability
and  positive impacts through  solid partnerships with
these  entities.  [SBM_1_01]
Prohibited products
None of the products  or services offered by La Banque Postale
Group 
are prohibited in certain markets. However,  the
Group is extremely vigilant with regard to a certain number
of sectors with high sustainability risks.
For 
example, La Banque Postale excludes the financing of
fossil fuels and infrastructure aimed at increasing  air traffic
(with the specific exception of financing aimed at improving
the safety of  staff and passengers, bringing infrastructure
up to  standard  or improving  its energy efficiency).
A Responsible Financing and  Investment Charter derived
from its operational risk management policy provides
guidance  to La  Banque  Postale  Group on financing and
lending 
to business and corporate loan customers. This
Charter specifies that companies operating in sensitive
sectors are excluded in terms  of financing or investment.
Moreover, companies involved in serious or repeated
controversies concerning environmental, social or governance
issues, may also be excluded from financing and investment.
For more details, see focus point La  Banque  Postale's
Financing and Investment Charter.
82 La Banque  Postale      2024 Universal Registration  Document Please see the glossary on page 808 for definitions of  the main CSR terms2Sustainable performance
General information on the preparation of sustainability reports  [ESRS 2]
La Banque Postale Group also  strives to prevent financial,
legal  and reputational risks  caused by investing in
jurisdictions known for a  lack of regulation, transparency
or cooperation regarding tax fraud, money laundering and
terrorism financing. As such, it is prohibited  from setting
up operations in the countries mentioned in the European
list of non-cooperative countries and territories for tax
purposes. Offers in these countries must be approved by
the Tax Department before they are marketed (additional
information is available  in Section 4 “Business activity and
results” of the Universal  Registration Document).
In addition, the Group has compiled a list of countries
excluded  from sovereign wealth funds due to corruption,
tax policy issues or the failure to respect  basic rights. It has
also clarified its  principles of intervention in  the defence
sector, which  came  into  force  on 1 July 2024. The Groupreaffirms the exclusion from its financing and investment
activity of all weapons and equipment prohibited by
international conventions or by European Union regulations,
as well as the players involved in these sectors.
In 
addition, the urgent need to protect ecosystems and
communities  from deforestation and the conversion of
ecosystems  has led La  Banque  Postale to  define a
commitment strategy to support its customers in  the
fight against deforestation, which came into force  on
1  January 2024. To ensure alignment with Caisse des
Dépôts’ 
biodiversity policy, this engagement strategy is
complemented 
by the exclusion of operators and traders
in 
the coffee, cocoa, rubber, palm oil, soya, cattle and
timber sectors from financing and investment unless the
company 
has implemented a recognised policy to
prevent  deforestation. [SBM_1_05]

title: La Banque Postale’s Financing and Investment Charter
heading:
La Banque Postale ’s Financing 
and Investment Charter
start_phrase: La Banque Postale’s Responsible Financing and Investment Charter embodies the Bank’s commitment to sustainable and community-minded finance.
summary:
- Section context: Part of La Banque Postale’s sustainable performance and ESRS 2 sustainability reporting framework.
- Risk and compliance stance: Prohibits operations in EU-listed non-cooperative tax jurisdictions; offers there require Tax Department approval. Maintains a list of countries excluded from sovereign investments due to corruption, tax policy, or fundamental rights concerns. Clarifies defence-sector intervention principles and excludes all weapons/equipment banned by international conventions or EU rules.
- Deforestation and biodiversity: From 1 January 2024, a commitment strategy to combat deforestation; aligns with Caisse des Dépôts’ biodiversity policy. Excludes financing/investment in operators and traders in coffee, cocoa, rubber, palm oil, soya, cattle, and timber unless they have a recognized deforestation-prevention policy.
- Responsible Financing and Investment Charter: Embeds ESG into lending/investment decisions via two pillars—exclusions and ESG controversy management.
  - Exclusions: Sensitive sectors (tobacco; controversial/banned/unconventional weapons; pornography; gambling; pesticides; fur; animal testing). Sovereign exclusions include tax havens or weak scores on political/civil liberties, workers’ rights, press freedom, and corruption.
  - Controversy management: Guided by UNGPs, ILO core conventions, and OECD Guidelines. A Controversies and Exclusion Committee updates a validated exclusion list quarterly; sources include public info, data providers, and counterparties. Procedure allows supervision, engagement, or exclusion if issues persist.
  - Implementation and scope: Governed by internal procedures; Sustainability Department ensures dissemination and understanding. Applies primarily to Corporate and Local Development Banking; not yet to bancassurance (France/abroad) or Wealth and Asset Management.
- Customer segments and propositions:
  - Public sector and social economy: Financing to local authorities and public hospitals via SFIL/CAFFIL for infrastructure and medical equipment; Hippocad supports local social action.
  - Corporates: Supports SMEs to large listed firms with tailored financing for productive investment, tech/ecological/social innovation, and energy transition; focus on climate-exposed sectors and strategic industries.
  - Financial institutions: Provides investment activities, structured financing, securities lending/borrowing, hedging, and cash management.
  - Retail customers: Serves 10.1 million active customers with nationwide accessibility (17,000 outlets, incl. 7,000 post offices); 647,000 new customers in 2024; 26% growth in complementary product sales.
  - Policyholders: Integration of CNP Assurances creates an integrated bancassurer offering life, retirement, personal risk, and protection, serving over 30 million personal risk/protection and 14 million savings/retirement policyholders in Europe and Latin America.
text:
La  Banque   Postale’s Responsible  Financing and
Investment Charter  embodies the Bank’s  commitment
to sustainable and  community-minded  finance.  This
document establishes the fundamental principles that
guide 
the bank’s  lending and investment decisions,
systematically  integrating environmental,  social and
governance  (ESG)  issues . It complements  the topical
commitments,  principles  of intervention  and  sectoral
risk management policies.  It is based on two main
pillars: exclusions and management of ESG controversies.
Exclusions
La  Banque  Postale has identified activities that are
incompatible with the targets of sustainable development,
health  and well-being for all. In addition, it does not
wish 
to contribute capital to countries where fundamental
rights  and international standards are not respected.
The Charter specifies that companies operating in sensitive
sectors (tobacco, controversial, banned or unconventional
weapons, pornography, gambling, pesticides, fur, animal
testing) are excluded from financing and investment.
With  regard to sovereigns, countries considered as tax
havens  or with an insufficient score in indices related to
fundamental  rights (in particular political rights and civil
liberties,  workers' rights, freedom of the press) and
corruption  are excluded.
Controversy  management
Companies  involved  in serious  or repeated  controversies
concerning  environmental, social  or governance issues,
may  also  be excluded  from  financing and investment.
The UN Guiding Principles,  the International Labour
Organization  Conventions  on fundamental  principles
and rights at work and the OECD Guidelines for
Multinational  Enterprises  serve  as guiding frameworks.La Banque Postale undertakes to verify, before investing
in or financing a company, that the company is not
involved in an ESG controversy, based on  an exclusion
list validated by the Controversies and Exclusion
Committee. 
This Committee meets quarterly to update
the exclusion list and make it available  to stakeholders.
Information relating to exclusion criteria and cases of
controversy  is obtained from  public information sources,
data suppliers and counterparties.
In the event of serious or repeated controversies over
ESG issues,  a procedure is put in place to assess the
companies concerned. The  Controversies and Exclusion
Committee examines these cases and may decide to
place the company under supervision, to initiate  a
dialogue, or, in the most serious cases,  to exclude  it from
the Corporate and Investment Banking portfolio if the
engagement does not yield satisfactory results.
Implementation
The 
implementation of the Charter is subject to a dedicated
and documented internal procedure, specifying the roles
and responsibilities of each stakeholder. The Sustainability
Department 
ensures that it is distributed to all employees
concerned by its application and  that it is properly
understood. The Charter is available on the La Banque Postale
website .
Scope of application
The provisions of the Charter apply in particular to the
activities  of La  Banque  Postale Group's Corpor ate and
Local Development Banking division. To date, they do
not 
apply to  the activities of the bancassurance divisions
in France and abroad, or to those of the Wealth and
Asset Management division.Please  see the glossary  on page 808 for definitions of the main CSR terms 2024 Universal  Registration Document     La Banque Postale 832Sustainable performance
General information on the preparation of sustainability 
reports [ESRS 2]
2.

title: Main types of customers
heading: 2.1.3.1.3 Main types of customers
start_phrase: True to its role as a bank dedicated to serving the community, La Banque Postale targets a diverse range of customers with an offer adapted to the specific needs of each segment, while integrating social, environmental and economic matters into its strategy.
summary:
- Context: Excerpt from La Banque Postale’s 2024 Universal Registration Document under ESRS 2, outlining sustainability reporting scope and key stakeholders, with glossary reference.
- Customer segments:
  - Public sector and social economy: Financing for local authorities and public hospitals via SFIL/CAFFIL; support for social action through subsidiary Hippocad.
  - Corporates: Tailored banking and financial engineering for SMEs to large listed firms; focus on productive investment, tech/ecological/social innovation, and energy transition; attention to climate-exposed sectors and strategic industries.
  - Financial institutions: Specialized solutions for banks, insurers, mutuals, asset managers, and funds (investment activities, structured financing, securities lending/borrowing, hedging, cash management) promoting responsible practices.
  - Retail customers: 10.1 million active customers; nationwide accessibility via 17,000 outlets (7,000 post offices); 647,000 new customers in 2024; 26% growth in complementary equipment product sales.
  - Policyholders: Integration of CNP Assurances creates an integrated bancassurance group offering life, retirement, personal risk/protection, and property insurance; 30 million personal risk/protection policyholders and 14 million savings/retirement policyholders across Europe and Latin America.
- Income and workforce:
  - Total income: €41.1 billion, defined as net turnover (interest, securities income, fees/commissions, financial transaction results, other operating income).
  - Workforce: 14,512 own workers (12,204 in France; 670 in Europe excl. France; 1,638 Rest of World).
- Sector positions and exclusions:
  - Not active in fossil fuels, chemical production, controversial/prohibited weapons, or tobacco growing; applies fossil fuel exclusion policies.
  - Reported revenues are zero from fossil fuel sectors (coal, oil, gas), chemical manufacturing, and controversial/banned weapons; taxonomy-aligned economic activities and fossil gas revenues reported as zero.
  - Cross-references provided to climate transition risk indicators and climate policies elsewhere in the document.
text:
1.3.1.3 Main types  of customers
True  to its role as a  bank  dedicated  to serving the
community, La Banque Postale targets a diverse range of
customers  with an offer adapted to the specific needs of
each  segment,  while  integrating  social, environmental
and economic  matters  into  its strategy.
Public  sector  and social  economy
La  Banque  Postale is a key player with local authorities
and public hospitals. Its strategic partnership with SFIL/
CAFFIL  (Société  de Financement  Local/Caisse Française
de Financement Local) enables it to finance structuring
projects,  such as the construction and renovation of
public  infrastructure  or the acquisition  of state-of-the-art
medical  equipment. In addition , through its subsidiary
Hippocad,  it supports local authorities in  social action
initiatives, thus  meeting  the needs  of the most vulnerable.
Corporates
La  Banque  Postale supports companies of all sizes, from
SMEs  and intermediate-sized enterprises  to large, listed
companies  (SBF 120, CAC 40), by offering them tailor-
made 
banking and financial engineering  solutions.
This offer aims to support productive investments, technological,
ecological and social innovation, as well as the energy
transition. 
Particular attention is paid to sectors exposed
to climate risks (transport, non-carbon energies) and to
industries  that  are strategic for  national  independence.Financial  institutions
La Banque Postale offers specialised solutions to financial
institutions, 
such as banks, insurance companies, mutual
insurance  companies, asset managers  and  funds.
These  solutions include investment  activities, structured
financing (fixed income or bank), securities borrowing and
lending, 
as well as hedging and cash management instruments.
This 
positioning consolidates its role as a major player in
the financial ecosystem, while promoting responsible and
sustainable practices.
Retail customers
La 
Banque Postale serves  10.1 million active retail customers
by offering them a comprehensive range of financial
products 
and services. It focuses on banking accessibility
and financial inclusion, with 17,000 retail outlets throughout
the country, including 7,000  post offices, guaranteeing
proximity to its customers. In 2024, La  Banque  Postale
welcomed 647,000 new retail customers and recorded a
26% 
increase in sales of complementary equipment products,
demonstrating 
its ability to meet the evolving needs of its
customers.
Policyholders
With 
the integration of CNP Assurances, La Banque Postale
has established itself as a major integrated bancassurance
group. 
This transaction strengthens its ability to offer a
complete 
range  of property and personal insurance,
covering areas such as life insurance, retirement, personal
risk and protection . With more  than 30 million personal
risk 
and protection policyholders and 14 million savings
and retirement policyholders on two continents (Europe
and  Latin America), CNP   Assurances consolidates
La  Banque  Postale’s commitment to offering solutions
adapted 
to the needs of its customers, while promoting
responsible and  sustainable practices. [SBM_1_02]84 La Banque  Postale      2024 Universal Registration  Document Please see the glossary on page 808 for definitions of  the main CSR terms2Sustainable performance
General information on the preparation of sustainability reports  [ESRS 2]

title: Breakdown of own workers and income
heading: 2.1.3.1.4 Breakdown of own workers and income
start_phrase: La Banque Postale Group is not considered to be a company active in the fossil fuel sector, given its financing, investment and insurance business, in accordance with the list defined by the regulations.
summary:
- Context and scope: Excerpts from La Banque Postale’s 2024 Universal Registration Document under “Sustainable performance” and ESRS 2, covering breakdowns of income and workforce, sectoral exclusions, and sustainability strategy/targets.
- Sectoral exclusions and zero revenues: The Group is not active in fossil fuels, chemical production, controversial/prohibited weapons, or tobacco growing. It reports zero revenues from these sectors (including coal, oil, gas, and tobacco cultivation) and applies fossil fuel exclusion policies outlined in its Responsible Financing and Investment Charter.
- Income definition and amount: Total income (aligned with the French Monetary and Financial Code definition of net turnover) aggregates interest, fees/commissions, gains on financial instruments, reinsurance items, and other operating income; reported at €41,100 million.
- Workforce breakdown: 14,512 own workers, with 12,204 in France, 670 in Europe (excl. France), and 1,638 in the Rest of the World.
- References to climate risk and reporting: Additional details on climate transition risk indicators appear elsewhere in the URD; disclosures reference ESRS 2 and specific SBM metrics.
- Mission, purpose, and governance: As a mission-led company, La Banque Postale articulates a purpose centered on social inclusion, regional development, and planetary boundaries. CNP Assurances (part of the Group) embeds its company purpose in its Articles of Association, with stakeholder commitments and monitoring indicators; it is positioned as a major green investor within the Caisse des Dépôts ecosystem.
- Sustainability targets and integration: By 2025, targets include 80% of new offers classified as sustainable via an ESG checklist and assessment of 87% of the Bank’s technical reserves using the Impact Weighting Factor (IWF).
- ESG in product innovation: ESG criteria are integrated into product design across Retail, Corporate, and Local Development Banking using common tools (ESG checklist; green/social/sustainable bond framework).
- Examples of “just transition” offerings: 
  - Financing for social home ownership and energy renovation (e.g., PAS loans, zero-interest eco-loan, Avance Rénovation, impact real estate loans) and green personal loans.
  - Community finance and solidarity products (SIS; LBP AM SRI Human Rights and Actions Solidaire funds).
  - SRI-labelled and ESG-screened savings solutions; transition-focused funds (e.g., Tocqueville Environnement SRI) and green bond issues.
  - Free services supporting customers’ carbon footprint tracking (Carbo) and youth financial inclusion (Youth Pass).
text:
1.3.1.4
Breakdown  of own  workers  and  income
La  Banque  Postale Group is not considered to be a
company  active in the fossil fuel sector, given its financing,
investment and insurance business, in accordance with

title: Sustainability strategy and targets
heading: 2.1.3.1.5 Sustainability strategy and targets
start_phrase: As a mission-led company, La Banque Postale is committed to meeting social, environmental and regional challenges.
summary:
- Scope and framework: Part of La Banque Postale’s 2024 Universal Registration Document on sustainable performance and ESRS 2 reporting, referencing exclusion principles in the Responsible Financing and Investment Charter and a glossary of CSR terms.
- Mission-led purpose: La Banque Postale’s company purpose centers on just transition, inclusion, and planetary boundaries; CNP Assurances’ purpose emphasizes responsible insurance/investment and an inclusive, sustainable society, embedded in its Articles of Association.
- 2025 sustainability targets: 80% of new offers to qualify as sustainable via an ESG checklist; 87% of Bank technical reserves assessed using the Impact Weighting Factor (IWF).
- ESG integration in products: Systematic use of shared tools (ESG checklist; green/social/sustainability bond framework) and methodologies (IWF, LBP AM’s GREaT) with innovation focus in 2024.
- Product and service examples for the just transition: financing for social home ownership, energy renovation and green vehicles; community finance (SIS) and SRI funds; transition-focused savings (e.g., Tocqueville Environnement SRI, green bonds); non-banking tools like Carbo carbon footprinting and Youth Pass. Tobacco cultivation/production revenues reported as zero.
- New impact card (Dec 2024, with WWF France): deposits fund mortgages with energy-efficiency works; card contribution supports WWF biodiversity programs; users receive carbon footprint tracking/advice via Carbo.
- Insurance and risk solutions: right to be forgotten for breast cancer survivors; microinsurance in Latin America; protection products (life, funeral, long-term care) and offerings tailored to seniors and people with chronic diseases.
- Sustainable investment offerings: launch of Tocqueville Biodiversity SRI (SFDR Art. 9) in July 2024; a green structured note (Green PAB 100 Autocall Nov 2032) linked to a Paris-aligned Eurozone PAB index under the Group’s Green/Social/Sustainability Bond Framework.
- Strategy and disclosure: Group transition plan; sectoral policies (coal, oil, gas, aeronautics, deforestation/ecosystem conversion); publication of a Climate and Nature report aligned with TCFD/TNFD, linking climate and biodiversity.
- Value chain and stakeholders: emphasis on collaboration across internal teams and external partners; stakeholder consideration through governance bodies—Mission Committee (18 members, 12 independent; meets at least 3 times/year; tracks 14 indicators and reports annually) and Customer Board (16 members; meets 3 times/year to inform offers, service quality, and customer experience).
text:
1.3.1.5 Sustainability strategy and targets
As a mission-led company, La Banque Postale is committed
to meeting social, environmental and regional challenges.
La Banque  Postale  Group's  company purpose
“Because  it was  created with  the purpose  of serving the public, La Banque  Postale believes that there can  be no long-
lasting value creation without redistribution, no economic growth without local prosperity, and no sustainable
development  without  respect  for planet boundaries.
By offering quality and accessible services, our purpose is to enable everyone to fulfil their potential and to contribute,
through their investment,  savings, insurance and consumption choices, to building a society that is more attentive to
the planet and all who live on it. As a committed banker and insurer, it is our desire to work towards this just
transition alongside  our customers and employees.”
By offering financial products and services to as many people
as possible, the Group fulfils its public service mission
while supporting  its customers  in the just  transition.
As part of  its transformation  into a  mission-led company,
the Group  has  set itself  ambitious targets  in terms of  the
sustainability of its products and technical  reserves, which
it is monitoring  closely.  By 2025,  for example,  it aims to
ensure that 80% of new offers are identified as sustainable
based  on the ESG checklist (see focus point: The ESGchecklist: 
responsible products “by design”) and to be
assessing 87% of the Bank’s technical reserves based on
the Impact Weighting Factor (see focus point: The Impact
Weighting Factor (IWF)).
Since 
2021, CNP Assurances has also included its company
purpose in its  Articles of Association.  It has  also set  out its
commitments to its various stakeholders, as well as specific
monitoring  indicators to ensure their  implementation.
CNP  Assurances’  company  purpose
“As a responsible insurer and investor,  driven by the community values of our Group, we work with our partners to
create an inclusive and sustainable society, providing solutions to as many people as  possible to protect and support
them on their  chosen  paths."
CNP  Assurances  stands out  for its  vision as  an insurer and
sustainable investor, its open and multi-partner model, as
well as its financial strength and impact on the economy.
Its model enables it to reach several hundred partners
and  tens of  millions of customers on two continents:
Europe and Latin America. As a member of the major
state-owned 
financial unit Caisse des Dépôts, CNP Assurances
is a leading  financial player  in green  investments and
major infrastructure  in its regions.  [SBM_1_21]
In 2024,  ESG  integration  was placed at the heart of the
Group's  product  innovation dynamic.
The inclusion  of ESG  criteria  in the  design of offers for
Retail Banking for individuals and professionals and in
Corporate 
and Local Development Banking is based on
shared  tools such as the ESG checklist and the issuance
framework  for green, social and sustainable bonds, which
defines  the rules  applicable  to thematic issues.
The ESG  checklist assesses offers and products in terms of
their contribution  to the  customer experience  and
satisfaction  as well as to the just transition. Within therange, certain product and
 service offerings are particularly
relevant to the just transition,  in particular:
•Financing offers that promote social home ownership
(PAS loans), energy renovation (impact  real estate loan,
zero-interest eco-loan, Avance Rénovation loan)  or that
support responsible  consumption projects  (personal
loans for green vehicles or green works);
•Community  finance offers such as the Solidarity Interest
Service (SIS), available for  regulated passbook savings
accounts as well  as the LBP AM SRI  Human  Rights and
LBP AM SRI Actions Solidaire funds;
•The range of committed financial  savings built on
obtaining the State SRI label for eligible products and on
strict ESG selection criteria for others;
•Savings solutions dedicated  to financing  the  transition,
such  as the Tocqueville Environnement SRI fund or
green bond issues;
•Free non-banking  services that support all customers in
calculating and managing the carbon footprint of their
banking 
expenses (Carbo) or, which help young customers
negotiate adulthood (Youth Pass).

Since  December 2024, La Banque Postale customers have
been  able to sign  up to a new impact card offer, in
partnership with WWF  France. This  offer  aims  to:
•contribute to the energy renovation of the French housing
stock, 
especially the  least  energy-efficient  housing.
To  this end, deposits in the associated accounts are
allocated to the  financing or  refinancing of real estate
loans  granted  by La  Banque  Postale to  those buying a
home,  where these also include a home improvements
budget  for energy and heat  efficiency;
•promote  actions to preserve and restore biodiversity: the
additional contribution of the impact card, compared to
a traditional  card, is  paid  in full  to WWF  France to
support its programmes;
•support holders  to adopt more responsible consumption
practices throughout  using  the  Carbo carbon  footprint
calculator  and  dedicated  advice.
Risk  management and insurance solutions also respond
to changes in society and the challenges of increased life
expectancy, 
preparing for retirement, and changing social
protection schemes. CNP Assurances has therefore introduced:
•The right to be  forgotten for women  who suffer from
breast  cancer;
•Microinsurance products in Latin America;
•A range of insurance products covering needs in terms of
protection  against life risks (life insurance, funeral costs,
long-term  care);
•Products  and services adapted to the specific needs of
the elderly  and  people  with  chronic diseases.
In financial savings, in addition to funds offering existing
sustainable 
investment solutions, the Group has expanded
its offer by listing  the Tocqueville Biodiversity SRI UCI in
July  2024.  This  fund, classified under  Article 9 of the SFDR
Regulation,  is offered to Retail Banking customers and
supports  investment in companies that, through their
goods  and services, directly and indirectly reduce the
impact of human activities on biodiversity. More information
on SFDR technical reserves is  available in paragraph 2.1.6.4
“Monitoring indicators for impact finance commitments”.
Also,  in the structured debt securities segment,
La  Banque  Postale Group continues to  innovate towards
greater ESG integration. In September 2024, it launched
a 
green issue – La  Banque  Postale Green PAB 100
Autocall  November 2032 – which can finance or refinance
projects  related to the  environmental transition identified
based  on its Green, Social and Sustainability Bond
Framework.  This also  provides an opportunity to use a
new underlying index (Euronext® Euro zone 60  PAB) in
line with the recommendations of the Paris Climate
Agreement.  [SBM_1_22]La Banque Postale Group  places sustainability matters at
the heart of its strategy, as evidenced by:
•the 
Group’s transition plan and the sectoral policies put in
place 
to direct financing and investments (coal, oil, gas,
aeronautics, deforestation and  ecosystem conversion);
•the publication of the Climate and Nature report
(aligned with the TCFD and TNFD recommendations),
which for the first time links climate and biodiversity
matters in a single publication;
•the ESG checklist, which helps to better qualify offers
(see  focus point: The ESG checklist: responsible products
“by design”);
•Use of the  Impact  Weighting Factor, an internally
developed sustainability and impact indicator (see focus
point:  The Impact Weighting Factor (IWF), as well as
GREaT, LBP  AM's  SRI analysis method (see focus point:
The GREaT methodology ). [SBM_1_23]

start_phrase: La Banque Postale Group’s value chain is presented in the following infographic.

- Launch of a new “impact card” with WWF France:
  - Deposits support financing/refinancing of real estate loans that include energy-efficiency renovations, particularly for poorly insulated housing.
  - The card’s additional contribution is fully donated to WWF France to fund biodiversity programs.

  - Green structured note issuance (La Banque Postale Green PAB 100 Autocall Nov 2032) to finance/refinance environmental transition projects per the Group’s Green, Social and Sustainability Bond Framework; uses Euronext Eurozone 60 PAB index aligned with the Paris Agreement.
- Embedding sustainability in strategy:
  - Group transition plan and sectoral policies guiding financing/investment (coal, oil, gas, aeronautics, deforestation and ecosystem conversion).
  - Publication of a combined Climate and Nature report aligned with TCFD and TNFD.
  - Tools and methods: ESG checklist for responsible products “by design,” the internal Impact Weighting Factor (IWF), and LBP AM’s GREaT SRI methodology.
- Value chain and collaboration:
  - Emphasis on internal and external collaboration to scale impact, share best practices, and ensure consistent, effective implementation of the sustainability strategy.
- Stakeholder engagement and governance:
  - Collaborative approach to decision-making; main stakeholders mapped via the value chain.

title: Consideration of stakeholders
heading: 2.1.3.1.7 Consideration of stakeholders
start_phrase: Details of how stakeholders are taken into account are presented in the following infographic “Main stakeholder challenges”.
summary:
- Scope and framing: Extract from La Banque Postale’s Universal Registration Document detailing ESRS 2 sustainability reporting, stakeholder integration, double materiality, and how sustainability is embedded in the Group’s strategy.
- New responsible offerings:
  - Impact card with WWF France: directs deposits to energy-efficient home renovation loans; channels card fee uplift fully to WWF biodiversity programs; supports responsible consumption via the Carbo carbon-footprint app and advice.
  - Insurance innovations by CNP Assurances: right to be forgotten for women with breast cancer; microinsurance in Latin America; coverage for life risks (life, funeral, long-term care); products tailored to seniors and people with chronic diseases.
  - Investment and structured products: Tocqueville Biodiversity SRI UCI (SFDR Article 9) added in July 2024; launch of a green structured note (Green PAB 100 Autocall November 2032) aligned with the Group’s Green, Social & Sustainability Bond Framework and Paris-aligned Euronext Eurozone 60 PAB index.
- Governance, tools and methodologies:
  - Group transition plan and sectoral policies (coal, oil, gas, aeronautics, deforestation/ecosystem conversion).
  - Climate and Nature report aligned with TCFD and TNFD, linking climate and biodiversity.
  - Product qualification via an ESG checklist; use of the Impact Weighting Factor (IWF) and LBP AM’s GREaT SRI analysis.
- Value chain and collaboration: Overview of upstream suppliers, own operations, and downstream customers/financed activities; emphasis on co-construction with teams, partners, and ecosystems to scale impact and consistency of the sustainability strategy.
- Stakeholder engagement architecture:
  - Mission Committee (18 members, 12 independent): meets at least three times a year, tracks 14 indicators, issues an annual mission report to the Supervisory Board.
  - Customer Board (16 members): triannual consultations to improve offer, service quality, and experience.
  - Initiative Against Banking Exclusion think-tank (25 members): financial inclusion, poverty insights, and solution co-creation.
  - Ongoing dialogue with NGOs and civil society (e.g., WWF) informing the IWF and sector policies; frequent consultation of public authorities, regulators, peers, and rating agencies.
- Stakeholder matrices: Detailed channels, purposes, and integration of feedback for shareholders/investors; public authorities and supervisors; NGOs/charities; industry peers; suppliers/subcontractors and their employees; employees and La Poste workers; financed entities and their employees; customers; planet; communities; and distributor/banking partners.
- Double materiality and IROs:
  - Positive impacts: access to bancassurance (including vulnerable populations), sustainable/positive-impact financing, strong corporate culture/working conditions, business ethics/general interest.
  - Negative impacts: own-operations climate/waste; environmental and human rights impacts from financed activities; customer impacts from cybersecurity breaches.
  - Risks: physical/transition climate and environmental risks and rising loss ratios; portfolio exposure to transition/physical risks; inadequate ESG integration in governance; HR health/safety risks; partner assessment gaps; customer protection risk.
  - Opportunities: growth in sustainable finance and employer attractiveness via culture.
  - Time horizons: environmental impacts assessed as current; social/governance as current or potential (short term for own operations/services; medium term for financed activities).
  - Trade-offs and dependencies acknowledged (e.g., home-loan decarbonization versus access to credit and pace of social housing renovation) within a just-transition approach; no material impacts from these dependencies identified in the analysis.
- Strategy linkage and execution:
  - Mission-led strategy centered on planet and people, a just transition, and transforming the bancassurance model; reinforces universal banking/insurance positioning and accessible banking mission.
  - Financed-activity impacts addressed through shareholder dialogue and financing of the public sector and social/solidarity economy.
  - Governance and business conduct treated as core to a regulated bancassurer.
  - 2030 strategic plan already aligned with most material ESRS topics; future updates will integrate double materiality results for the full conglomerate (including CNP Assurances); no near-term structural changes planned.
  - Strategic model emphasizes differentiation, diversification, and digitization across customers, co-workers, and communities, mapping objectives to ESRS E1–E5 and S1–S4, including access, impact financing, portfolio risk prevention, corporate culture, HR and customer-protection (including cybersecurity).

1.3.1.7 Consideration of stakeholders
Details  of how  stakeholders are taken into account are
presented in the following infographic “Main stakeholder
challenges”.
La  Banque  Postale Group seeks to work  collaboratively
with its stakeholders in as many decisions as possible.
[SBM_2_01]
The Group’s main stakeholders are presented in the
infographic showing the value chain. 
[SBM_2_02]
Several bodies ensure that the interests of the Group’s
stakeholders are understood  and  taken into  account.
Composed  of 18 members,  including 12 independent
experts from the economic, financial, academic and civil
society worlds, the Mission Committee monitors and
develops  La  Banque   Postale ’s sustainability strategy. It
meets at  least  three times a  year,  and ensures that the
actions implemented effectively  contribute  to meeting
the Group’s targets. It assesses the action plan on the
basis 
of 14 indicators  and  publishes a  mission report each
year, which is presented to  the Supervisory Board.
The Customer Board, a partner of the Executive Committee,
aims to improve the offer, the quality of service and  the
customer experience. To this end, it collects customer
opinions 
on the Group’s projects or strategic  decisions
three times a year. Its  16 members  embody the  diversity of
La Banque Postale’s customers.Please  see the glossary  on page 808 for definitions of the main CSR terms 2024 Universal  Registration Document     La Banque Postale 872Sustainable performance

The strategy’s sustainability pillars include serving our company purpose as a mission-led 
company, deﬁ  ned by our commitment to a society which works towards the interests of our planet and its inhabitants, a just transition, and the transformation of the bancassurance model. This strategy aims to mitigate our impacts and promote adaptation (economic resilience and diversiﬁ  cation) in a context of environmental and societal transition. It also systematically includes ESG matters to ensure sustainability and positive impact.
The Group’s strategy reinforces its differentiating position as a universal banking and insurance 
provider, in line with our accessible banking mission and regional network. Furthermore, La Banque Postale Group recognises the impact of its ﬁ  nanced activities and 
acts accordingly through both shareholder dialogue with companies, and the ﬁ  nancing of the 
public sector and the social and solidarity economy. [SBM_2_08] [SBM_2_09]
With regard to CSRD topics not covered in the current strategy, the issues of governance and 
business conduct are intrinsic to the business model of a particularly regulated bancassurance company, and are the subject of daily attention.The implementation of the 2030 strategic plan takes stakeholder issues into account. There are currently no scheduled structural changes to the strategic plan. However, when it is updated, the interests of stakeholders identiﬁ  ed through the double materiality analysis will be integrated into a conglomerate vision, which includes CNP Assurances. [SBM_2_10]
The affected stakeholders will therefore not be
impacted in the short term by a change in the strategy. [SBM_2_11]La Banque Postale’s ten-year strategic plan (2021-2030) is the result of an approach that takes on board the concerns of stakeholders (customers, community and co-workers). It also incorporates the expectations of investors and rating agencies.It was developed before the CSRD, but it is based on the Group’s 
sustainable values  and is already 
aligned with the majority of the issues identiﬁ  ed in the materiality analysis.Our strategy focuses on our main stakeholders: customers, community and co-workers. For La Banque Postale, the term “sustainability” encompasses environmental and societal issues, particularly those of the regional public sector, and the Group’s ability to provide responsible products and services (banking services, insurance, credit and investment). In this respect, it is aligned with the main ESRS.

title: Description of material impacts, risks and opportunities (IRO)
heading: 2.1.3.2 Description of material impacts, risks and opportunities (IRO)
start_phrase: The positive and negative impacts, risks and material opportunities for La Banque Postale Group are set out in the diagram below presenting the list of IROs.
summary:
- Focus: ESRS 2 general disclosures in La Banque Postale’s 2024 Universal Registration Document covering material impacts, risks and opportunities (IROs), their interaction with the business model, and related financial effects.

- Double materiality and IROs:
  - Identification of positive and negative IROs for own operations, service activities, and financed activities, with a reminder that actions to mitigate one impact may create trade-offs elsewhere.
  - ESG interdependencies are integrated into a “just transition” strategy; no material impacts from these dependencies were identified.
  - Time horizons: environmental impacts considered current; social and governance impacts can be current or potential. Potential impacts are assessed short term for own operations/service activities and medium term for financed activities.
  - A matrix summarizes which topics (E1–E5, S1–S4, G1) are material/non-material/not assessed across impacts and risks/opportunities for both own and financed activities.

- Interaction with the business model and strategy:
  - The Group is adapting its mission-led bancassurance model to enhance positive impact and resilience without questioning the core activity.
  - Adjustments include service offering changes, investment and commercial decision processes, and support to business lines; “impact” is added as a third decision axis alongside risk and return.
  - Example: CNP Assurances implements reinsurance coverage for excess mortality linked to climate risks (e.g., pandemics, heat waves). Internal functions (HR, purchasing, compliance) integrate climate-related social and governance considerations.
  - No immediate strategic overhaul is planned; ongoing stakeholder dialogue will keep the strategy relevant.

- Main impacts:
  - Negative environmental impacts largely stem from financed activities: GHG emissions, pollution, water and marine resource use, biodiversity impacts, and waste across supported sectors. Potential negative customer impacts include cybersecurity breaches or inadequate insurance.
  - Positive impacts arise from strategic choices: green loans for climate adaptation, favorable working conditions, financing for local authorities, accessible banking; as a responsible insurer, CNP seeks to enhance positive effects on people.

- Where impacts arise:
  - Environmental, employee, and governance impacts relate to own operations, service activities, and financed activities.
  - Social impacts on workers in the value chain, affected communities, and customers mainly arise through business relationships (e.g., La Poste workers, suppliers, local/regional authorities, customers).

- Financial effects of material risks:
  - 2024 provisions include climate-related risks in financed activities:
    - Transition risk in the Corporate portfolio (impact of carbon price increases on counterparties’ solvency).
    - Physical flood risk in the home loan portfolio (effects on expected recoveries in litigation).
  - Provisions will be refined each reporting period; details are in the consolidated financial statements notes.
  - Provisions for social factors (HR disputes) are recognized; no provisions for governance risks at 31 Dec 2024.
  - No assessment yet of the financial impact of material opportunities.

title: Interactions between material IROs and La Banque Postale Group's business model
heading: 2.1.3.3 Interactions between material IROs and La Banque Postale Group 's business model
start_phrase: In a context of environmental and social transition, La Banque Postale Group is adapting its business model to have a positive impact and ensure its resilience.
summary:
- Purpose and context: La Banque Postale Group is adapting its mission-led bancassurance business model to environmental and social transitions, embedding sustainability into strategy, governance, and product design to enhance resilience.

- Integration of impacts, risks, and opportunities (IROs): A third “impact” lens now complements the traditional risk-return analysis in strategic decisions. Current material impacts and risks are already factored into the strategy; stakeholder dialogue will keep it relevant, with no short-term strategic change planned.

- Business model and offering evolution:
  - Expansion of services and decision processes to address environmental and social issues.
  - Example: CNP Assurances’ global protection approach adds reinsurance against excess mortality (pandemics, heat waves).
  - Internal functions (HR, purchasing, compliance) integrate climate effects on social and governance aspects.
  - Financing and investment activities incorporate impact criteria across lending and asset management.

- Material impacts overview:
  - Negative: Primarily from financed activities—financed GHG emissions, pollution, water and marine resource pressure, biodiversity impacts, and waste; plus potential customer harm via cybersecurity breaches or inadequate insurance.
  - Positive: Driven by strategy and mission—green loans for climate adaptation/mitigation, favorable working conditions, financing local authorities, and accessible banking; responsible insurance for over 30 million policyholders.

- Impact linkages:
  - Environmental, employee, and governance impacts tied to own operations, service activities, and financed activities.
  - Social impacts on workers in the value chain, affected communities, and customers arise mainly via business relationships (La Poste workforce, suppliers, local/regional authorities, customers).

- Financial effects and provisions:
  - 2024 provisions added for climate risks:
    - Transition risk in the Corporate portfolio (counterparty solvency under higher carbon prices).
    - Physical flood risk in the home loan portfolio (impact on recoveries).
  - ESRS E1 risks addressed; methodology to be refined at each close.
  - Provisions for social factors (HR disputes) recorded under ESRS S1.
  - No provisions for governance risks as of 31/12/2024; no quantified assessment of opportunity financial impacts.

- ESRS-aligned risks and opportunities mapped across scopes:
  - Own operations/service activities: energy use and GHG (E1), waste (E5), employee health/safety, DEI, fair pay and work rights (S1), value chain labor risks and improvements (S2), societal sponsorship and local authority financing (S3), customer protection and cybersecurity (S4), governance, ethics, AML/CFT, supplier payment practices and culture (G1).
  - Insurance and own operations: physical and transition climate risks, customer protection risks, partner assessment failures, governance decision-making risks, and culture as a strategic asset.
  - Financed activities: portfolio exposures to physical/transition risks, energy price impacts, financed emissions and high-GHG sectors, financing of adaptation/mitigation and renewables, environmental pressures financed (E2–E5), labor and human rights in portfolios (S2, S3), consumer safety risks (S4), and governance failures in investees (G1).
  - Time horizons considered: current, short-, medium-, and long-term; impact finance IROs flagged.

- Strategy and business model resilience:
  - Anchored in long-term service to retail customers, accessible protection, and support for France’s public/private players; strengthened by Caisse des Dépôts shareholding, mission status, and CNP Assurances’ purpose.
  - Strong national footprint via the postal network; international growth through insurance; diversified activities (banking, insurance, asset management) bolster resilience.
  - IRO list established in 2024 and to be updated annually.

- Specific issues beyond ESRS:
  - Impact-awareness culture (G1), financing local/regional authorities (S3), and cybersecurity (S4) identified as additional material topics and integrated into the IRO set.

- IRO management methodology:
  - Two-part approach: impact materiality (using ENCORE) and financial materiality (ESG risk map).
  - Scope covers own operations, banking services, insurance, credit, and investment; aligned with CNP Assurances.
  - Inclusion of sectors significantly contributing to climate change for financing/investment analysis and linkage to duty-of-care risk mapping.
  - Validation through workshops with external stakeholders and internal experts (e.g., WWF France, EcoAct, I4CE, BL Évolution, OREE, INEC, HR, Caisse des Dépôts, LBP AM).
text:
1.3.3 Interactions  between  material 
IROs  and La Banque Postale 
Group 's business model
In a context of environmental and social transition,
La Banque Postale Group is adapting its business model
to have a positive impact and ensure its resilience.
This  approach is part of its strong focus on sustainability,
expressed by La Banque Postale’s mission and the company
purpose of CNP  Assurances. Although the impacts and
risks  identified do not call  into question the Group’s
bancassurance activity, they do lead to changes  in the
conduct of its  service activities, its investments  and its
commercial offers.  Therefore, La  Banque   Postale  Group’s
strategy  is adapting at all levels, in  line with its status as a
mission-led  company.
The effects of material impacts and risks, particularly current
ones,  are already included in this strategy. The Group will
continue to enhance it to take into account the potential
impacts,  risks and  opportunities identified in the future. In
the short  term,  no change to the  strategy is planned but
an ongoing dialogue with stakeholders  will ensure that it
continues  to be relevant.
La  Banque  Postale’s  business model has also evolved to
take account  of these  challenges.
The service offering has been expanded to  take into
account environmental  impacts,  risks and opportunities.
This required  adapting the decision-making processes
and supporting the business  lines in redefining the role of
the bancassurer. For example, in a context in which the
scale  and frequency of climate events is creating new
challenges for insurers, CNP Assurances has implemented
a global protection approach that includes  climate risks
via reinsurance  coverage  against  the  risk  of excess
mortality.  This coverage thus protects against pandemics
or heat waves. In addition, for its own operations, changes
in decision-making processes and the initiatives in progress
in the Group’s HR, purchasing and compliance functions
reflect  the consideration of the  effects of  climate change
on social and governance aspects.  Lastly, the Group has
integrated  the effects  related to financed activities as part
of an impact investor, financier and creditor approach.
A  third “impact” focus area therefore complements the
risk-return ratio in the analysis  of strategic decisions, and
can also  be a way  of identifying opportunities.  [SBM_3_03]
The Group’s main negative  environmental impacts are
related  to the  activities it finances, in particular GHG
emissions, 
pollution, water consumption, the  use of marine
resources, impacts on biodiversity  and waste production
by sectors  supported through  loans and investments.
There  are also  negative impacts on  customers  in the  event
of a cybersecurity breach or inadequate insurance.
They   are linked to the Group’s business model, and
therefore affect  all economic  sectors.
The positive  impacts, on  the  other hand,  do not only stem
from the business  model but also from the Group’s
strategy. As a mission-led company, La  Banque  Postale
has adopted an impact-awareness  culture and pursues
ambitious social and environmental  targets. Thus, thepositive impacts related,  for example, to green loans for
climate 
change adaptation, favourable working conditions
for employees and workers in the value chain, the
financing of local  authorities and accessible banking result
from the Group’s desire to  pursue  societal targets.
Similarly, as a  responsible insurer covering more than 30
million 
policyholders, CNP  Assurances has material
impacts on people,  and strives to promote the positive
effects of  these  impacts. [SBM_3_05]
These impacts may be related to La  Banque  Postale
Group’s activities as well as its business relationships:
•The environmental, employee  and governance impacts
are linked to the Group’s activities (own operations,
service activities  and  financed activities);
•The social impacts related to workers in the value chain,
affected communities  and customers  are mainly related
to its business relationships (links  with the parent company
La Poste via La Poste  workers working for  and on behalf
of La Banque Postale, links with  suppliers,  link with  local
and  regional authorities, links with customers).  [SBM_3_07]
Estimation of the financial effects of material risks
The 
current financial effects of material risks are considered
through 
provisions for environmental, social or governance
risks. All provisions detailed below are included in the
consolidated  balance sheet of the financial statements in
Section 5.1 “Consolidated financial statements” of the
Universal Registration  Document.
In 2024, La Banque Postale included provisions for climate
risks . These provisions were defined in addition to the
sectoral provisions already in place by addressing two main
portfolios:
•the 
transition risk on the Corporate portfolio, in particular
by assessing the impact of  an increase in carbon prices
on the solvency of counterparties;
•the physical risk of flooding on the home loan portfolio
and the impact that this may have on expected recoveries
in the event of litigation.
These 
assessments cover the material risks of the ESRS E1
within the  scope of the financed activities. They will be
refined and supplemented at  each  closing of financial
statements and as the system matures. These provisions
are presented in Note 4.6 “Impairment and provisions for
credit 
risk” in Section 5.2 “Notes to the consolidated
financial statements” of the Universal Registration Document.
Provisions for  social factors, covering HR disputes, are
described 
in Note 7.7 “Provisions” in Section 5.2 “Notes to
the consolidated financial statements” of the Universal
Registration 
Document. The ESRS S1 material risk “HR risk
relating  to any failure of the Group’s employment and
employee health, safety, diversity  and inclusion practices”
is therefore recorded in  the financial statements.
At 31 December 2024, La  Banque Postale Group’s financial
statements did not include provisions for governance risks.
In 
addition, no assessment of the financial impact of the
material opportunities was carried out. [SBM_3_08]ESRS

title: Strategy and business model resilience
heading: 2.1.3.4 Strategy and business model resilience
start_phrase: The resilience of La Banque Postale Group's strategy and business model is driven by:
summary:
- Extract from La Banque Postale’s 2024 Universal Registration Document (CSR/ESRS 2), outlining strategy and sustainability reporting approach.
- Strategy and business model resilience built on: a mission-led, long-term vision serving retail customers and public/private players; ties to Caisse des Dépôts and CNP Assurances; strong national footprint via the postal network (nearly 10 million active retail customers; 12th-largest eurozone bank by assets end-2023); international growth through CNP Assurances; and diversification across banking, insurance, and asset management.
- Resilience reinforced by a structured view of impacts, risks and opportunities (IROs); first comprehensive IRO list created in 2024 with annual updates from 2025.
- Double materiality identified three Group-specific issues beyond ESRS requirements: impact-awareness culture (linked to ESRS G1), financing of local and regional authorities (ESRS S3), and cybersecurity focused on customer protection (ESRS S4). These IROs are integrated into the material IRO list; all other IROs are covered by ESRS disclosures.
- IRO methodology: two-pronged assessment—impact materiality using the ENCORE database; financial materiality based on the Group’s ESG risk map. Applied across Own Operations, Banking Services, Insurance, Credit, and Investment; methodology aligned with CNP Assurances.
- Impact materiality carried out Group-wide and across geographies, including portfolio exposure to sectors with significant climate contribution for Credit and Investment. All CSRD topics assessed due to the bancassurance scope.
- Integration with the Company’s duty of care via due diligence risk mapping to ensure consistency.
- Stakeholder engagement through workshops with external experts and internal teams (e.g., WWF France, EcoAct, I4CE, BL Évolution, OREE, INEC, Caisse des Dépôts, LBP AM, HR) to validate methods and results.
- Cross-references provided to the Group business model/value chain section and to Section 6.8 on ESG risks for loan portfolio details.
text:
1.3.4
Strategy  and business 
model  resilience
The resilience of La Banque Postale Group's strategy and
business model  is driven  by:
•its long-term  vision  of supporting retail customers,  the
accessibility of insurance solutions that protect and facilitate
all life pathways, and the  development of public and
private  economic players in France.  This vision is based
on its connection to a major state-owned group through
its shareholder, Caisse des Dépôts, its status as a
mission-led  company and the  company purpose of
CNP   Assurances, which underlines its desire to ensure
that  its social and environmental credentials guide its
development  and performance;
•its roots in France. La Banque Postale is now the twelfth-
largest  bank in the euro zone(1), with nearly 10 million
active  retail customers. Thanks to the postal network, it is
present throughout France;
•its international  development through  its insurance
business and  its subsidiary  CNP  Assurances;
•the diversity of its activities (insurance, banking, asset
management), which  combined with its geographical
diversification, strengthens its ability to face socio-economic
cycles and  geopolitical crises with  more resources.
For more information on the  Group’s business model, see
paragraph 2.1.3.1 “Group business model and value chain”.
[SBM_3_10]This resilience is strengthened by the Group’s understanding
of 
its impacts, risks and opportunities. Established for the
first 
time in 2024, the list of IROs will be updated annually
from 2025. 
[SBM_3_11]
Specific  issues were identified as part of the double
materiality  analysis, in addition to  the issues covered by
the ESRS disclosure requirements. These issues were
identified during double materiality work, based on sectoral
benchmarks 
and consultations with internal or external
experts. They are  as follows:
•Impact-awareness  culture: this issue, specific to the
Group, 
is linked to La  Banque  Postale’s mission. It is
related to ESRS G1;
•Financing of local and regional authorities: this issue
represents La  Banque  Postale’s specific positioning in
the financing of regional players, and is linked to ESRS S3;
•Cybersecurity: 
this issue, common to all players  in the
bancassurance 
sector, focuses on customer protection
(ESRS S4).
These 
issues were linked to  the most relevant thematic
ESRS.  The IROs associated with these specific issues are
included in the list of material impacts, risks and opportunities
resulting from the double materiality analysis as presented
in the previous  tables. With  the exception of IROs
associated with the  specific issues listed above, all IROs
are covered by ESRS disclosure requirements.  [SBM_3_12]

title: Methodology for identifying and assessing IROs - Introduction
heading: 2.1.4.1 Methodology for identifying and assessing IROs
start_phrase: The procedure for identifying and analysing IROs was carried out in two parts:
summary: Introduces the Group’s 2024 methodology for identifying and assessing IROs via a two-part approach: a materiality impact analysis using the ENCORE database (Exploring Natural Capital Opportunities, Risks and Exposure) and a financial materiality analysis based on the Group’s ESG risk map. Methodology  for identifying 
and assessing IROs
The procedure for identifying and analysing IROs was
carried  out in two parts:

title: Impact materiality
heading: 2.1.4.1.1 Impact materiality
start_phrase: The impact materiality analysis was carried out on the Group scope, taking into account, in all geographic areas, Own Operations (including Banking Services), as well as the Insurance and Credit businesses and Investment.
summary:
- Context: Extract from La Banque Postale’s 2024 Universal Registration Document (ESRS 2) covering strategy/business model resilience and the management of impacts, risks and opportunities (IROs) via a double materiality approach.
- Strategy and business model resilience: Grounded in a long-term, mission-led vision tied to Caisse des Dépôts; strong French footprint through the postal network; international development via CNP Assurances; diversified activities (insurance, banking, asset management) that enhance resilience; first formal IRO list established in 2024 with annual updates.
- Scope and alignment: Double materiality spans Own Operations, Banking Services, Insurance, Credit and Investment; methodological alignment with CNP Assurances.
- Entity-specific material topics beyond ESRS: Impact-awareness culture (linked to ESRS G1); financing of local and regional authorities (ESRS S3); cybersecurity focused on customer protection (ESRS S4). These are integrated into the IRO list; all other IROs are covered by ESRS requirements.
- Impact materiality methodology: 
  - Environmental impacts (ESRS E1–E5) for financed activities assessed using the ENCORE database at sector/portfolio level; a sector is material if ENCORE rates the impact High/Very High and technical reserves exceed defined thresholds.
  - Materiality criteria: scale, scope, irreversibility (negative only), probability (potential only), and long-term impact; for human rights, severity overrides probability.
  - Social/governance impacts assessed using internal management data and stakeholder interviews due to limited quantification tools.
  - Data gaps: several E2/E4 subtopics (e.g., microplastics, substances of concern, species state, ecosystem dependencies) not assessed this year pending external data.
- Stakeholder engagement: Workshops with external experts (e.g., WWF France, EcoAct, I4CE) and internal stakeholders (Sustainability, Group Risk, CNP Assurances, LBP AM, La Poste Group); no direct consultations with communities potentially affected by financed activities; in insurance, CNP operational teams integrate stakeholder views.
- Financial materiality methodology:
  - Risks mapped via the Group ESG risk map; opportunities identified by Risk and business lines; CNP conducts a coordinated assessment with governance review by its Executive bodies and committees.
  - Climate-related risks (physical and transition) emerge as material; other environmental risks currently not deemed material due to lack of methodologies linking them to economic variables.
  - Assessment criteria: potential financial effect, probability, and time horizon weighting; expert-based scoring where topics are not yet on the ESG risk map; opportunities include financing to mitigate environmental impacts (green loans, circular economy, decontamination).
- Materiality thresholds: Portfolio-based thresholds for technical reserves in Credit/Investment (e.g., €1 billion for banking portfolios ≈ 1.3% of outstanding loans); a unified scoring threshold applied to all IROs across scopes for consistency.
- Internal control and governance: No existing internal control procedure specifically for impacts; controls to be phased in after the first CSRD impact analysis; risk management overseen by independent committees within a three-lines-of-defense framework; clear separation between Executive Board (operations) and Supervisory Board (oversight).
- Cross-references: Business model and value chain; governance role in IRO management; ESG risks (Section 6.8).
text:
Impact  materiality
The impact materiality analysis was carried out on the
Group scope, taking into account, in all geographic areas,
Own 
Operations (including Banking Services), as well as
the Insurance and Credit businesses and Investment. For
the latter two scopes,  the exposures of the portfolios to
sectors that contribute significantly to climate change
were integrated into the analysis,  in order to assess the
impacts  related to financing and investment activities.
Additional  information on the loan portfolios is available in
Section 
6.8 “Environmental, social  and governance (ESG)
risks” of  the Universal  Registration Document.  [IRO_1_03]
As the scope of bancassurance activities is very broad, due
to 
the Credit and Investment businesses, all the topics
listed in the CSRD were analysed.
The process also included the link with  the Company’s
duty of care. A mapping of the risks arising from due
diligence 
was also examined to ensure overall consistency.
[IRO_1_04]
In 
order to incorporate the views of affected stakeholders,
workshops 
with external stakeholders and internal experts
were held to confirm the methodologies, enhance the
analysis 
and validate the results obtained. WWF France,
EcoAct, I4CE, BL Évolution, OREE, INEC, La Banque Postale
Group’s Human Resources Department, Caisse des Dépôts
and  LBP AM took part in  these  workshops.
(1) In terms of assets, end-2023.Please  see the glossary  on page 808 for definitions of the main CSR terms 2024 Universal  Registration Document     La Banque Postale 1012Sustainable performance
General information on the preparation of sustainability 
reports [ESRS 2]
The following internal stakeholders were consulted on all
environmental  topics:  the Sustainability  Department, the
Group Risk Department (GRD), CNP Assurances, LBP AM,
Louvre  Banque Privée and La Poste Group. Apart from the
consultation  of external  experts,  direc t consultations with
the communities potentially affected  by the financed
activities  were  not carried  out.
Furthermore, in the insurance scope, the double materiality
assessment  is carried out by the CNP  Assurances Group
operational and business  line management  teams , who
have  a good  perception  of the  interests and points of view
of stakeholders.
The structured stakeholder dialogue process is also presented
in Section 2.1.3.1. “Group business model and value chain”.
[IRO_1_05]
La Banque Postale Group (including CNP Assurances) used
two methodologies for the impact materiality analysis, for
all 
activities (Own  Operations, Banking Services, Insurance,
Credit and  Investment).
Materiality  of financed activities 
for environmental  matters
The identification and assessment of environmental impacts
(ESRS  E1 to E5) on the Credit and Investment portfolios
were  carried out  using the ENCORE database, with an
analysis specific  to each portfolio.
For each  line  in the  portfolio,  each impact was rated using
the ENCORE database. A sector is thus considered material
for a specific  impact if the corresponding ENCORE rating
is “High”  or “Very  High”.  The sum  of technical  reserves in
the sectors considered as material was calculated for each
impact.
An impact is  considered material for La  Banque  Postale
Group 
if the total technical reserves meeting this definition
are greater than the defined thresholds (see Section 2.1.4.1.3
“Materiality  thresholds  used”).
For each of the identified impacts, this  analysis was able
to determine:
•their  scale, defined  as the average ENCORE rating of
the portfolio;
•their  scope, assessed according to the total technical
reserves  in the material  sectors.The approach used to analyse the materiality of  environmental
impacts is therefore based on the sectors of activity
financed, 
rather than by geographic areas, due to the
scale  of the  financing activities and the difficulty of
identifying all the sites in question.
The ENCORE database does not cover all  environmental
sub-topics of the CSRD. This is why the materiality  of the
following sub-topics was not assessed during this financial year:
•“Pollution of  living  organisms and food resources” (E2);
•“Substances of concern” (E2);
•“Substances of very  high concern”  (E2);
•“Microplastics”  (E2);
•“Impacts on the  state of  species”  (E4);
•“Dependencies  on ecosystem services” (E4);
Their assessment will be updated in future years, depending
on the availability of  external data.
Materiality  of other  matters
In addition, in the absence of tools to quantify the scale of
social  and governance impacts,  the identification and
assessment of these were carried out based on the Group’s
internal management data and interviews with the Group's
various 
stakeholders. The result of this analysis made it
possible 
to rate all the impacts (see the infographic
“Impact materiality assessment criteria” below). [IRO_1_02]
The quantitative assessment of the impact materiality was
carried  out, at  Group  level, based  on the following  criteria:
•Scale: indicates to what extent the impact is negative, or
on the contrary  beneficial, for the population  or the
environment;
•Scope: indicates how widespread the negative or positive
impact is;
•Whether the impact is irreversible (only for negative impacts);
•Probability of occurrence (only for potential  impacts);
•Long-term impact: weighting of the duration of the impact.
In accordance with ESRS 1 (3.4, paragraph 45), potential negative impacts relating to human rights are subject to an
exception: the criterion  of severity  prevails over that of  probability. [IRO_1_06]
