title: Financial materiality
heading: 2.1.4.1.2 Financial materiality
start_phrase: The identification and assessment of La Banque Postale Group’s risks was based on the Group’s ESG risk map (see infographic Financial materiality assessment criteria below).
summary:
- Context and scope: Excerpt from La Banque Postale’s 2024 Universal Registration Document (ESRS 2) detailing how the Group prepares sustainability reporting through a financial materiality lens, within a double materiality framework.
- Financial materiality approach: Group-level identification and assessment of risks and opportunities using an ESG risk map; opportunities (e.g., green loans, circular economy financing, decontamination) identified by Risk and business-line experts.
- CNP Assurances methodology: Uses risk and due-diligence impact mapping plus expert assessments; broad internal consultation (business lines, subsidiaries, shareholder sustainability reps); Sustainability and Accounting ensure consistency and set a materiality threshold; review by Executive Committee and Board, presented to Audit & Risk and CSR Committees; annual reassessment.
- Environmental topics: Climate-related negative impacts create both financing opportunities and material physical/transition risks. Other environmental risks currently deemed non-material due to lack of robust assessment methodologies and their limited reflection in economic variables/regulation/consumer behavior.
- Quantitative assessment: Risks scored on four levels (Minor, Moderate, Major, Critical) against three criteria—potential financial effect, probability, and time horizon (short/medium/long with weighting multipliers). Topics not yet on the ESG risk map and all opportunities are assessed using expert judgment.
- Materiality thresholds: Defined for Credit and Investment to determine material impacts using ENCORE; example threshold of €1 billion for banking portfolios (1.3% of outstanding loans). A consistent materiality threshold is also set on the IRO rating scale across all scopes.
- Internal control and governance: No internal control procedure yet for impact scope; controls to be integrated following the first CSRD impact analysis. Broader risk management relies on independent committees, clear separation of Executive vs. Supervisory Boards, and a three-lines-of-defense internal control framework.
- Decision rule: Material risk/opportunity determined via a composite score combining potential financial effect, probability, and time-horizon weighting against a defined materiality threshold.
text:
1.4.1.2
Financial  materiality
The identification and assessment of La   Banque  Postale
Group’s risks was based  on the  Group’s  ESG  risk map  (see
infographic Financial materiality assessment criteria below).
The identification  and assessment  of all opportunities
were  carried out  by the  internal experts  of the Risk  team
and  the relevant  business lines.
CNP Assurances has used its own methodology based on
the mapping of risks, the mapping of the due diligence
impacts, as well as expert assessments. In order to assess
the risks, we  consulted the business line departments, the
CNP  Assurances Group subsidiaries, the sustainability
representatives of the shareholder La Banque Postale, and
the sustainability officers within  the CNP  Assurances
Group  subsidiaries. The Sustainability  Department and the
Accounting Department ensured the overall consistency
of the assessment and proposed a materiality threshold,
which  was reviewed by the members of the Executive
Committee and the Board of Directors. This analysis was
presented to the  Audit and  Risk Committee and to
CNP  Assurances Group's CSR  Committee. The assessment
will be reviewed each year by the dedicated teams. [IRO_1_07]
The environmental impacts of the financed activities, i.e.
negative  impacts related to global warming, pollution,
water  and marine resource  management, biodiversity andwaste,  give rise to opportunities for financing activities to
limit, 
reduce or remedy these impacts (green loans, financing
of circular economy projects, decontamination solutions, etc.).
The 
negative impacts related to the climate also give rise
to physical and transition risks that stand out as material
in the financial analysis.
Other than climate risk, environmental risks  are not
material. This is due to the fact that there is currently no
methodology  to assess them. Indeed, the assessment of
risks is based on economic variables, yet the outcomes
generated  by environmental impacts  other than climate
are not currently included in these variables, in the absence
of regulations or changes in consumer behaviour. [IRO_1_08]
The quantitative assessment of  financial materiality was
carried  out, at Group  level, based on the ESG risk map,
where the various risks are rated according to four levels
(Minor,  Moderate, Major and Critical).  For all activities (Own
Operations, Banking Services, Insurance,  Credit and
Investment), the following  criteria are considered:
•The potential  financial effect;
•The probability of  occurrence;
•The time horizon based on which the duration of the
risk is  weighted.
The topics  that  have  not yet been  included  in the Group’s
ESG risk map have been considered and assessed on an
expert  basis,  pending  methodologies for a more detailed
assessment. All opportunities were also assessed by experts.
[IRO_1_09]
2.

title: Materiality thresholds used
heading: 2.1.4.1.3 Materiality thresholds used
start_phrase: In the Credit and Investment scopes, materiality thresholds have been defined in order to determine the material impacts: the impacts with material technical reserves higher than these thresholds were considered as material during the impact analysis, carried out using the ENCORE database (see Section 2.1.4.1.1 “Impact materiality”).
summary:
- Focus and framework: Explains La Banque Postale Group’s financial materiality assessment within ESRS 2 and the broader double materiality approach used for sustainability reporting.
- Risk and opportunity identification: Uses the Group ESG risk map; opportunities and topics not yet mapped are assessed by internal experts. CNP Assurances applies its own methodology (risk and due‑diligence impact mapping, expert input, consultations), with thresholds set by Sustainability and Accounting, reviewed by the Executive Committee and Board, and presented to Audit & Risk and CSR Committees; reassessed annually.
- Environmental lens: Financed activities’ environmental impacts create financing opportunities (e.g., green loans, circular economy, decontamination) and material climate-related physical and transition risks. Other environmental risks are currently deemed non‑material due to lack of methodologies and limited reflection of these impacts in economic variables, regulation, or consumer behavior.
- Quantitative assessment method: Group-wide scoring based on potential financial effect (0–3), probability of occurrence (0–3), and time horizon weighting (0.8 short‑term, 1 medium‑term, 1.1 long‑term). Materiality is determined via a combined score compared against a threshold; risks are categorized from Minor to Critical. Expert judgment is used where methodologies are pending; opportunities are also expert‑assessed.
- Materiality thresholds: For Credit and Investment, thresholds are set using ENCORE-based impact analysis and material technical reserves; example: €1 billion threshold for banking portfolios (1.3% of outstanding loans). A consistent materiality threshold is also defined on the IRO rating scale across all scopes to align portfolio thresholds with IRO ratings.
- Internal control and governance: No dedicated internal control over impacts yet; controls will be phased in following the first CSRD impact analysis. The Group relies on a three-lines-of-defense risk management framework, overseen by independent committees, with clear separation between the Executive Board (operations) and the Supervisory Board (oversight).

1.4.1.3
Materiality thresholds used
In the Credit and Investment scopes, materiality thresholds
have  been defined in order to determine the material
impacts: the  impacts  with material  technical reserves
higher than these  thresholds  were considered as  material
during  the impact analysis, carried  out using the ENCORE
database  (see  Section  2.1.4.1.1  “Impact  materiality”).
By way of illustration, this threshold was set at €1 billion for
the portfolios in the banking scope, which  represents 1.3%

In order to ensure consistency between the results obtained
with 
the thresholds applied to the portfolios and the rating

the rating  scale . This  threshold  applies to  all IROs across all
scopes. [IRO_2_13]2.1.4.1.4

title: Internal control process
heading: 2.1.4.1.4 Internal control process
start_phrase: Currently, there is no internal control procedure concerning impacts.
summary:
- Scope and standards: Excerpt from La Banque Postale’s 2024 Universal Registration Document under ESRS 2, detailing double materiality, IRO (Impacts, Risks, Opportunities) methods, governance, and data sources across Own Operations, Banking Services, Insurance, Credit, and Investment.
- Financial materiality approach:
  - Group ESG risk map underpins identification and assessment, with risks/opportunities evaluated by the Risk team and business lines; topics not yet on the map assessed by experts.
  - CNP Assurances uses its own methodology combining risk mapping, due diligence impact mapping, and expert input; results reviewed by Executive bodies and presented to Audit & Risk and CSR Committees; annual review planned.
  - Environmental impacts of financed activities create financing opportunities (green loans, circular economy, decontamination), while climate-related negatives drive material physical and transition risks.
  - Other environmental risks (non-climate) deemed not currently material due to lack of methodologies and absence of economic/regulatory signals.
  - Quantitative scoring: potential financial effect, probability of occurrence, and time horizon weighting (short 0.8, medium 1.0, long 1.1). Materiality determined when (effect + probability) × time horizon exceeds threshold.
- Materiality thresholds:
  - Defined for Credit and Investment to flag material impacts via ENCORE; example threshold €1 billion for banking portfolios (1.3% of outstanding loans).

  - No dedicated internal control yet for impacts; controls to be phased in following the first CSRD impact analysis.
  - ESG risks managed within existing enterprise risk framework and three lines of defense; clear segregation of duties between Executive Board (operations) and Supervisory Board (oversight).
  - ESG Risk unit within Group Risk assesses exposure, alignment with commitments, and reports to governance; ESG risks integrated into the Risk Appetite Framework and managed like other risks. Opportunities management not yet embedded in the overall framework.
- Data sources and updates:
  - ENCORE for environmental impact identification/assessment in Credit and Investment.
  - Internal management data for positive impacts and own operations.
  - Group ESG risk map for risk identification/assessment.
  - IRO assessment to be updated next financial year, incorporating ENCORE’s July 2024 update and ESG risk map refresh.
- Climate-related IROs:
  - Impact materiality: GHG impacts assessed across all scopes; ENCORE used for Credit/Investment sector impacts; 2023 carbon data for own operations.
  - Financial materiality—physical risks: portfolio- and operations-specific mapping of extreme events (floods, wildfires, storms, clay shrink–swell) and chronic risks (temperature rise, precipitation change, drought, heat waves), over short/medium/long horizons; CNP updated real estate physical risk and found low operational exposure; details in Pillar III (URD Section 6.8.8).
  - Financial materiality—transition risks: analysis via NGFS scenarios, focusing on exposure to carbon‑intensive sectors and financed emissions; details in Pillar III (URD Section 6.8.7).

title: Risk and opportunity management
heading: 2.1.4.2 Risk and opportunity management
start_phrase: La Banque Postale Group treats Environmental, Social and Governance (ESG) risks as a risk area in its own right, but also as a risk factor for other risk areas (credit, operational, market, etc.).
summary:
- ESG risk management approach: La Banque Postale treats ESG as both a standalone risk class and a cross-cutting factor for other risks (credit, operational, market). ESG risks are integrated into existing risk governance and the Group Risk Appetite Framework, overseen by a dedicated ESG Risk unit within the Group Risk Department that assesses exposures, ensures alignment with commitments, coordinates with subsidiaries, and reports to the Executive and Supervisory Boards. Opportunity management is not yet embedded in the overall framework.
- Data sources and scope: Analyses draw on the ENCORE tool (negative environmental impacts for Credit and Investment), internal management data (positive impacts and own operations), and the Group ESG risk map. Covered scopes include Own Operations, Banking Services, Insurance, Credit, and Investment. The inaugural IRO analysis will be updated next year with the July 2024 ENCORE update and refreshed ESG risk map.
- Climate impact materiality: GHG impacts are assessed across all scopes. For Credit and Investment, sectoral impacts are evaluated using ENCORE; for own operations, 2023 carbon data underpin the assessment.
- Financial materiality—physical risks: Risk mapping quantifies physical risk scenarios over short-, medium-, and long-term horizons for Commercial and Real Estate Loans, covering extreme events (floods, wildfires, storms, clay shrink–swell) and chronic risks (rising temperature and precipitation, drought, heat waves). CNP Assurances updated physical risk assessments for its real estate in 2023 to inform 2024 adaptation plans. Own operations are judged not severely exposed to climate hazards likely to disrupt business.
- Financial materiality—transition risks: Transition risks are assessed using NGFS scenarios, focusing on exposures to carbon-intensive sectors and the Group’s financed emissions. Further methodological and indicator details are referenced in Pillar III sections of the Universal Registration Document.
text:
1.4.2 Risk  and opportunity  
management
La  Banque  Postale Group  treats Environmental, Social
and Governance (ESG) risks as a risk  area in its own right,
but also as a risk factor for other risk areas (credit, operational,
market, etc.).  Dedicated  risk management  frameworks
provide appropriate responses to the knock-on effects of
ESG  risks  on existing risk factors. [IRO_1_10]
The Group  Risk  Department's dedicated  ESG Risk unit
leads  studies  and  analyses to assess whether the level of
exposure  to ESG risks is acceptable, and  complies with the
commitments made by La Banque Postale Group.  It then
reports on this work  to the Group’s  Executive Board and
Supervisory  Board. It coordinates  and harmonises  work on
the risk  management framework  with  the subsidiaries
and  within  the Group.
In order  to encourage their inclusion in  all of the Group’s
risk control and management  frameworks and ensure
that  they are managed efficiently, they are covered by  the
existing organisations and bodies, rather than by dedicated
bodies. The principles applicable to La  Banque  Postale
Group’s  Risk Appetite F ramework are therefore also
applicable  to the  management  of ESG risks . ESG risks are
controlled  in the same way as other risks. For more
information, please refer to Section 2.1.2.7.1 “Risk management
and internal control system ”; additional information is
also  available in Section 6.8.2 “ESG risk governance” of the
Universal Registration  Document.  [IRO_1_11]  [IRO_1_12]
At this stage, the management of opportunities is not
integrated 
into the Group’s overall management framework.
[IRO_1_13]

title: Financial materiality – physical and transition risks
heading: 2.1.4.4.2 Financial materiality – physical and transition risks
start_phrase: To assess the physical risks related to climate change, La Banque Postale has carried out risk mapping work.
summary:
- Scope and governance of ESG risks: La Banque Postale treats ESG risks both as a standalone risk class and as drivers of other risks (credit, market, operational). ESG risks are integrated into existing risk appetite and control frameworks, not managed by separate bodies. A dedicated ESG Risk unit within the Group Risk Department coordinates analyses across subsidiaries and reports to the Executive and Supervisory Boards. Management of opportunities is not yet embedded in the overall risk framework.

- Data, tools and perimeter: The analysis uses ENCORE (for environmental impacts on credit and investment), internal management data (for positive impacts and own operations), and the Group ESG risk map. Coverage spans Own Operations, Banking Services, Insurance, Credit and Investment. The IRO assessment will be updated next year with the July 2024 ENCORE refresh and the updated ESG risk map.

- Climate IROs:
  - Impact materiality: Assessment of GHG impacts across all scopes; portfolios evaluated via ENCORE, own operations via 2023 carbon data.
  - Financial materiality: Physical risks mapped for commercial and real estate loans, covering extreme events (floods, wildfires, storms, clay shrink-swell) and chronic risks (temperature rise, precipitation change, drought, heatwaves). CNP Assurances updated physical risk assessment for real estate; own operations considered not severely exposed. Transition risks assessed using NGFS scenarios, focusing on carbon-intensive sector exposures and financed emissions. Assets incompatible with the transition plan identified (fossil fuels, Paris-Aligned Benchmark exclusions). Opportunities from transition assessed qualitatively (no scenario analysis). Risk scenarios align with financial statement assumptions; provisions use NGFS short-term disorderly transition scenarios and a flood scenario for physical risks.

- Biodiversity and ecosystems IROs:
  - Impact materiality: ESRS E4 is non-material for own operations but material for credit and investment, based on exposure to high-impact sectors. Results align with the 2023 Climate and Nature report (TCFD/TNFD), which locates key impact areas.
  - Financial materiality: ESRS E4 not currently financially material, but a deeper analysis using the Global Biodiversity Score assessed dependencies on 21 ecosystem services via average and critical dependency scores. Four portfolios analyzed (commercial/residential real estate, corporate finance, public sector/social economy) covering 39% of exposures. Sectoral qualitative grids developed for five priority sectors: Real estate; Food and beverage manufacturing; Transport and warehousing; Energy production and distribution; Health and pharmaceuticals. CNP Assurances’ BIA-GBS analysis (covering 98% of directly held equities/bonds) shows low average but significant critical dependencies, indicating potential business model risks (e.g., water scarcity in leather). An initial assessment of nature-related physical and transition risks was completed; systemic risk not yet included.

- References: Further details on ESG risk governance, transition and physical risk indicators, and credit quality are provided in the Universal Registration Document (Sections 2.1.2.7.1, 6.8.2, 6.8.7, 6.8.8).

title: Impact materiality
heading: 2.1.4.5.1 Impact materiality
start_phrase: The impacts on biodiversity and ecosystems were examined, within the scope of La Banque Postale Group’s own operations, based on internal management data and on the Group’s ESG risk map.
summary:
- Context: Excerpt from La Banque Postale’s 2024 Universal Registration Document covering sustainability reporting (ESRS 2) and climate/biodiversity impact, risk, and opportunity (IRO) assessments.
- Transition alignment: Identification of assets/activities potentially incompatible with the Group’s transition plan, including exposures to fossil fuels and companies excluded from the Paris-Aligned Benchmark; further credit quality details referenced in Section 6.8.7.1.
- Transition opportunities: Assessed qualitatively on an expert basis without scenario analysis.
- Scenario use and financial alignment: Climate scenarios used are consistent with assumptions in the financial statements; transition risk provisions based on NGFS short-term disorderly scenarios; physical risk provisions use a flood scenario.
- Biodiversity and ecosystems (ESRS E4) – Impact materiality:
  - Own operations: ESRS E4 assessed as non-material based on internal data and ESG risk mapping.
  - Downstream value chain (credit and investment): ESRS E4 assessed as material; impact analysis focused on exposures to high-biodiversity-impact sectors per the document’s methodology; findings align with the 2023 Climate and Nature report (TCFD/TNFD), which maps the geographic location of impacts.
- Biodiversity and ecosystems – Financial materiality:
  - Currently not financially material for La Banque Postale, but deeper analysis conducted using the Global Biodiversity Score (GBS) across 21 ecosystem services and four IPBES pressures.
  - Two dependence metrics used: average dependency score and critical dependency score (indicating non-substitutable, high/very high dependencies).
  - Portfolio coverage: Four portfolios analyzed—commercial and residential real estate, corporate finance, public sector and social economy—covering 39% of on- and off-balance sheet exposures.
  - Sectoral deep-dives: Qualitative grids developed for five priority sectors—real estate; food and beverage manufacturing; transport and warehousing; energy production and distribution; health and pharmaceuticals.
- CNP Assurances’ analysis: Applied BIA-GBS to 98% of directly held equities and bonds; average dependency is low, but critical dependencies are significant for a share of companies, implying potential financial risks (e.g., water scarcity risks in the leather sector).
- Nature-related risk assessment: Initial assessment of physical and transition risks completed; systemic nature risk not yet incorporated.
text:
1.4.5.1 Impact  materiality
The impacts
 on biodiversity and ecosystems were examined,
within the scope of La  Banque  Postale  Group’s own
operations, based on internal management data and on
the Group’s ESG risk map. The assessment of this data
highlighted  ESRS E4 – Biodiversity and Ecosystems as
non-material for  this scope.
The biodiversity matters  for La Banque Postale Group are
therefore 
concentrated in the activities of the downstream
value chain, namely credit and investment activities.
In  these scopes, the impact analysis was carried out on
the basis of technical reserves  exposed to sectors with
significant  impacts  on biodiversity and ecosystems,
following the methodology presented in Section 2.1.4.1.1
“Impact  materiality”. This assessment  highlighted ESRS E4
as material  in terms  of impacts on the credit and
investment scopes.
A more in-depth  analysis of  the impacts  on biodiversity
was carried out  as part of  La Banque  Postale Group's 2023
Climate and Nature report (in accordance with the
recommendations 
of the TCFD and TNFD) published in
October  2024. This study provides visibility as to the
location  of the  impacts on  biodiversity and ecosystems of
the activities in the portfolios analysed. The results  of the
impact analysis carried out as part of the double materiality
analysis 
are generally consistent with the results  of the
nature report  according to the  TNFD  recommendations.
The full study is available in La  Banque  Postale’s 2023
Climate  and  Nature report.  [E4_IRO_1_01]

title: Financial materiality
heading: 2.1.4.5.2 Financial materiality
start_phrase: The identification and assessment of risks related to biodiversity and ecosystems was carried out based on the methodology detailed in Section 2.1.4.1.2 “Financial materiality”.
summary:
- Context and framework: Extract from La Banque Postale’s 2024 Universal Registration Document covering ESRS 2 sustainability reporting preparations and double materiality work, with links to glossary and cross-references to risk and exposure disclosures.

- Transition plan alignment: Identification of assets/activities potentially incompatible with the transition plan (including fossil fuel exposures and Paris-Aligned Benchmark exclusions). Transition opportunities assessed on an expert basis (no scenario analysis). Climate scenarios aligned with financial statements; transition risk provisions based on NGFS short-term disorderly scenarios and physical risk provisions using a flood scenario.

- Biodiversity and ecosystems (ESRS E4):
  - Impact materiality: Own operations assessed as non-material; material impacts identified in downstream value chain (credit and investment). Analyses align with the 2023 Climate and Nature report (TCFD/TNFD).
  - Financial materiality: Currently not material, but detailed dependency assessment performed using the Global Biodiversity Score across IPBES pressures. Two portfolio dependency metrics used (average and critical). Four portfolios analyzed (commercial/residential real estate, corporate finance, public sector, social economy) covering 39% of exposures. Sectoral qualitative grids developed for five priority sectors (real estate; food & beverage manufacturing; transport & warehousing; energy production & distribution; health & pharma).
  - CNP Assurances: BIA-GBS methodology applied to 98% of directly held equities/bonds; low average dependency but significant critical dependencies on at least one ecosystem service, implying potential financial risk (e.g., water scarcity in leather).
  - Nature-related risks: Initial assessment of physical and transition risks completed; systemic risk not yet included.

- Stakeholder engagement and operations context: Stakeholders consulted include WWF France, CDC Biodiversité, and BL Évolution. As a service bank, the Group does not source raw materials, has no production sites, and reports no biodiversity-sensitive sites or community impacts within own operations; therefore, no specific biodiversity mitigation measures (EU Birds/Habitats Directives, EIA, IFC PS6) deemed necessary for own operations.

- Pollution (ESRS E2):
  - Own operations: Non-material.
  - Downstream credit/investments: Material for impacts, non-material for financial materiality. High-impact sectors identified include metal products manufacturing; wearing apparel; paper; construction and civil engineering; pharmaceuticals; motor vehicles/trailers; aviation and defense; electric power generation/transmission/distribution; and IT services (programming/consulting).

- Water and marine resources (ESRS E3):
  - Own operations: Non-material.
  - Downstream credit/investments: Material for impacts, non-material financially. Sectors with very significant water use include paper; mineral and metal products manufacturing; renewable energy production; construction and civil engineering; mining and quarrying; leather manufacturing; and electric power generation/transmission/distribution.
text:
1.4.5.2 Financial  materiality
The identification and assessment of risks related to
biodiversity  and ecosystems was carried out based on the
methodology detailed in Section 2.1.4.1.2 “Financial materiality”.
Although ESRS E4 is not currently material from a financial
point  of view, a more in-depth analysis  of the  risks  and
dependencies  related to biodiversity was carried out as
part  of the 2023 Climate and Nature  report (following the
recommendations of the TCFD and TNFD), published in
October  2024.The Global Biodiversity Score (GBS)-based work carried
out assessed the dependency  of La  Banque  Postale’s
portfolios 
on the 21 ecosystem services provided by nature
with regard to four of the five pressures defined by the
IPBES (change in land use, overexploitation of natural
resources, pollution and climate  change).
Two ecosystem service dependency  scores are available:
•An average dependency score, which represents the
average of dependencies across all ecosystem services
and  sectors in the portfolio;
•A critical dependency score, which represents the portion
of 
the portfolio that is critically dependent - i.e.  highly or
very highly - on  at least  one ecosystem service.
Indeed, if the dependence is strong or very strong, this
ecosystem service is considered as  non-substitutable.
Four  portfolios  were analysed, covering 39%  of
La  Banque  Postale’s  on-balance sheet and  off-balance
sheet  exposures:  commercial and  residential  real estate,
corporate finance and public sector and social economy
financing.
In addition,  sectoral qualitative grids have been developed
to define, identify and qualify the impacts and dependencies
related 
to the nature of the priority sectors for La Banque Postale.
This 
exercise was  conducted in five sectors identified as
priorities (Real estate, Food and beverage manufacturing,
Transport and warehousing, Energy production and
distribution and Health and the pharmaceutical sector).
The results of these analyses are available in  the 2023
Climate and Nature report.
For its part, CNP Assurances used the BIA-GBS™ methodology,
which 
assigns each business sector a biodiversity dependency
score. 
Once these scores have been aggregated for companies
and then for the CNP  Assurances portfolio, this work
made 
it possible to measure the direct  dependency (Scope 1)
and  the upstream  value chain dependency (Scope 3) on
ecosystem services of the activity of the companies to
which 
CNP  Assurances is exposed. The  measurement
covers 98% of CNP  Assurances'  directly held equity and
bond portfolio. The result  shows that the average
dependency of  CNP  Assurances’ investment portfolio is
low both in terms  of its own activities and  the  upstream
value chain of the financed companies. Nevertheless, this
average 
dependency score must be supplemented by the
critical dependency score. This reveals  a significant
percentage  of companies that are highly or very heavily
dependent on at least one ecosystem service.  In other
words, this means that the business model and the
sustainability  of a company may present a risk without
corrective action (example: water scarcity for the leather
sector),  and therefore  represent a risk for the financial
value of CNP Assurances' investment. [E4_IRO_1_02] [E4_IRO_1_03]
Wishing  to anticipate the impacts and dependencies that
the erosion of biodiversity could have on the sustainability
of 
its business model, La  Banque  Postale  carried out an
initial assessment of its nature-related physical and transition
risks. Systemic (1) risk has not yet been included. [E4_IRO_1_04]

title: Involvement of stakeholders and affected communities
heading: Involvement of stakeholders and affected communities
start_phrase: As part of the double materiality analysis, La Banque Postale Group consulted internal and external stakeholders on the various subjects.
summary:
- Context: Extract from La Banque Postale’s 2024 Universal Registration Document (Sustainable performance) detailing ESRS-based sustainability reporting preparations and double materiality outcomes.
- Methodology: Use of double materiality analysis with internal management data, ESG risk mapping, and references to methodologies in sections on impact materiality (2.1.4.1.1) and financial materiality (2.1.4.1.2).
- Stakeholder engagement: Consultation with internal stakeholders and external experts—WWF France, CDC Biodiversité, and BL Évolution—for topics including biodiversity and pollution.
- Biodiversity (ESRS E4):
  - Own operations: No raw material sourcing or production sites; no significant impacts on biodiversity or ecosystem services; no sites in/near sensitive areas; ESRS E4 deemed non-material for own operations.
  - Mitigation measures under EU nature directives and IFC PS6 considered unnecessary given activity profile.
- Pollution (ESRS E2):
  - Own operations: Not a significant source of pollution; not located in pollution risk areas; ESRS E2 non-material for these scopes.
  - Downstream value chain (credit and investment): ESRS E2 material for impact analysis but non-material for financial materiality. High-impact sectors identified include metal products manufacturing, apparel, paper, construction/civil engineering, pharmaceuticals, motor vehicles/trailers, aviation/defence, electric power generation/transmission/distribution, and IT services.
- Water and marine resources (ESRS E3):
  - Own operations: No significant water/marine resource use; ESRS E3 non-material for these scopes.
  - Downstream value chain: ESRS E3 material for impact analysis but non-material for financial materiality. High water-use sectors include paper, mineral and metal products manufacturing, renewable energy production, construction/civil engineering, mining/quarrying, leather products, and electric power generation/transmission/distribution.
- Overall conclusion: Environmental materiality for La Banque Postale largely resides in financed and invested sectors rather than the Group’s direct operations, with clear identification of high-impact sectors to inform risk and impact management.
text:
Involvement of stakeholders and affected communities
As part of the double  materiality analysis, La Banque Postale
Group consulted internal  and external stakeholders on the
various subjects.
In addition to the internal stakeholders presented in
Section  2.1.4.1.1 “Impact materiality”, the following stakeholders
were  consulted on the topic of Biodiversity:  WWF France,
CDC Biodiversité and BL  Évolution.  [E4_IRO_1_05]
Not being a manufacturing company, La Banque Postale
Group  does not  source raw materials and  does not  have a
production site that could have  a negative  impact on
biodiversity and  ecosystems.  [E4_IRO_1_06]
Thus, the Group’s own operations do not affect communities
in terms  of biodiversity. [E4_IRO_1_07]
In the  operational  scope,  the  Group  also  has no impact on
the ecosystem services that are of interest to the affected
communities.  ESRS E4  - Biodiversity and ecosystems is in
fact not material for this scope. [E4_IRO_1_08]
Sites  located in or  near sensitive areas
La Banque Postale Group does  not have any sites located
in or near  biodiversity-sensitive areas.  [E4_IRO_1_14]  [E4_IRO_1_15]
Given  the  nature of  the  Group’s  activities,  it was not
considered  necessary to  implement mitigation  measures
on its  own  operations,  such as the  measures  referred  to in:
Directive 2009/147/EC of the European Parliament and
the Council on the conservation of wild  birds; Council
Directive 92/43/EEC on the conservation of natural habitats
and of wild  fauna and flora; an environmental impact
assessment (EIA) as defined  in Article 1  (2) (g) of  Directive
2011/92/EU of the European Parliament and of the Council
(76) on the  assessment  of the effects  of certain  public and
private projects on the environment; and, for activities in
third 
countries, national provisions or equivalent international
standards,  such as the International Finance Corporation
(IFC)  Performance  Standard  6: Biodiversity  conservation
and  sustainable management of  living natural resources.
[E4_IRO_1_16]

title: Assessment of pollution‑related IROs
heading: 2.1.4.6 Assessment of pollution‑related IROs
start_phrase: La Banque Postale Group’s own operations and service activities are not the source of significant pollution, and are not located in areas at risk of pollution.
summary:
- Context and scope: Extract from La Banque Postale’s 2024 Universal Registration Document detailing sustainability reporting preparation under ESRS 2, with a focus on double materiality and impact/risk/opportunity (IRO) assessments.
- Stakeholder engagement: Internal and external stakeholders consulted; for biodiversity and pollution topics, external experts included WWF France, CDC Biodiversité, and BL Évolution.
- Biodiversity and ecosystems (ESRS E4): 
  - As a non-manufacturing bank, the Group does not source raw materials or operate production sites; its own operations do not negatively impact biodiversity, ecosystems, or related community ecosystem services.
  - No sites are located in or near biodiversity-sensitive areas.
  - Given the nature of activities, no specific mitigation measures (EU Birds/Habitats Directives, EIA Directive, IFC PS6) are deemed necessary for own operations.
  - ESRS E4 is not material for the Group’s operational scope.
- Pollution (ESRS E2):
  - Own operations and service activities are not significant pollution sources; ESRS E2 is non-material for these scopes based on internal data and the ESG risk map.
  - Pollution issues arise in the downstream value chain (credit and investment). For these scopes, ESRS E2 is material for impact analysis but non-material for financial materiality.
  - High-impact financed sectors identified: manufacture of metal products; wearing apparel; paper; building construction and civil engineering; pharmaceuticals; motor vehicles, trailers and semi-trailers; aviation and defence; electric power generation, transmission and distribution; programming/consulting/IT.
- Water and marine resources (ESRS E3):
  - Own operations require no significant water/marine resource use; ESRS E3 is non-material for these scopes.
  - In the downstream (credit and investment) scopes, ESRS E3 is material for impact analysis but non-material for financial materiality.
  - High water-consumption financed sectors identified: paper; manufacture of mineral and metal products; renewable energy production; building construction and civil engineering; mining and quarrying; leather and related products; electric power generation, transmission and distribution.
- Methodologies: Impact analyses based on exposure of technical reserves to high-impact sectors per Section 2.1.4.1.1 (Impact materiality); risk assessments per Section 2.1.4.1.2 (Financial materiality); own-operations assessments used internal management data and the ESG risk map.
text:
1.4.6 As sessment  of 
pollution‑ related IROs
La  Banque  Postale Group’s own operations  and service
activities are not the source  of significant pollution, and
are not  located in  areas  at risk of  pollution. The impacts,
risks and opportunities identified for these activities were
examined  based on internal management data, and on
the Group’s ESG  risk map. This assessment showed ESRS
E2 – Pollution  as non-material for these scopes.
The challenges in terms of pollution are concentrated in
the activities of the downstream value chain, namely
credit  and investment activities. For these scopes, the
impact  analysis was carried out  on the basis of technical
reserves  exposed to sectors causing significant pollution,
following the methodology presented in Section 2.1.4.1.1
“Impact  materiality”. The risk assessment was carried out
based  on the  methodology presented  in Section  2.1.4.1.2
“Financial  materiality”.For the credit and investment scopes, ESRS  E2 is material
for the impact analysis and  non-material for the financial
materiality  analysis. [E2_IRO_1_01]
The analysis highlighted the following sectors as very
material in terms of pollution (considering the average
impact  score of air, water and soil  pollution):
•Manufacture of metal products;
•Manufacture of wearing apparel;
•Paper industry;
•Building construction  and  civil engineering;
•Pharmaceutical industry;
•Manufacture of motor vehicles,  trailers  and  semi-trailers;
•Aviation  and  defence;
•Electric power generation, transmission and distribution;
•Programming, consulting and other IT activities. [E2_IRO_1_03]
In 
addition  to the internal stakeholders presented in
Section 2.1.4.1.1 “Impact materiality”, the following organisations
were consulted as part of the double materiality analysis
on the topic of pollution: WWF France, CDC Biodiversité
and BL Évolution.  [E2_IRO_1_02]

title: Assessment of water and marine resources-related IROs
heading: 2.1.4.7 Assessment of water and marine resources-related IROs
start_phrase: As a commercial bank, La Banque Postale Group’s own operations and service activities do not require significant use of water or marine resources.
summary:
- Context: Extract from La Banque Postale’s 2024 Universal Registration Document (Sustainable performance), explaining how sustainability reporting is prepared under ESRS 2 and summarizing double materiality assessments.

- Stakeholder engagement: Internal and external consultations conducted. External stakeholders include WWF France, CDC Biodiversité, BL Évolution (biodiversity, pollution, water) and OREE (circular economy).

- Biodiversity and ecosystems (ESRS E4):
  - As a bank with no raw materials or production sites, own operations have no significant biodiversity impacts and do not affect communities or ecosystem services.
  - No sites in or near biodiversity‑sensitive areas.
  - No need for mitigation measures under relevant EU directives or IFC PS6 for own operations.
  - ESRS E4 is non‑material for the operational scope.

- Pollution (ESRS E2):
  - Own operations and services are not significant pollution sources and are not in high‑risk areas; ESRS E2 non‑material for operations.
  - Downstream (credit and investment) activities: material for impact, non‑material for financial materiality.
  - Very material sectors for pollution: manufacture of metal products; wearing apparel; paper; construction and civil engineering; pharmaceuticals; motor vehicles/trailers; aviation and defence; electric power generation/transmission/distribution; programming/consulting/IT.

- Water and marine resources (ESRS E3):
  - Own operations require limited water/marine resources; non‑material for operations.
  - Downstream activities: material for impact, non‑material for financial materiality.
  - High water consumption sectors: paper; mineral and metal products manufacturing; renewable energy; construction and civil engineering; mining and quarrying; leather and related products; electric power generation/transmission/distribution.
  - Significant marine resource use sectors: construction and civil engineering; mining and quarrying; agriculture/forestry/fishing; renewable energy.

- Resource use and circular economy (ESRS E5):
  - Operational scope: material for impact, non‑material for financial materiality.
  - Downstream (credit/investment) scope: material for impact, non‑material for financial materiality.
  - High waste‑producing sectors: real estate; renewable energy; automotive; pharmaceuticals; mining; aviation and defence; leather and related products; electric power generation/transmission/distribution.

- Disclosure framework:
  - EU legislative data points and coverage detailed in Sections 2.5.1.1 and 2.5.1.2.
  - Non‑disclosure choices include voluntary data points, delayed disclosure, non‑material topics, unmet disclosure conditions, and selection among alternative disclosures.
  - Minimum Disclosure Requirements applied for each ESRS.

title: The impact-awareness culture at the heart of the mission-led company
heading: 2.1.6.1 The impact-awareness culture at the heart of the mission-led company
start_phrase: La Banque Postale is committed to serving its purpose as a mission-led company.
summary:
- Focus on La Banque Postale’s mission-led model and impact-awareness culture, governed by a dedicated Mission Committee and embedded across the Group, including ESG-linked remuneration and comprehensive employee training.
- Commitment to exceed regulatory expectations and co-construct practices with independent third parties (NGOs, Mission Committee), while promoting accessible banking, and offers/services that enable customers’ environmental and social transitions.
- Strong ethics and compliance stance: zero tolerance for integrity breaches, fraud, anti-competitive behavior; adherence to sanctions, financial transparency, data protection, health, environmental safeguards, and human rights.
- Rising employee engagement in ESG: higher training completion, greater participation in sustainability initiatives, and a doubling of volunteer hours between 2023 and 2024.
- Impact culture metrics show 2024 progress and 2025 targets, including:
  - Employees trained in CSR/sustainable finance (69.7% in 2023 to 80% in 2024; 90% target).
  - Non-financial targets in remuneration (20% to 28.8%; target ≥20%).
  - Growth in customer carbon-footprint awareness initiatives.
  - CNP Assurances social inclusion and community impact: significant increase in internships/work-study for youth from deprived areas, higher sponsorship spending, and more employees mobilized for societal actions.
  - Other indicators: bank card carbon footprint tracked with refined LCA methodology (2023 restated; 2024 increase linked to higher card issuance), 100% SRI in employee savings (LBP AM range fully SRI), increased hours devoted to community outreach, and stable support for L’Envol.
- Detailed explanation of bank card emissions significance for the banking activity, methodological improvements in carbon accounting, and market context (high daily usage in France and higher new card issuance in 2024).
- Group-wide impact finance approach aligned with Finance for Tomorrow’s pillars (intentionality, additionality, measurement), steered by the Sustainability Department (DEC) since 2021 to ensure strategy coherence and avoid greenwashing.
- Strategic integration of impact finance in mission targets: transforming the bancassurance model through impact culture, developing products/services for environmental, social, and regional challenges, and advancing best practices and standards in sustainable finance.
- Application across financing and services: support for environmental solutions and local authorities, improving working conditions in the value chain, managing negative impacts of financed activities, and promoting access to bancassurance (accessible banking mission).
- Monitoring via CSRD indicators and concrete sector commitments: LBP AM’s leadership in research support, issuer transparency, SRI development, collaborative engagement, participation in impact/biodiversity/climate working groups, and governance roles.
- Methodological tools and innovations: Impact Weighting Factor for financing selection and LBP AM’s GREaT investment analysis methodology integrating sustainability considerations.
text:
1.6.1 The  impact-awareness culture  
at the heart  of the  mission-led 
company  
La Banque Postale is  committed to serving its purpose as
a mission-led company. This commitment is supported by
a specific governance structure, embodied by the  Mission
Committee.
This company purpose, enshrined in the Company’s Articles
of Association, focuses specifically on the impact-awareness
culture,  which  commits all employees  to actions which
serve  and protect the environment, and is implemented
operationally  in all activities  within  the banking scope.Within La Banque Postale Group, all employees, including
the members of the Executive Board, are committed to a

start_phrase: Finance for tomorrow defines impact finance as an investment or financing strategy that aims to accelerate the just and sustainable transformation of the real economy, by providing evidence of its beneficial effects.
summary:
- Context and scope: Excerpt from La Banque Postale’s 2024 Universal Registration Document (Sustainable performance; ESRS 2) detailing impact finance strategy, governance, indicators, and selected CSR performance highlights.

- Customer and product CSR insights:

Methodology updates using life-cycle analysis improved accuracy; the 2023 baseline was revised from 563 tCO₂e to 408 tCO₂e.

  - Social programs: Slight increase in employee participation and youth beneficiaries in the L’Envol program, confirming its long-term relevance.

- Impact finance approach:
  - Definition aligned with Finance for Tomorrow (intentionality, additionality, impact measurement).
  - Governance: Centralized in the Sustainability Department (DEC, created 2021) to steer the 2030 plan, ensure Group-wide consistency, and prevent greenwashing.
  - Strategic integration: Embedded in the mission-led company targets—transform the bancassurance model with impact culture, develop solutions for environmental/social/regional needs, and advance sector best practices and standards.
  - Scope of impacts: 
    - Positive impacts via financing environmental solutions, local authorities, and improving conditions in the downstream value chain.
    - Exemplary management to assess and mitigate negative environmental and social impacts in financing and investments.
    - Access to bancassurance services enhanced through regional networks and inclusive offerings (accessible banking mission).
  - Monitoring: Impact tracked through CSRD indicators.

- Tools, methodologies, and initiatives:
  - Impact Weighting Factor (IWF): An impact scoring tool co-developed with WWF France, used in retail and corporate lending to assess environmental, societal, and regional impacts alongside risk and financial performance; also a change-management lever for teams and customers.
  - LBP AM leadership: Supports academic research, issuer environmental transparency, SRI development, and advanced collaborative engagement; active in impact finance, biodiversity, and climate working groups at the Institute for Sustainable Finance (board member).
  - GREaT methodology: LBP AM’s Group-wide investment analysis framework integrating sustainable development issues.

- Impact finance instruments and offers (illustrative portfolio):
  - Regional financing for local authorities, social housing, charities, healthcare, and companies.

  - Inclusive retail support: Livret A, Simplicité account, L’Appui; accessible branch network (including for people with disabilities).

text:
1.6.2 La  Banque  Postale Group’s  impact
finance approach
Finance  for tomorrow defines impact finance as an
investment  or financing strategy that  aims to accelerate
the just and sustainable transformation of the real
economy,  by providing  evidence of its beneficial effects. It
is based on  the pillars of intentionality,  additionality and
impact measurement. The  latter is at the heart of the
Group’s 
governance, through the Sustainability Department
(DEC) created  in 2021,  which  has made it possible to  adapt
and steer the implementation of the roadmap of the
2030 strategic plan. Amongst other things, the DEC's role
is to ensure that  this strategy is consistent and credible
across the entire Group to consolidate La Banque Postale’s
leadership  in impact finance. The DEC plays an innovative
role in the construction of the offer and ensures overall
consistency  by building internal principles to avoid any
reputational  risk of greenwashing.Impact  finance is a cross-functional subject, covered by
various policies and  concrete actions  that are detailed in
the thematic ESRS. At the strategic level, this topic is
specifically present in the targets set by La Banque Postale
as 
a mission-led company (Transform our bancassurance
model  through an impact-awareness  culture,  Develop
and promote the products and services needed to meet
environmental, 
social and regional challenges and Advance
best 
practices and regulatory standards in the bancassurance
sector  through La Banque Postale’s  exemplary actions).
Within the scope of the financed activities, the topic of
impact  finance is present in the positive impacts of the
financing  of environmental solutions and local authorities
as well as actions to  create favourable  working conditions
in the downstream value chain. For La  Banque  Postale
Group, impact finance also involves exemplary management
of financing and investments, which is primarily reflected
in 
the assessment and mitigation of negative impacts of
the financed activities on the environment and people. In
insurance business and banking services, it is rolled  out
through actions to promote access  to bancassurance
services and the regional network (the accessible banking
mission  is presented in 2.3.4.5.2 “Actions implemented to
generate positive impacts”).
Impact  finance is also managed through the monitoring
of various  indicators published in the  CSRD.
Lastly, La  Banque  Postale Group has made practical
commitments to impact finance  in the various scopes.
For example, LBP  AM, La  Banque  Postale 's main asset
management subsidiary, is involved in several financial
sector initiatives to support academic research and enhance
the 
environmental transparency of issuers, SRI development
and state-of-the-art collaborative shareholder engagement
actions. These initiatives include LBP AM's participation in
a number of working groups  on impact finance, biodiversity
and climate within the Institute for Sustainable Finance,
of which  it is also a Board member.
In addition, La  Banque  Postale has created the Impact
Weighting 
Factor to improve  the way in which it selects
its financing projects (see focus  point below).
LBP  AM has also developed an investment analysis
methodology  integrating  sustainable development issues,
which is used across the Group (see focus: The GREaT
methodology).

title: The Impact Weighting Factor (IWF)
heading: The Impact Weighting Factor (IWF)
start_phrase: The Impact Weighting Factor is an impact scoring tool used to grant loans to retail customers and for Corporate and Investment Banking.
summary:
- Context: Excerpt from La Banque Postale’s 2024 Universal Registration Document under “Sustainable performance” and “General information on the preparation of sustainability reports [ESRS 2],” with references to CSR glossary and terminology.

- Impact finance framework: Overview of La Banque Postale’s approach to “impact finance” aimed at accelerating a just and sustainable transformation of the real economy, covering:
  - Regional financing for local authorities, social housing, charities, healthcare, and companies, plus shareholder engagement.
  - Consumer impact offerings (impact home loans, renovation loans like Prêt Avance Rénovation, responsible current account, impact bank card).
  - Sector and exclusion policies; financing of green projects.
  - Accessibility and inclusion in bancassurance (universal access, support for financially vulnerable customers, accessible products such as first insurance kits, carer guarantees; services like Livret A, Simplicité account, L’Appui; accessible branch network).
  - Portfolio commitments tied to concrete GHG reduction pathways.

- Impact Weighting Factor (IWF): A proprietary impact scoring tool co-developed with WWF France to guide lending and investment decisions by assessing environmental, territorial, and inclusion impacts.
  - Scope and use: Applied at counterparty level or by financing purpose across retail and corporate activities; embedded in onboarding, credit analysis, annual reviews, and portfolio management; data from customers, external providers, public sources, and sector inputs.
  - Operational effects: Influences retail loan pricing (preferential rates for positive-impact or energy-efficiency renovation financing); in corporate real estate/asset/project finance, unfavorable scores escalate decisions to higher approval levels.
  - Deployment: Already built for five priority lines (home loans; commercial real estate; asset and project finance; large corporate loans; trading room). Next phases include local authorities, social housing, public health, SMEs/mid-caps, and consumer loans. Progress tracked by a mission-led metric (share of activities covered by the IWF).
  - Strategic outcomes: Steers capital toward positive environmental and social sectors and away from high-negative-impact activities (e.g., fossil fuels, polluting counterparties). Incorporated into Executive Board variable remuneration.
  - Structure: Three pillars—Environment (aligned with EU Green Deal, Taxonomy, SFDR: climate, biodiversity, water, pollution), Territory (economic and social characteristics within France/EU: regional economic development, sustainable territorial development), Inclusion (human rights, diversity and inclusion, universal product/service accessibility).
  - Impact scale: Five levels from Very negative (1) to Very positive (5).

- LBP AM GREaT methodology: Integration of ESG in La Banque Postale Asset Management’s investment processes through its SRI approach.
  - SRI pillars: (1) Integrate sustainable development issues in investment selection; (2) Engage companies to improve practices; (3) Exclude firms in major controversies or sensitive sectors (controversial/prohibited weapons, tobacco, gambling, thermal coal, certain oil and gas).
  - GREaT analytical framework: G – responsible Governance; R – sustainable management of natural and human Resources; E – Energy transition; T – Territorial development.
  - Consumer-focused criteria: Data protection, product/service quality and safety, customer relationship management (privacy), mitigation of negative impacts on customer rights, access to essential services, and human rights respect.
  - Application: Covers all asset classes with SRI ratings for ~12,000 companies; ratings used via quantitative methods and certified thresholds in portfolio construction. The GREaT Committee oversees engagement and exclusion policies, including exclusion decisions.

title: The GREaT methodology
heading: The GREaT methodology
start_phrase: LBP AM, La Banque Postale Group’s asset management company, places responsibility at the heart of its strategy.
summary:
This excerpt from La Banque Postale’s 2024 Universal Registration Document outlines how sustainability reporting is prepared under ESRS 2 and details LBP Asset Management’s integration of ESG across all investment processes. It presents LBP AM’s SRI approach—built on (1) embedding sustainable development in investment selection, (2) engaging issuers to improve practices, and (3) excluding sensitive sectors and major controversies (e.g., controversial/prohibited weapons, tobacco, gambling, thermal coal, and certain oil and gas). The proprietary GREaT methodology—covering Governance, Resources (natural and human), Energy transition, and Territorial development—assesses issuers on topics including product/service quality and safety, data privacy, consumer relationships, access to essential services, and human rights. It is applied to all asset classes, assigns SRI scores to roughly 12,000 companies, and feeds quantitative selection thresholds audited for SRI certification. A GREaT Committee oversees engagement and exclusion policies and makes exclusion decisions.

The text also positions impact finance as a core strategic pillar addressed across the Group’s double materiality analysis. It references monitoring indicators and links them to climate action (E1), regional and community commitments (S3), and consumer/end-user interests (S4). Impact finance IROs span:
- Negative impacts: environmental and social harms from financed activities; potential customer detriment from inadequate insurance.
- Positive impacts: sustainable/positive-impact financing; improved access to bancassurance for all customers including vulnerable groups; enhanced working conditions in the downstream value chain.
- Opportunities: growth in sustainable finance markets and new business openings.
- Risks: portfolio exposure to physical and transition climate risks.
The section emphasizes exemplary management of financing and investments, proactive mitigation of environmental and social impacts, voluntary positive-impact actions, market development, and business model resilience.

The GREaT  methodology
Integrating  ESG issues into LBP AM’s asset 
management  business
LBP  AM, La Banque Postale Group’s asset management
company, 
places responsibility at the heart of its strategy.
LBP 
AM’s Socially Responsible Investment (SRI)* approach
is therefore integrated into all of its management processes.
It is based  on three  areas:
1. Incorporate sustainable development issues  into  the
selection of investments;
2. Encourage companies to  improve  their practices;
3. Exclude  companies involved  in major  controversies
or operating in sensitive sectors (controversial and
prohibited  weapons,  tobacco, gambling, thermal
coal and  certain oil and gas companies).
GREaT investment analysis methodology
The aim of  the proprietary GREaT methodology is to
integrate 
sustainable development issues into the analysis
of LBP AM’s investments. It aims to assess companies in
terms  of respect for human  rights,  product  quality
and  managing societal impacts. To achieve this goal,
LBP  AM bases  its analysis  on four pillars:
•G – responsible Governance;
•R – sustainable management  of natural and human
Resources;
•E – Energy  transition;
•(and) T – Territorial  development.The GREaT approach includes specific criteria related  to
consumers, such as:
•protection of personal data;
•quality  and  safety of products and services;
•managing relationships with consumers (privacy, data
protection);
•preventing and addressing negative impacts on the
rights of customers and end users, access to essential
services (health, communication);
•respect for  human rights.
This methodology applies to all asset classes and makes it
possible to assign SRI ratings to the sustainable development
practices 
of nearly 12,000 companies. These SRI ratings
are 
incorporated into the asset selection process mainly
through quantitative methods and thresholds established
and audited within the framework of the SRI certification.

start_phrase: La Banque Postale Group is committed to a broad approach to impact finance.
summary:

- Reported outstandings (2022–2024):
  - LBP AM & Louvre Banque Privée: growth in total assets; mix across SFDR Articles 6/8/9 and non-SFDR; rising Article 8 and 9 volumes.
  - CNP Assurances, LBP AM & Louvre Banque Privée: total outstandings increase; stable total responsible finance assets; breakdown between SRI/Greenfin-compliant and other ESG-filtered assets.
- Environmental information on climate change (E1):
  - Material IROs and link to strategy/business model; reference to detailed climate IRO assessment.
  - Climate risk types (physical and transition) per materiality analysis.
  - Resilience analysis and stress testing:
    - Internal framework using NGFS scenarios aligned with ACPR/ECB exercises; short-term (1–3 years) projections on retail/non-retail portfolios with plans to extend beyond 10 years.
    - Sensitivity analyses for market, liquidity, and operational risk; integration into ICAAP and risk management (risk mapping, materiality matrix).
    - Physical risk scenarios: floods for real estate, drought for corporates; operational risk scenario of a 100-year Seine flood to calibrate insurance coverage.
    - Findings: overall performance aligned with eurozone bank averages; limited exposure and low concentration to carbon-intensive sectors.
  - CNP Assurances ACPR climate stress test (France scope, end-2022 data): assessed sensitivity to high-rate environments; demonstrated resilience due to portfolio decarbonization, coal exposure reduction, and increased green investments.

SFDR  technical reserves (Sustainable  Finance  Disclosure

defined by Regulation (EU) 2019/2088 of the European
Parliament  and of the Council: Article 6(1), Article 8(2) and
Article  9(3) funds.
Definition of “Responsible  technical reserves 
of financial  assets ” for LBP  AM:
The selected technical reserves take into account environmental,
social  or governance (ESG) criteria in the financial analysis
and in the building  of portfolios.  These are:
•Either  SRI technical reserves, with the systematic and
traceable integration of ESG criteria considerations, with
a high degree of selectivity (or significant improvement
in an average ESG score vs. the portfolio’s analysis
universe)
. These may be:
•portfolios of funds or discretionary management portfolios
that  have  obtained the  SRI or Greenfin  label,
•portfolios of funds or discretionary management portfolios
whose  SRI approach is considered equivalent to the
SRI certification  specifications (V2);
•Or responsible technical reserves which are not classified
as SRI:  these  are funds (such as  SFDR  8) that comply
with a list of exclusions and filters established on the
basis of ESG criteria  with a lesser degree of selectivity.
For example, these are funds with an average SRI rating
better  than that of the universe (but not higher than
20%,  unlike a “V2”  SRI fund).Responsible  technical  reserves not classified as SRI, and
portfolios 
whose approach is considered to be very close
to the certification (Greenfin, SRI V2) without being
certified, 
comprise the technical reserves of financial
assets with other ESG filters.
Technical 
reserves marketed but not managed by LBP AM
are not disclosed in this sustainability report.
Definition  of “Responsible technical reserves 
of financial  assets” for Louvre Banque Privée:
The benchmark technical reserves used are limited to the
technical 
reserves under discretionary management; freely
managed 
technical reserves are structurally excluded, as
customers are free to choose and freely  manage their
investments (ESG/non-ESG) at any time.
The ESG methodology consists of applying the following
exclusion criteria cumulatively:
•Exclusion from the investment universe of companies
operating  in whole or in part in certain controversial
sectors or types  of business  sectors;
•Then, standards-based exclusion based on ratings assigned
by the  “Sustainalytics”  social  and environmental rating
agency;
•Finally, the critical analysis of Louvre  Banque  Privée's
management and analysis team is used to refine this list.
With regard to listed securities funds:
•Internal 
and external funds are either SRI-certified or rated
at least three Morningstar Globes  (on a scale of 1  to 5);
(1) Article  6: Products  without  sustainability targets.
(2) Article  8: Products that promote environmental and/or social characteristics.
(3) Article  9: Products  whose target  is to have a positive  impact on the  environment  and society.

text:
2.1.1.2 Resilience  analysis
An internal stress test framework  has been developed by
La Banque Postale to measure the impacts of climate risk
on its business model and study its resilience based on
the scenarios of  the Network  for Greening  the Financial
System (NGFS) used in the exercises of the French
Prudential 
Supervision and  Resolution Authority (ACPR)
and the European Central Bank (ECB). By projecting over
a horizon of  one  to three years with constant  assets, the
analysis covers the Retail and Non-Retail loan portfolios.
La  Banque   Postale aims to roll out this exercise over a
period of more  than 10  years  in 2024.
Ad hoc sensitivity  scenarios were  also developed  to assess
the materiality  of the climate  risk  in terms of  market risk,
liquidity  risk and  operational  risk.
The data, combined with the ESG risk management work,
provided a basis  for incorporating climate issues  in the
Bank’s Internal  Capital  Adequacy Assessment  Process
(ICAAP) and  led to an increase  in the coverage  of climate
risks  by capital. They are also used in the context of risk
management: in the mapping of climate risks and the
work  to produce  the materiality  matrix.In relation to physical risks,  these  tests are based on the
“flood”  scenario for  real estate exposures and the
“drought” scenario for companies. Physical operational
risks 
were also studied with the 100-year Seine flood
scenario;  with assumptions that  deliberately target a
strong  shock over a  limited time horizon  (1 year) and are
used to calibrate the Bank’s insurance coverage needs
(flood of the Seine) . [E1_IRO_1_07]  [E1_IRO_1_08]  [E1_IRO_1_13]  [E1_IRO_1_15]
Additional information is available in Section 6.8.4.5
“Incorporation 
of short, medium and long-term effects of
environmental 
and social factors and associated risks into
the Bank’s risk management framework” of the Universal
Registration Document.
La  Banque  Postale therefore assesses its exposure to
carbon-intensive  sectors and its  ability to cope with
climate shocks. Based on the  results of these exercises,
La Banque Postale’s  overall performance is in line with the
average for euro zone banks. Its portfolio’s exposure to
the most carbon-intensive sectors is limited, and its
concentration  on the most  carbon-intensive  firms is  low.
In 2024,  CNP Assurances SA was also  asked by the ACPR
to participate in the climate stress test on the scope of its
activities  in France on the  basis of its data  at the  end of
2022. The test quantified CNP Assurances’ exposure to the
climate scenarios proposed by  the ACPR, and in
particular 
its sensitivity to a high-interest rate
environment in the various scenarios. It also highlighted
CNP   Assurances’ resilience to climate risk: the measures
implemented  in recent years (reduction of the investment
portfolio carbon footprint, reduction of exposure to the
thermal coal sector, increase in green investments) enable
CNP  Assurances to fare  better in the event of an
unfavourable transition scenario for companies that emit
the most greenhouse gases. [E1_SBM_3_02] [E1_SBM_3_03]
[E1_SBM_3_04] [E1_SBM_3_05]  [E1_SBM_3_06]

heading: 2.2.1.2.1 Presentation of the transition plan
start_phrase: In 2021, through its Chairman of the Executive Board, La Banque Postale made an ambitious commitment to achieve net zero emissions by 2040, i.e. ten years ahead of the targets set by the Paris Agreement, conditional upon consistent measures from governments and companies.

- Sector policies and scientific alignment: Stringent coal, oil, and gas risk policies aligned with a 1.5°C trajectory using IPCC SR15, IEA NZE 2050, and CRREM 1.5°C; strategy designed to be climate-resilient.

text:
2.1.2.1 Presentation  of the transition  plan
In 2021, through  its Chairman of the Executive Board,
La  Banque  Postale made an ambitious commitment to
achieve net  zero  emissions by 2040, i.e. ten years ahead of
the targets set by the Paris Agreement, conditional upon
consistent measures  from  governments  and  companies.
La Banque Postale is putting its pledges into action both
in its offerings, by publishing low-carbon pathways, and in
its sector-specific policies. All internal  actions are aligned
to this transition, as regards both the organisation’s operational
scope and  the operations  of its various  business  lines.
In 2025, La Banque Postale Group reached a new milestone
with  the publication(1) of its transition plan covering its
main 
entities (La Banque Postale, CNP Assurances, LBP AM
and Louvre Banque  Privée). With a forward-looking purpose,
this transition plan details the actions to be implemented
over  the next 5 years to meet the decarbonization targets
set by the  Group.  It makes  it possible to  anchor long-term
targets in the overall strategy by aligning the climate targets
with the financial planning horizon. The implementation
of this plan  thus requires transformative thinking on how
to 
develop the business model, which involves all employees
on all subjects: governance, monitoring of the plan’s execution,
financing 
dedicated to actions, etc. For La Banque Postale
Group, the implementation of this plan will align with the
commitments 
already made with the operational and
commercial  challenges of  the Group’s business lines and
subsidiaries,  and  will send a clear  strategic message.  [E1_1_01]La  Banque  Postale has relied  on two distinct but
complementary 
methodological frameworks to define its
low-carbon pathways:
1.the 
Science Based Targets initiative (SBTi): the worldwide
standard for CO2 emissions reduction pathways and
validation of company pathways;
2.
the Net Zero Banking Alliance  (NZBA): a United
Nations-convened group of banks that establishes CO2
emission  baselines  and  pathways. La  Banque   Postale
has been a  member of the NZBA’s Steering Group
since  2021. La  Banque  Postale’s two subsidiaries,
CNP  Assurances and LBP AM , are members of the Net
Zero Asset Owner Alliance and  the Net Zero Asset
Managers  Initiative respectively, both of which are
aiming to help their members achieve net zero
emissions  by 2050.
The commitment to the SBTi dates from 2017.
La Banque Postale contributed to the development of the
first 
methodology specific to the financial sector, and took
part  in the methodological road tests in June 2019. This
step was important for La Banque Postale in several ways,
including  the development and strengthening of internal
skills, 
the Bank’s business lines taking on board the
challenges related to the setting of low-carbon pathways
(own operations and portfolios), and initial estimates of the
Bank’s performance in  terms of alignment with the Paris
Agreement. 
The methodology was published in October
2020. 
One year later, La  Banque  Postale became  one of
the first three banks in  the  world to have  its low-carbon
pathways validated by the SBTi, both in its operational
scope and in its Corporate and Investment Banking
activities. 
In 2023, La Banque Postale continued to implement
its low-carbon pathways with the development of a
steering tool for residential and commercial property, and
the ongoing development of a tool for corporate counterparties
(Corporate 
and Investment Banking). For the operational
scope,  La  Banque  Postale’s pathway was reviewed and
included in an overall  target presented by  La Poste Group.
The latter was validated by the  SBTi in  March 2024.
In addition, La Banque Postale has implemented stringent
sectoral risk management policies in the coal, oil and gas
sectors that guarantee it is aligned with 1.5°C in these
sectors. Here again, its approach is based on scientifically
validated 
scenarios such  as the “IPCC Special Report on
Global 
Warming of 1.5°C (SR15)”,  the IEA Net  Zero by 2050
or the Carbon Risk  Real Estate  Monitor (CRREM) 1.5°C.
Thus, La  Banque  Postale’s pathways are based on the
scientifically 
credible scenarios presented above. Through these
analyses, La Banque Postale can consider all the impacts
related 
to climate change which are beyond its control,
and  ensure that its  strategy is resilient to climate change.
La  Banque  Postale’s subsidiaries have also implemented
strategies to align with the Paris Agreement, taking into
account the specificities of their activities.
(1)
The full transition  plan is published  separately and is available on La Banque Postale’s institutional website from spring 2025.118 La Banque  Postale      2024 Universal Registration  Document Please see the glossary on page 808 for definitions of  the main CSR terms2Sustainable performance
Environmental information
CNP   Assurances has  also set targets for reducing direct
and indirect  green house  gas emissions, aligned  with the
Paris  Agreement. At the end  of 2024,  approximately 28%
of CNP Assurances ’ investment portfolio was covered  by a
target aligned  with  the Paris Agreement.  CNP  Assurances'
targets  are based  on the  recommendations of the Net
Zero  Asset Owner Alliance. As data is  not always available
for all asset  classes, the exercise was carried out with a
view  to continuous improvement. Participation in the
work  of the Net Zero Asset Owner Alliance makes it
possible  to refine  these  results  from  year to year.
In 2022, LBP  AM committed to achieving a “Net Zero”
alignment for 80% of assets  under management by 2030,
and  100%  by 2040.
Louvre   Banque  Privée follows  an asset management
strategy  expressed as an  “implied rise in temperature”.
Each  company in the portfolio is assessed according to its
low-carbon  pathway, based on SBTi and CDP (Carbon
Disclosure  Project) data. Companies receive a score based
on their compatibility with global warming scenarios
ranging  from an alignment  at 1.5°C to  scenarios above 3°C.
The implied temperature of a portfolio is the weighted
average 
of the temperatures of the companies held. Thus, if
this average  is 1.5°C,  it means  that the companies in the
portfolio  have transition  plans aligned with the target of
1.5°C. [E1_1_02]
La  Banque  Postale, as well as its subsidiaries, are not
excluded  from the benchmarks of the Paris Agreement.
For information, these financial benchmarks, like the EU
PAB,  bring together companies  and securities whose
pathway  is compatible with limiting global warming to
1.5°C  above  pre-industrial levels by  2050. [E1_1_12]

text:
2.1.2.2 Incorporating the transition plan  
into the Group’s  overall strategy 
and financial forecasts
La Banque Postale Group has included its decarbonization
target s in its  overall target s. In order  to achieve  them, each
business  line, including the subsidiaries, has drawn up a
specific  roadmap  aligning its decarbonisation projects
and initiatives with the Group’s ambitions. They have been
particularly  mindful of aligning  commercial targets with
climate  targets. This direct involvement of the business
lines  was key to raising awareness and empowering each
department in achieving La Banque Postale’s decarbonization
ambitions.
Decarbonization  initiatives are managed in the short and
medium  term within the divisions, with overall monitoring
by the Executive  Committee. On  the financial side, the
transition plan projects are gradually incorporated into
strategic  and budget reviews,  allowing for rigorous
monitoring  of execution, costs and the value of positive
outcomes.  They also strengthen  the integrated planning
process  (financial,  non-financial  and  strategic).  [E1_1_13]Construction of the transition plan, led by the Sustainability
Department, involved all  of La  Banque  Postale Group’s
business lines in the construction of their  own roadmap.
This plan was validated at each stage by the Executive
Committee. The members of the Supervisory Board were
informed  of the progress of  work on this transition  plan,
while  the Mission Committee contributed to its advance
preparation and approved the final content.
For 
CNP  Assurances , the transition plan is approved and
monitored 
by the Board of Directors. LBP AM’s transition
plan 
will be approved in 2025 by the  Sustainable Finance
Committee and by LBP  AM’s Supervisory Board.
Louvre Banque Privée's plan was adopted by its Executive
Board 
in 2024, and will be published  jointly with  that of
La Banque Postale in  2025. [E1_1_14]

heading: 2.2.1.3 Climate change mitigation and adaptation policies
start_phrase: Through its climate policies, La Banque Postale Group aims to address the following sustainability issues:
summary:
- Focus of the excerpt: La Banque Postale Group’s climate strategy and governance, integration of transition plans into overall strategy and finance, and detailed climate mitigation/adaptation policies across the Group and key subsidiaries (CNP Assurances, LBP AM, Louvre Banque Privée).
- Investment alignment and targets:
  - CNP Assurances: Paris Agreement–aligned decarbonization targets; ~28% of the investment portfolio covered by Paris-aligned targets at end-2024; targets based on Net-Zero Asset Owner Alliance (NZAOA) recommendations; iterative improvement due to data gaps.
  - LBP AM: Commitment to “Net Zero” alignment for 80% of AUM by 2030 and 100% by 2040.
