title: Policies related to resource use and the circular economy
heading: 2.2.5.1 Policies related to resource use and the circular economy
start_phrase: In 2024, La Banque Postale implemented a Resources and Circular Economy policy whose scope includes La Banque Postale SA as well as its main subsidiaries (CNP Assurances, LBP AM, La Banque Postale Consumer Finance, Louvre Banque Privée, Domiserve and Easybourse, LBP Leasing & Factoring).
summary:
- Focus on water and marine resources:
  - Use of the Impact Weighting Factor (IWF) with WWF France to guide financing/investment.
  - Green loans for local authorities targeting water and sanitation; bridging loans to pre-finance water agency subsidies (e.g., network leak reduction, reuse of treated wastewater).
  - Climate and Biodiversity Impact Fund financing projects to reduce water consumption.
  - Subsidiary actions: CNP Assurances’ Green Works Charter (limit/ensure quality of water use in real estate), LBP AM’s participation in CERES’ Valuing Water initiative, Louvre Banque Privée’s strengthened monitoring of “emissions to water” (SFDR PAIs).
  - Post-2023/2024 impact measurement will inform expanded impact-reduction actions.

- Water risk mapping and priorities:
  - 2024 analysis identified financed activities in sensitive areas using criteria including water stress; about 65% of financed areas have at least two high-risk criteria.
  - Priority locations: Île-de-France (significant potential building land, medium overall risk) and parts of South-East France (very high overall risk).
  - Next steps: define concrete actions to limit impacts in water-risk areas.
  - CNP Assurances to map financial assets in high/extremely high water-stress areas by end-2027 and real estate/sites by end-2026; LBP AM engaging portfolio companies to map abstraction sites, identify high-stress areas, and study local impacts.

- Targets and results for water:
  - Quantified impact-reduction targets to be set progressively following 2023–2024 assessments.

- Circular economy strategy:
  - 2024 Resources and Circular Economy policy covering La Banque Postale SA and main subsidiaries (CNP Assurances, LBP AM, LBP Consumer Finance, Louvre Banque Privée, Domiserve, Easybourse, LBP Leasing & Factoring).
  - Commitment to reduce at source and optimize resource use and end-of-life by 2030, with a life-cycle approach and subsidiary-specific roadmaps.
  - Promotion of recycled and renewable materials; eco-design of products (e.g., bank cards) prioritizing recycled content and recyclability.
  - Financing/investment activities considered but without specific targets; policy governed and monitored by the Sustainability Department and shared internally/externally.
  - No waste policy yet for Corporate & Investment Banking due to measurement methodology gaps; collaborative work with La Poste Group to develop resource footprint and reduction pathways.

- Action plans for resource use and waste:
  - Reduce consumption and waste:
    - Plastics: identify high-consuming suppliers, implement reduction plans, integrate material criteria in procurement, raise buyer/specifier awareness.
    - Paper/cardboard: trace waste origins, embed criteria in tenders, train influencers/buyers on alternatives.
    - Electrical/electronic equipment (EEE): optimize allocation policies and raise user awareness.
  - Optimize end-of-life:
    - Comprehensive waste mapping, supplier progress plans prioritizing reuse and recycling over energy recovery/landfill, employee training on sorting/recovery.
    - Reduce undelivered bank cards; integrate recovery with providers; consider extending card validity.
    - Promote reuse via stricter supplier requirements, donation channels, life-cycle analyses, and awareness.
  - Annual roadmap coordinated by the Sustainability Department; no specific budget allocation; no waste roadmaps for credit/investment portfolios.

- Waste management practices:
  - Contracts apply the waste hierarchy; reuse considered before recycling.
  - Majority of waste handled by operators committed to 100% recycling (e.g., Recygo, Les Joyeux Recycleurs).

2.5.1
Policies related  to resource use  
and the circular  economy
In 2024, La  Banque  Postale implemented a Resources
and   Circular Economy policy  whose scope includes
La  Banque  Postale SA as well as its main subsidiaries
(CNP  Assurances, LBP AM, La Banque Postale Consumer
Finance, 
Louvre Banque Privée, Domiserve and Easybourse,
LBP Leasing & Factoring). This scope covers the policy,
actions and indicators presented
 in this section.The policy is part of the general ESG approach implemented
by La  Banque   Postale  Group,  and  is based on  the key
commitment to reduce at source and optimise the use
and end-of-life of the  Group’s resources by 2030. This policy
incorporates 
the management of waste  flows as part of a
resource 
“life cycle” vision. It applies to the entire scope of
La  Banque  Postale's operational activities. Financing and
investment  activities were considered in the  drafting of
this policy, but are not subject to specific targets or
commitments. The policy is validated and monitored by
La Banque Postale’s Sustainability Department. This policy
and  the monitoring of the associated targets have been
circulated 
to all interested internal contributors, and are
freely circulated  internally and externally on request.158 La Banque  Postale      2024 Universal Registration  Document Please see the glossary on page 808 for definitions of  the main CSR terms2Sustainable performance
Environmental information
The 
policy is broken down into roadmaps for all subsidiaries
based  on their  operational specificities and the way in
which they  use resources. [E5_MDR_P_01_06]
In addition  to the  targets  set,  the Resources and  Circular
Economy  policy  supports specifiers  in the  systematic use
of recycled resources, both for paper/cardboard and plastic
and for waste electrical and electronic equipment (WEEE).
All products (bank cards, for  example) put into circulation
by 
La Banque Postale are subject to an eco-design approach.
This approach is reflected by prioritising recycled materials
and 
paying particular attention to the recyclability of plastics,
cardboard  and computer equipment put into circulation.
This eco-design approach also aims to promote renewable
resources  in the Group’s supply  policies. [E5_1_02]
As part of the management of its Corporate and Investment
Banking portfolio, La  Banque  Postale  does not have a
waste management policy. This is due to the fact that there
are currently no methodologies to measure the resource
footprint (incoming, outgoing and waste) or to manage
the waste  related  to these activities.
Work  carried out by  La Poste  Group has been initiated to
establish the resource footprint  and associated reduction
pathways 
at Group level. La Banque Postale  has also been
involved  in this work. As a result, it should be possible to
enhance  the way in which waste impacts are reflected in
La  Banque  Postale’s Corporate and Investment Banking
activities.  [E5_MDR_P_07_08]

title: Action plans related to resource use and the circular economy
heading: 2.2.5.2 Action plans related to resource use and the circular economy
start_phrase: The main actions deployed under the Resources and Circular Economy policy include:
summary:
- Scope and policy: La Banque Postale’s environmental/CSR approach includes a Group-wide Resources and Circular Economy policy, translated into subsidiary-specific roadmaps based on operational needs and resource use.
- Eco-design and materials: All products placed on the market (notably bank cards) follow an eco-design approach prioritizing recycled inputs, recyclability of plastics/cardboard/IT equipment, and promotion of renewable resources. Procurement supports systematic use of recycled materials for paper/cardboard, plastics, and WEEE.
- CIB perimeter: No waste management policy currently applies to Corporate & Investment Banking due to the absence of robust methodologies to measure resource footprints. Group-level work (with La Poste Group) is underway to establish footprints and reduction pathways, which should enable better integration of waste impacts in CIB in the future.
- Action plans to reduce resource use and waste:
  - Plastics: Identify highest-consuming suppliers, deploy plans to reduce plastic supply, embed materials criteria in tenders, and raise awareness among specifiers/buyers.
  - Paper/cardboard: Map waste origins across activities, add dedicated procurement criteria, and raise awareness of alternatives.
  - Electrical/electronic equipment (IT): Review allocation/management policies, optimize allocation processes, and train employees on responsible use.
- End-of-life optimization:
  - Waste management: Assess volumes and types across sites; implement supplier progress plans; favor reuse and recycling while avoiding incineration and landfill; train employees on sorting and recovery.
  - Bank cards: Reduce undelivered cards, organize recovery of non-delivered products, and consider extending card validity to limit renewals.
  - Reuse: Strengthen supplier requirements for WEEE reuse, set up internal/external donation channels, conduct LCAs, and train specifiers on reuse methods.
- Governance and implementation: Actions are consolidated in an annual roadmap shared across entities and adapted to each operational scope. The Sustainability Department leads execution; efforts focus on human-resource prioritization and influencer awareness. No specific budget allocations were attached to these roadmaps.
- Exclusions: No waste management roadmaps exist for the credit and investment portfolio.
- Waste handling: Contracts apply the waste treatment hierarchy, systematically considering reuse before recycling. Most waste is processed by operators committed to 100% recycling (e.g., Recygo, Les Joyeux Recycleurs).
text:
2.5.2 Action  plans related to resource 
use and the circular  economy
Main actions  implemented
The main actions deployed under the Resources and Circular
Economy policy  include:
•the reduction of waste volumes and resources consumed:
•for plastics, identifying the suppliers that consume the
most  and implementation of a progress plan to help
them move away from the supply of plastics, integration
of specific “materials” criteria during renewal consultations,
awareness-raising  of specifiers and  buyers on these
topics  and  the alternatives available  on the market;
•for paper and cardboard, identifying the origin of
paper/cardboard waste across  all activities,  integration
of dedicated  criteria during consultations,  awareness-
raising of influencers and buyers on these subjects
and  the alternatives  available on  the market;
•for electrical  and  electronic equipment,  identifying  the
policies and practices in force concerning the allocation
and  management of IT  equipment, optimisation  of
the IT equipment allocation process and raising awareness
among  all employees on  the rules of use;•end-of-life optimisation for raw and secondary materials:
•for waste management, identifying the volume and
specific  nature of all waste produced on  the sites,
implementing the progress  plan (PQSE appendix)
with contracted suppliers, with the exclusion of energy
and material recovery (incineration  and landfill), and
awareness-raising among all employees regarding on-
site sorting and recovery methods;
•awareness-raising with retail customers to limit undelivered
bank 
cards (NPL), and with service providers in order to
integrate 
the recovery of NPL, considering the extension
of bank card validity contracts in order to limit renewals;
•for reuse: identifying suppliers in charge of WEEE
management and end-of-life management procedures,
increased  requirements for  suppliers to  implement
reuse initiatives, internal and external donation process
to promote reuse, carrying out a life cycle analysis (LCA),
raising awareness among specifiers about reuse
approaches and methods.
These 
actions are  based on an annual roadmap specifying
the methods for achieving  the targets set by the policy.
It  is shared with  the  various contributors  as well as with
the subsidiaries of  La  Banque  Postale. For all interested
stakeholders, the roadmap is adapted to their own operational
scope. The implementation  and operational  management
of these actions are the responsibility of  the Sustainability
Department. The actions require  prioritization in terms of
human resources, and in particular a strong  awareness of
the main influencers. There were no financial estimates
associated 
with the implementation of the roadmaps, as
the actions did  not involve a specific or measurable
budget  commitment.  [E5_MDR_A_01_12]
La  Banque   Postale does not have waste management
roadmaps 
as part of the management of its credit and
investment portfolio. [E5_MDR_A_13_14]
Managing, recovering and reducing our waste
In all waste management contracts for the La Banque Postale
SA scope and its subsidiaries, the waste treatment
hierarchy is taken into account and reuse is systematically
considered 
(when relevant) before recycling is implemented.
The majority of waste is handled by operators that are
committed  to 100% recycling, such as Recygo or
Les Joyeux  Recycleurs. [E5_2_06]Please  see the glossary  on page 808 for definitions of the main CSR terms 2024 Universal  Registration Document     La Banque Postale 1592Sustainable performance
Environmental information
Strengthening  the circular economy
The Group’s ambition through its Resources and Circular
Economy policy is to go beyond the actions and partnerships
already  in place, primarily by more actively developing
specific  internal and external donation rules via the
consolidation of a donation hierarchy shared with all entities
to ensure the effective and efficient implementation  of
the circular  economy  for materials. [E5_2_08]
La  Banque  Postale holds discussions with institutional
players  such as CITEO in order to monitor the application
of Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) within its scope
and  to benefit  from  its ecosystem  coordination actions.
In  addition, all employees are involved in awareness-
raising  initiatives  to promote  the circular  economy. [E5_2_09]
Suppliers  are committed and involved in these matters
through annual monitoring  bodies and the implementation
of 
associated progress plans. La Poste Group’s internal experts
and, 
in particular, the Sustainability Department members
responsible for managing circular economy initiatives, work
with institutional  stakeholders on  these  issues.  [E5_2_10]
CNP   Assurances takes into account resources and the
circular  economy in the ESG filters of listed equities and
bonds.  The  non-financial rating  of the  companies/issuers
used is based  on a specific methodology that measures
the commitment,  responsibility,  opportunities  and risks
for companies on four pillars, including the sustainable
management  of resources. The  latter is studied according
to four criteria, including waste, and aims to ensure that
the principles of the circular economy are taken into account
in the design, production and use phases of products /
services  to reduce  pollution and promote recycling.
For real estate, ESG criteria are rolled out operationally in
the real  estate  assets  under management in the form of
the so-called “Green Works” Charter, whereby the management
companies  of CNP Assurances undertake to carry out the
work in accordance with the rules of  the Charter. Issues
surrounding resource use  and  the  circular  economy  are
included  therein,  including looking at,  as far as possible for
each operation, the option of using deconstruction processes
for the reuse and recovery of materials, as well as the priority
use of materials from redeployment channels, where possible.
The management companies of CNP  Assurances are
responsible  for the risks associated with this  charter.
CNP Assurances  expects  them to  manage  these risks in a
balanced  and appropriate manner on a case-by-case
basis , depending on the materiality  of the  matters at
stake. [E5_MDR_A_01_12]2.2.5.3

title: Targets
heading: 2.2.5.3.1 Targets
start_phrase: A number of operational targets have been set and are managed annually by the Sustainability Department.
summary:
- Focus: La Banque Postale’s Resources and Circular Economy policy within its 2024 Universal Registration Document, covering governance, targets to 2030, eco-design and procurement practices, waste management approach, and performance metrics.
- Governance and engagement:
  - Strengthens circular economy via a shared donation hierarchy and specific internal/external donation rules.
  - Works with institutional actors (e.g., CITEO) to monitor Extended Producer Responsibility and coordinates ecosystem actions.
  - Engages all employees through awareness initiatives; involves suppliers via annual reviews and progress plans.
  - CNP Assurances integrates resource/circular-economy criteria into ESG filters for listed assets and applies a “Green Works” Charter in real estate (deconstruction, reuse/recovery, priority for redeployed materials), with risk management by asset managers.
- Targets to 2030 (base year 2023; set by the Sustainability Department; monitored quarterly; annual assessments):
  - Reduce plastic waste by 50% and paper/cardboard by 30%.
  - Sort and recover 100% of site-generated waste (excluding plastic), prioritizing recycling.
  - Ensure 100% of plastic waste is recyclable, reusable, or compostable.
  - Reduce WEEE by 30% vs 2021 and maintain recovery rates above 85%.
  - Achieve a minimum 50% “second life” rate (one-third reuse, two-thirds redeployment).
  - Apply eco-design to 100% of products put into circulation.
  - Collect 30% of expired bank cards; recover 100% of expired and 100% of undistributed cards.
  - Note: No waste-management targets for loan and investment portfolios.
- Eco-design and procurement:
  - All offers/services pass an internal ESG project grid assessing resource use and waste.
  - Purchasing embeds circularity, especially for IT: repairability indices, spare parts availability, take-back of replaced/EOL equipment, and robust redeployment/recycling/destruction channels.
- Waste management approach:
  - Prioritizes reduction at source and follows the European waste hierarchy (recycling, then material recovery, then energy recovery).
  - Voluntary, mission-driven policy exceeding regulatory requirements.
- Key metrics and results:
  - Total waste generated: 1,435 tonnes.
  - Waste diverted from disposal: 1,325 tonnes; waste sent for disposal: 110 tonnes.
  - Non-recycled waste: 253 tonnes (17.6% of total).
  - WEEE: 575 tonnes; classified as hazardous waste under EU Directive 2008/98/EC. No radioactive waste.
  - 36 tonnes of electrical/electronic equipment reused.
  - Main streams: office paper; WEEE (batteries, bulbs, phones, computers), containing rare metals, aluminum, plastics.
- Reporting:
  - Centralized by DEC teams using service-provider data; estimates used for some multi-tenant sites based on employee counts.
- Additional:
  - Targets mapped to circular economy levers (eco-design, circular material use, minimization of primary raw materials, sustainable sourcing, waste management).

- Waste management scope and priorities:

title: Background and regulatory requirements of the European Green Taxonomy
heading: 2.2.6.1 Background and regulatory requirements of the European Green Taxonomy
start_phrase: The European Green Taxonomy Regulation (EU) 2020/852 dated 18 June 2020 defines sustainable economic activities by establishing substantial contribution technical criteria (CCS), for at least one of the environmental and Do No Significant Harm (DNSH) targets and five other targets.
summary:
- Context and scope: La Banque Postale’s Universal Registration Document outlines how the European Green Taxonomy applies to the Bank’s activities, focusing on environmental information and sustainable performance.
- EU Green Taxonomy framework: Explains Regulation (EU) 2020/852, defining sustainable activities through substantial contribution criteria, Do No Significant Harm (DNSH), and Minimum Social Safeguards (MSS). Notes Article 8 disclosure obligations and the technical screening criteria set by Delegated Regulations 2021/2139 (climate objectives) and 2023/2486 (the other four environmental objectives). Lists the six environmental objectives (climate mitigation, climate adaptation, water/marine, circular economy, pollution prevention, biodiversity/ecosystems).
- Implementation at the Bank: Integration of the Taxonomy into the business model, including updates to green loan and green bond frameworks and front-office enablement to help clients meet green criteria.
- Reporting perimeter and timing: The Bank currently discloses eligibility/alignment for the first two objectives (climate mitigation and adaptation). It deems the remaining four objectives non-material for current portfolios but plans best-efforts analysis from next year. Acknowledges interpretation and data limitations; cites the EC FAQ of 8 Nov 2024 that could not be incorporated this cycle and will be addressed in future reporting.
- Green Asset Ratio (GAR) methodology:
  - Definition: GAR measures the share of Taxonomy-aligned assets in total assets; key KPI under the Taxonomy.
  - Denominator (covered assets): Total assets minus sovereign, central bank, supranational exposures, and trading book.
  - Numerator scope: Applies technical criteria to selected products/counterparties; excludes certain items only from the numerator (e.g., companies not subject to the NFRD, derivatives, on-demand interbank loans), ensuring eligibility/alignment ratios are inherently below 100%.
  - Eligibility boundaries: Only activities with defined technical criteria are eligible; some sectors (e.g., farming) are currently out of scope.
  - Alignment rules: Specialized/project financing that meets criteria is treated as aligned; general-purpose loans rely on counterparties’ published alignment ratios. Each asset can align to only one environmental objective to avoid double counting.
  - Stepwise calculation flow: Total assets → covered assets (after exclusions) → assets analyzed for eligibility → Taxonomy-eligible assets (after removing non-eligible portions) → Taxonomy-aligned assets (after removing non-aligned portions), based on project- or counterparty-level indicators.
- Disclosures: Results of the analyses and required qualitative information are provided, with a commitment to refine future publications as data quality and regulatory guidance improve.
text:
2.6.1 Background and regulatory requirements of the European Green Taxonomy
The European  Green  Taxonomy  Regulation  (EU)  2020/852 dated  18 June  2020  defines sustainable economic activities  by
establishing substantial contribution technical criteria (CCS), for at least one of the environmental and Do No Significant
Harm  (DNSH) targets and five other targets.. In addition, the economic activity must meet Minimum Social Safeguards
(MSS) criteria  corresponding to compliance with international principles and conventions. 
The Green  Taxonomy  targets
Article 8 of the Taxonomy Regulation requires the publication
of indicators on how and to what extent the Bank’s
activities are associated with economic activities that qualify as
environmentally  sustainable. 
Commission  Delegated  Climate  Regulation (EU) 2021/2139
of 4 June 2021 establishes the technical screening criteria for
determining the conditions under which  an economic
activity  qualifies as contributing substantially  to the first or
second  target without causing significant harm to any of
the 
other four environmental targets. Similarly, Commission
Delegated Environment  Regulation  (EU)  2023/2486 of
27  June 2023  establishes the criteria applicable to the
other four targets.
This  new  sustainability  framework is  gradually being
incorporated into the Bank’s business model. Among other
things,  the framework of its green  loans and green issues
have been reviewed in light of these requirements.
In  addition, front-office teams have been made aware ofthe issues and equipped to help customers ensure that
their projects meet green criteria.
In 
line with the regulations, the Bank publishes information
on the alignment of its exposures with the first two targets (1).
We considered that the analysis of eligibility and
alignment 
with the last four targets did not present  a
material issue with regard to our portfolios. We will use
our best efforts to carry it out based on the data available
from next year.
The results of these analyses, together with all the qualitative
disclosures required  by the Taxonomy Regulation, are
described 
in this section. However, given the remaining
uncertainty with regard to the interpretation of certain
aspects of the Taxonomy Regulation and the unavailability
of actual data to assess the degree of Taxonomy eligibility
or alignment of certain assets, the information published
by La  Banque   Postale will be further clarified in future
publications.

On 8 November 2024, the European Commission  published an FAQ-style document clarifying certain provisions of the Taxonomy Regulation
(EU) 2020/852. For this fiscal year, the information provided that was not already planned for production could not be  taken into account due to delays.
The Bank
 is currently reviewing its reporting process in order to incorporate this  information at the next reporting date.

title: Alignment analysis principles
heading: 2.2.6.2 Alignment analysis principles
start_phrase: The GAR is the ratio of Green Taxonomy-aligned assets to total assets, and is the Taxonomy’s key performance indicator.
summary:
- Source and context: Excerpt from La Banque Postale’s 2024 Universal Registration Document (Sustainable performance – Environmental information) detailing EU Green Taxonomy alignment analysis and Green Asset Ratio (GAR) methodology and results.
- GAR definition and purpose: GAR measures the share of total assets aligned with the EU Green Taxonomy; it is the Taxonomy’s key KPI identifying investments in sustainable economic activities.
- Scope and calculation principles:
  - Denominator (covered assets): Total assets excluding exposures to sovereigns, central banks, supranationals, and the trading book.
  - Numerator: Assets meeting Taxonomy technical screening criteria among selected products/counterparties.
  - Scope differences: Certain exposures (e.g., companies not subject to NFRD, derivatives, on-demand interbank loans, some interbank loans) are excluded from the numerator or from eligibility analysis, ensuring eligible/aligned ratios are always below 100% (e.g., an SME wind farm loan cannot enter the numerator if the SME is outside NFRD scope).
  - Eligibility constraints: Only activities with specified technical criteria can be assessed; some (e.g., farming) are not yet Taxonomy-eligible.
  - Alignment rules: Specialized (project) financing aligned when it meets criteria; general purpose financing included based on counterparties’ published alignment ratios; each asset is aligned to only one environmental objective to avoid double counting.
- Process flow: Total assets → Covered assets → Assets analyzed for eligibility → Taxonomy‑eligible assets → Taxonomy‑aligned assets.
- Four-stage Taxonomy assessment:
  1) Eligibility (activity listed in the Taxonomy),
  2) Substantial contribution (to one of six environmental objectives),
  3) DNSH (no significant harm to the other five objectives),
  4) MSS (minimum social safeguards).
- Mandatory vs voluntary GAR:
  - Mandatory GAR: Asset-by-asset assessment without estimates, per regulation.
  - Voluntary GAR: Supplementary indicator with estimates and a slightly broader scope; includes special purpose SME green loans excluded from mandatory GAR; complemented by Pillar III ESG Table 10 on green products not in GAR.
- Portfolio-specific application principles:
  - Households – Real estate:
    - Mandatory: Uses actual energy use data and a physical risk model aligned with Pillar III ESG (for DNSH); MSS presumed met for French financing.
    - Voluntary: Uses estimated energy use from external data provider with the same risk model; MSS presumed met.
  - Other household loans (e.g., motor vehicles, home renovation): Included in eligibility per regulations where applicable, but generally excluded from alignment if treated as general purpose financing.
  - Corporates:
    - Special purpose financing: Mandatory uses actual client data; voluntary may use estimates or partial analysis (e.g., only substantial contribution).
    - General purpose financing: Mandatory collects alignment ratios published by NFRD-reporting counterparties.
- Methodology governance: Despite unresolved interpretive issues in the texts, the Bank developed an internal reference framework to operationalize the Taxonomy’s technical screening criteria.
- Reported outcome: As of 31 December 2024, the regulatory GAR is 5.7% (€10.3bn) based on turnover, mainly from energy‑efficient household real estate financing aligned with climate change mitigation; includes some general purpose financing where counterparties publish alignment indicators; level is stable versus 5.5% (31 Dec 2023) and 5.9% (30 Jun 2024).
text:
2.6.2
Alignment  analysis principles
Green  Asset  Ratio  (GAR) calculation  principles
The GAR is the ratio of Green  Taxonomy-aligned assets to total assets, and is the Taxonomy’s  key performance indicator.
It identifies  the proportion of the Bank’s total assets  invested  in sustainable  economic  activities.
* Non-Financial Reporting  Directive
Based  on total assets, the assets included in the GAR’s
numerator  are identified by applying the Green Taxonomy
technical  screening criteria to selected types of products
and  counterparties.
a) The  assets covered  by the analysis correspond to total
on-balance sheet assets minus sovereign, central bank
and  supranational exposures and the trading book.
These covered assets represent the GAR’s denominator.
b) Some  assets, such as exposures to companies not subject
to the Non-Financial Reporting Directive (NFRD) and
interbank 
loans, are only excluded from the numerator,
such that only certain exposures are analysed for Taxonomy
eligibility. 
Due to this difference in scope between the
GAR numerator and denominator, a bank’s Taxonomy-
eligible asset ratio and alignment ratio will always be less
than 100%. This is because the exposures concerned bythe 
exclusion rules will not be subjected to any alignment
analysis 
separately from the analysis of the assets’
environmental 
characteristics. For example, a loan to an
SME for the construction of a wind  farm could not be
included in the GAR’s numerator.
c)An activity qualifies for inclusion in the alignment analysis
provided 
that the technical criteria are specified in the
regulation. Certain activities, such as farming, do not qualify
as Taxonomy-eligible at this stage.
d)Among the Taxonomy-eligible assets, specialised financing
that meets the Taxonomy criteria is considered as aligned.
Loans 
qualified as general purpose financing are included
based on  the alignment ratios published by the
counterparties. An asset may only be considered as
aligned with a single environmental target to avoid it
being counted twice.

title: Alignment indicators - Introduction
heading: 2.2.6.3 Alignment indicators
start_phrase: At 31 December 2024, the Bank’s regulatory green asset ratio was 5.7% (€10.3 billion) based on turnover.
summary: Overview of La Banque Postale’s EU Taxonomy alignment metrics and methodology: at 31 Dec 2024 the regulatory Green Asset Ratio (GAR) was 5.7% (€10.3bn) based on turnover, mainly from energy‑efficient household real estate financing aligned to the climate change mitigation objective; some general purpose financing is included where counterparties’ alignment indicators exist. This is broadly stable versus 5.5% (31 Dec 2023) and 5.9% (30 Jun 2024). The Taxonomy assessment follows four stages: eligibility, substantial contribution, Do No Significant Harm (DNSH), and minimum social safeguards (MSS). Data limitations on existing technical reserves constrained alignment determinations, while new production data are captured at issuance; enhanced data collection is underway for real estate, asset, and project finance and integrated with broader ESG initiatives (Impact Weighting Factor, low‑carbon pathway, Equator Principles). Voluntary (non‑regulatory) GAR is 8.0% (€14.2bn; 2.3% voluntary component). Off‑balance sheet alignment ratios are 0.0% for financial guarantees and 3.0% for assets under management at LBP AM. Required Delegated Regulation (EU) 2021/2178 tables are presented, with exposures shown twice using counterparties’ turnover then CapEx alignment ratios; Green Taxonomy/Pillar III ESG Tables 6–8 are published once in the Green Taxonomy format, with insurance/asset management details in Section 2.5.1.7.

The GAR obtained from this financial year reflects the

To permit more detailed analyses in future  periods, data
collection efforts are being stepped up with a particular

basis, taking into  account participation in all the Bank’s

alignment ratios and then their CapEx ratios.

start_phrase: The following table presents the main key performance indicators (KPIs), as calculated using the information reported in the Taxonomy tables presented in Section 6.8.9.3. “Alignment indicators”.
summary:
- Focus on sustainable performance reporting in La Banque Postale’s 2024 Universal Registration Document, covering environmental (EU Taxonomy) and social (workforce) disclosures.
- Environmental information:
  - Green Asset Ratio (GAR) reflects limited reliable data for Taxonomy alignment on existing technical reserves; data is available for new production at issuance.
  - Enhanced data collection underway, prioritizing real estate loans, asset and project finance, aligned with broader ESG initiatives (Impact Weighting Factor, low‑carbon pathway, Equator Principles).
  - As of 31 Dec 2024: voluntary (non-regulatory) GAR at 8.0% (€14.2bn) based on turnover; off-balance sheet alignment ratios: 0.0% for financial guarantees, 3.0% for assets under management (LBP AM); further work to expand green asset coverage.
  - Reporting follows Delegated Regulation (EU) 2021/2178; exposures are presented using counterparties’ turnover and CapEx alignment ratios; insurance/asset management metrics detailed elsewhere.
  - Consolidated publication of overlapping Green Taxonomy and Pillar III ESG tables (6, 7, 8) in the most detailed Green Taxonomy format.
  - Summary KPIs provided under Article 8, including GAR (stock and flow), financial guarantees, and assets under management, with notes on KPI coverage, exclusions, and timelines (trading book and fee/commission KPIs effective from 2026; SME inclusion conditional; specific loan types included per regulation).
- Social information:
  - Scope covers La Banque Postale Group (banking, insurance, asset management). Many distribution employees are La Poste SA staff working “for and on behalf of” La Banque Postale and are treated as value chain workers, with HR management by La Poste SA.
  - Double materiality analysis identifies:
    - Potential negative impacts: harmful working conditions (stress, MSDs), discrimination/harassment, pay deterioration/job quality issues, and breaches of work-related rights.
    - Positive impacts: inclusion, equal opportunity, upskilling, career development, and favourable working conditions (hours, social dialogue, fair pay, protections).
  - Key risks/opportunities: HR compliance risks in employment, H&S, diversity/inclusion; opportunities via workforce skills development supporting innovation.
  - Emphasis on inclusion, diversity, and equal remuneration; strong social dialogue and “employee experience” central to strategy; 2025–2030 cultural transformation with a managerial model focused on efficiency and well‑being.
  - No climate adaptation risks identified for employees; a 2025 transition plan includes projects and training across business lines for 2025–2029.

start_phrase: La Banque Postale, a subsidiary of La Poste Group, is structured around a multi-business line organisation, which includes banking, insurance and asset management functions.
summary:

  - Negative impacts: harmful working conditions affecting physical/mental health (stress, burnout, MSDs); discrimination/inequality/harassment; potential deterioration in pay, employment levels or contract types reducing purchasing power; non-compliance with work-related rights under EU regulations.
  - Positive impacts: initiatives on inclusion, protection, equal opportunities, skills and career development; favourable working conditions (hours, social dialogue, fair pay, social protection, collective agreements).

  - Risks: potential failure in employment, health and safety, diversity and inclusion practices; heightened vigilance on diversity, inclusion and equal pay due to bancassurance model.

- Strategy and governance:
  - Emphasis on the employee experience, diversity and inclusion, strong social dialogue.
  - 2025–2030 strategic plan targets cultural transformation and a new managerial culture focused on efficiency and employee well-being.

title: Note on La Poste employees working for and on behalf of La Banque Postale
heading: Note on La Poste employees working for and on behalf of La Banque Postale
start_phrase: To develop its distribution activities, La Banque Postale relies on a network located in post offices and in remote customer relations centres (retail customers), and lastly on its business centres (professional customers).
summary:
- Focus: Social information on guaranteeing favorable working conditions for all employees within La Banque Postale Group (LBP), part of a multi-business bancassurance organization (banking, insurance, asset management).
- Scope: Workforce covered is LBP SA and its subsidiaries. A large portion of distribution activity is performed by La Poste SA employees (retail and business centers), classified as “value chain workers,” not part of LBP’s own workforce; their HR management and risk prevention are handled by La Poste SA. Details provided separately in Section 2.3.2.1.
- Material impacts, risks, and opportunities (IROs) from a double materiality analysis:
  - Negative impacts: harmful working conditions affecting physical/mental health (stress, burnout, MSDs); discrimination, inequality, harassment; potential deterioration in remuneration, job levels or contract types reducing purchasing power; non-compliance with work-related rights.
  - Positive impacts: actions supporting inclusion, protection, equal opportunity, skills and career development; favorable working conditions (working hours, social dialogue, fair pay, social protection, collective agreements).
- Sector-specific emphasis: Given bancassurance exposure, strict monitoring of inclusion, diversity, and equal remuneration. “Employee experience” is a strategic priority, aiming for strong working conditions, diversity and inclusion, and robust social dialogue.
- Risks and opportunities:
  - Risks: potential failure in employment, health and safety, diversity and inclusion practices; H&S risks seen as limited; higher risk around D&I, including wage inequality and discrimination.
  - Opportunities: upskilling employees to drive innovation and new product/service development; leveraging the mission-led company model and the 2025–2030 strategic plan to strengthen employment, D&I, and cultural transformation, including a project to evolve managerial culture toward efficiency and employee well-being.
- Climate aspect: No climate adaptation risk identified for employees; a 2025 transition plan includes projects and training across banking lines from 2025–2029 (referenced in Section 2.2.1).

title: IRO relating to the Group’s workforce
heading: 2.3.1.1.2 IRO relating to the Group’s workforce
start_phrase: Various positive and negative impacts, as well as risks and opportunities, relating to the Group’s workforce were identified during the double materiality analysis.
summary:
- Context: Social information section detailing how La Banque Postale (LBP) ensures favourable working conditions for all employees as part of its CSR approach.
- Scope: Reporting covers LBP SA and its subsidiaries. La Poste SA employees who work for and on behalf of LBP are not part of LBP’s own workforce; they are treated as “value chain workers” and covered elsewhere.
- Material IROs: Results of a double materiality analysis identifying workforce-related impacts, risks and opportunities.
- Negative impacts identified: harmful working conditions affecting physical/mental health (stress, burnout, MSDs); discrimination, inequality or harassment; potential deterioration in pay, jobs or contract types affecting purchasing power; non-compliance with EU work-related rights.
- Positive impacts identified: actions promoting inclusion, protection, equal opportunities, skills and career development; favourable working conditions (working hours, social dialogue, fair remuneration, social protection, collective agreements).
- Governance focus: Strong monitoring of inclusion, diversity and equal pay; “employee experience” is a strategic priority supported by a culture of social dialogue.
- Risks and opportunities: Risk of shortcomings in employment, health and safety, and diversity/inclusion practices; opportunity to develop employee skills that drive innovation and new products/services. Health and safety risks are limited for bancassurance, but D&I and pay inequality/discrimination risks require attention.
- Strategy: Mission-led company model seen as an opportunity for employment, diversity and inclusion; embedded in the 2025–2030 strategic plan aimed at cultural transformation and a new managerial culture focused on efficiency and well-being.
- Climate dimension: No specific climate adaptation risks identified for employees; a 2025 transition plan includes cross-business projects and training from 2025 to 2029.
text:
3.1.1.2 IRO  relating  to the Group’s  workforce
Various  positive and negative impacts, as well as risks and
opportunities, relating to the Group’s workforce were identified
during  the double materiality  analysis. Details concerning
these  IROs are  available in paragraph 2.1.3.2 “Description of
material impacts, risks and opportunities (IROs)”.
The following actual and potential negative impacts have
been identified:
•Working conditions that could harm the physical or mental
health  of employees  (stress,  burnout,  musculoskeletal
disorders);
•Cases of discrimination, inequality or harassment  in the
workplace, with negative consequences for employees;
•Deterioration  in remuneration levels, the number of jobs
or the  type of  contract leading to  a decrease in the
purchasing  power  of employees  (potential impact);
•Failure  to respect other work-related rights (covered by
European  regulations).  [S1_SBM_3_03]The following  actual and potential positive impacts have
been identified:
•Actions to promote inclusion, protection, equal opportunities,
skills  development and  professional development of
employees;
•Favourable working conditions for La Banque Postale Group
employees 
(working hours, social dialogue, fair remuneration
system, social  protection, collective agreements, etc.).
Due  to the  market exposure and the structure of
La  Banque  Postale Group’s bancassurance activities,
compliance 
with the  rules in terms of inclusion, diversity
and equal remuneration are specifically monitored to
minimise 
the negative impacts of its activities on
employees. The focus on the 'employee experience' is a
key component of La  Banque  Postale Group’s strategic
plan, 
demonstrated by real ambition in the areas of favourable
working 
conditions, both material and organisational and
respect for diversity and inclusion in the context of a strong
culture of social dialogue. [S1_SBM_3_04]
The risks and opportunities related to  the impacts and
dependencies identified are as follows:
•HR risk relating to the failure of the Group’s employment,
health and safety, diversity and  inclusion  practices;
•Development of the skills of the Company’s employees
promoting innovation and the creation of  new products
and services.
As a  player in the bancassurance sector, the risks of
La  Banque  Postale  Group’s health and safety practices
failing remain  limited.  However,  the  business  model  may
present risks in terms of  diversity and inclusion, including
wage  inequalities  and  risks of discrimination.
La  Banque  Postale Group’s  strategy of  being part of the
mission-led company business model is therefore an
opportunity in terms of employment, diversity and inclusion.
This 
opportunity forms part of the 2025-2030 strategic
plan, dedicated to the Company’s cultural transformation.
There 
is a special project in place to create a new managerial
culture, focused on efficiency and employee well-being.
[S1_SBM_3_05]
The Group has not identified any climate change adaptation
risk 
relating to its employees. Nevertheless, the Group's
transition plan, published in 2025, provides for projects for
all banking business lines – including training  – between
2025 and  2029.  For more information  on this plan, refer to
Section 2.2.1 “Combating and adapting to climate change
[E1]” . [S1_SBM_3_06]

heading: 2.3.1.1.2 IRO relating to the Group’s workforce
start_phrase: Various positive and negative impacts, as well as risks and opportunities, relating to the Group’s workforce were identified during the double materiality analysis.
summary:
- Scope and organization: La Banque Postale (LBP) Group—covering LBP SA and subsidiaries across banking, insurance, and asset management—is the perimeter for social reporting. Many frontline distribution roles are performed by La Poste SA employees, treated as “value chain workers” and addressed separately.
- Value chain workers: La Poste SA staff working on behalf of LBP are managed under La Poste’s HR strategy; their impacts, risks, and opportunities (IROs) are integrated there.
- Double materiality IROs for LBP’s own workforce: 
  - Negative impacts: risks to physical/mental health (stress, burnout, MSDs); discrimination/inequality/harassment; potential deterioration of pay, jobs, or contracts affecting purchasing power; non-compliance with work-related rights.
  - Positive impacts: inclusion, protection, equal opportunities; skills and career development; favourable working conditions (hours, social dialogue, fair pay, social protection, collective agreements).
- Risk and opportunity profile: Limited health and safety risks typical of bancassurance; higher focus on diversity, inclusion, and equal pay to prevent discrimination and wage gaps. Strategic emphasis on employee experience, strong social dialogue, and a cultural transformation (2025–2030) to build a managerial culture centered on efficiency and well-being. Skills development seen as a lever for innovation.
- Climate dimension: No specific employee climate-adaptation risk identified; 2025 transition plan includes cross-business projects and training through 2029.
- Forced and child labor: Assessed as not at risk; adherence to international labor standards; 88% of workforce in France/Europe where such risks are tightly regulated.
- Vulnerable groups: While job roles do not create higher H&S risk, older employees, ethnic minorities, and people with disabilities may face higher exposure to discrimination risks.
- Policy framework (covers permanent and fixed-term staff within LBP’s Economic and Social Unit and Group/subsidiaries):
  - Quality of Work Life and Working Conditions: comprehensive QWLWC and occupational risk prevention.
  - Diversity and Inclusion: disability, intergenerational diversity, gender parity, LGBT+ inclusion, social and ethnic inclusion; dedicated disability policy; anti-sexism/discrimination/harassment measures.
  - Health & Safety Prevention: risk assessments, accident analyses, workstation adjustments, traffic risk awareness, annual prevention plan.
  - Remuneration: fairness and equal pay (notably gender), recognition of performance, support for professional development.
  - Employee Experience: career progression, daily work-life improvements, commitment to a just transition.
  - Social Dialogue: strong framework for employee representation and consideration of employee interests.
  - Training: skills development aligned with the Group’s strategic plan.
text:
3.1.1.2 IRO  relating  to the Group’s  workforce
Various  positive and negative impacts, as well as risks and
opportunities, relating to the Group’s workforce were identified
during  the double materiality  analysis. Details concerning
these  IROs are  available in paragraph 2.1.3.2 “Description of
material impacts, risks and opportunities (IROs)”.
The following actual and potential negative impacts have
been identified:
•Working conditions that could harm the physical or mental
health  of employees  (stress,  burnout,  musculoskeletal
disorders);
•Cases of discrimination, inequality or harassment  in the
workplace, with negative consequences for employees;
•Deterioration  in remuneration levels, the number of jobs
or the  type of  contract leading to  a decrease in the
purchasing  power  of employees  (potential impact);
•Failure  to respect other work-related rights (covered by
European  regulations).  [S1_SBM_3_03]The following  actual and potential positive impacts have
been identified:
•Actions to promote inclusion, protection, equal opportunities,
skills  development and  professional development of
employees;
•Favourable working conditions for La Banque Postale Group
employees 
(working hours, social dialogue, fair remuneration
system, social  protection, collective agreements, etc.).
Due  to the  market exposure and the structure of
La  Banque  Postale Group’s bancassurance activities,
compliance 
with the  rules in terms of inclusion, diversity
and equal remuneration are specifically monitored to
minimise 
the negative impacts of its activities on
employees. The focus on the 'employee experience' is a
key component of La  Banque  Postale Group’s strategic
plan, 
demonstrated by real ambition in the areas of favourable
working 
conditions, both material and organisational and
respect for diversity and inclusion in the context of a strong
culture of social dialogue. [S1_SBM_3_04]
The risks and opportunities related to  the impacts and
dependencies identified are as follows:
•HR risk relating to the failure of the Group’s employment,
health and safety, diversity and  inclusion  practices;
•Development of the skills of the Company’s employees
promoting innovation and the creation of  new products
and services.
As a  player in the bancassurance sector, the risks of
La  Banque  Postale  Group’s health and safety practices
failing remain  limited.  However,  the  business  model  may
present risks in terms of  diversity and inclusion, including
wage  inequalities  and  risks of discrimination.
La  Banque  Postale Group’s  strategy of  being part of the
mission-led company business model is therefore an
opportunity in terms of employment, diversity and inclusion.
This 
opportunity forms part of the 2025-2030 strategic
plan, dedicated to the Company’s cultural transformation.
There 
is a special project in place to create a new managerial
culture, focused on efficiency and employee well-being.
[S1_SBM_3_05]
The Group has not identified any climate change adaptation
risk 
relating to its employees. Nevertheless, the Group's
transition plan, published in 2025, provides for projects for
all banking business lines – including training  – between
2025 and  2029.  For more information  on this plan, refer to
Section 2.2.1 “Combating and adapting to climate change
[E1]” . [S1_SBM_3_06]Please  see the glossary  on page 808 for definitions of the main CSR terms 2024 Universal  Registration Document     La Banque Postale 1672Sustainable performance
Social information

title: Policies regarding quality of life and working conditions
heading: 2.3.1.2.1 Policies regarding quality of life and working conditions
start_phrase: The policies presented below respond directly to positive impacts concerning favourable working conditions for the Group’s own workforce, negative impacts concerning working conditions that harm the physical or mental health of employees, and risks related to the quality of life at work and working conditions of employees.
summary:
- Outlines La Banque Postale Group’s Quality of Work Life and Working Conditions (QWLWC) policy: workload regulation, protection of physical and mental health, work-life balance, and tackling information overload, delivered through a multidisciplinary, indicator-driven, continuous improvement approach with broad stakeholder involvement.
- Confirms compliance with French Labour Code and sector agreements; details a QWLWC agreement signed on 11 Sept 2023 with trade unions, published for all employees, and monitored annually; notes CNP Assurances’ parallel QWLWC agreement and international diversity and inclusion governance.
- Describes the employee skills policy and Group training framework supporting the Strategic Plan: career‑long upskilling, onboarding, transformation support, and mandatory/regulatory training (EU/national banking, GDPR, RGAA), with plans co-built by business lines and HR and validated across the Group.
- Lists HR’s core missions: recruiting and onboarding, skills assessment, career path management, professional development, and talent development.
- States four HR policy principles: co-constructed career management, cross-entity mobility within La Banque Postale/La Poste ecosystem, talent acquisition, and managerial development.
- Details the remuneration policy’s governance (Executive and Supervisory Boards; HR Director) and principles: fairness and transparency, market alignment and internal consistency, gender pay equality, recognition of long‑term individual and collective performance, alignment with long‑term Group objectives, and support for internal mobility and career advancement.
text:
3.1.2.1 Policies  regarding quality of life 
and working conditions
The policies presented below respond directly  to positive
impacts concerning favourable working conditions for the
Group’s 
own workforce, negative impacts concerning working
conditions  that harm the physical or mental health of
employees, and risks related to  the quality of life at work
and working  conditions of  employees.
The Quality of Work Life and Working Conditions (QWLWC)
policy has been implemented by the Human Resources
Department for the companies of La  Banque  Postale's
Economic  and Social Unit (UES), and meets the following
targets:
•Define  and implement a global QWLWC approach for
all stakeholders in the Company, based on the following
topics:
•Work 
content: streamlining the organisation and working
methods in order to promote workload regulation;
•Prevention and health at work: protecting the physical
and mental  health of employees;
•Work  relations : facilitating work-life balance;
•tackling information overload (infobesity);
•Create  a multi-disciplinary approach to the primary
prevention  of occupational risks, in order to protect the
physical and mental health and safety of employees
and,  more generally, contribute to their well-being at
work,  broken  down  into  various phases:
•Analyse  and objectify situations  by relying specifically
on indicators;
•Build the approach by involving the various stakeholders;
•Involve  all stakeholders in the Company in QWLWC
issues;
•Use trial and error as part of a continuous improvement
approach;
•Monitor the actions implemented  and  progress made;
•Promote  good work relationships at every stage of
employees’  professional lives by  making integration a
driver of alignment with the Company's values and culture
and by ensuring a work-life balance throughout their career.
These provisions are in line with the legal and regulatory
framework  laid down  in particular by the  French Labour
Code, as well as by any regulations applicable in the business
segment, via the  French National Collective  Agreement
on Banking for La  Banque  Postale and other branch
agreements  for the  business  segments of each entity.
After  in-depth  negotiations,  the QWLWC agreement  was
signed on 11 September 2023 by three representative trade
unions. The provisions are published on the intranet, and
are accessible to  all employees.  An annual commission
monitors  the QWLWC agreement. This enables both the
stakeholders who have contributed to its drafting and are
responsible for its implementation, and the social partners,
to monitor  the proper implementation of the agreement.
In addition, CNP  Assurances has a QWLWC agreement
that  addresses  the level of  employee  engagement  and
well-being.  It is therefore committed to structuring and
organising 
diversity and inclusion initiatives and stakeholders
by setting up  diversity and inclusion governance at the
international  level, including for its subsidiaries. [S1_1_01]
[S1_MDR_P_01_06]2.

title: Employee skills policy
heading: 2.3.1.2.2 Employee skills policy
start_phrase: The policies presented in this paragraph aim to reinforce the positive impacts and opportunities of upskilling employees.
summary:
- Focus: CSR social information detailing La Banque Postale Group’s employee-related policies on quality of work life and working conditions (QWLWC), skills development, and remuneration, aimed at enhancing positive impacts (well‑being, upskilling) and mitigating risks (health, work conditions, pay deterioration).

- QWLWC policy:
  - Objectives: workload regulation; protection of physical and mental health; work–life balance; reducing information overload; fostering good work relationships across the employee lifecycle.
  - Approach: multidisciplinary primary risk prevention; data-driven analysis with indicators; broad stakeholder involvement; test-and-learn continuous improvement; monitoring of actions and progress.
  - Governance and compliance: aligned with French Labour Code and sectoral collective agreements; QWLWC agreement signed 11 Sept 2023 by three representative unions; provisions published on intranet; annual commission oversees implementation.
  - Group scope: CNP Assurances has a QWLWC agreement emphasizing engagement and well‑being, and sets international diversity and inclusion governance across subsidiaries.

- Employee skills policy:
  - Purpose: support the Group’s Strategic Plan through upskilling and continuous learning across the employee journey (onboarding, transformation support, new offerings).
  - Coverage: continuous, regulatory, and mandatory trainings (EU/national banking standards, GDPR, RGAA).
  - Process: skills development plan co-built by business lines and HR, validated and shared across the Group.
  - HR missions and principles: recruit and onboard, assess skills, manage careers, promote development and potential; four pillars—co‑constructed career management, cross-entity mobility within La Banque Postale/La Poste ecosystem, talent acquisition, and managerial development.

- Remuneration policy:
  - Governance: approved by Executive and Supervisory Boards; implemented by the HR Director.
  - Principles and targets: recognition of performance, fairness, transparency; fair pay based on expertise, tenure, experience with market benchmarking and internal equity; gender pay equality; recognition of long-term individual and collective performance; alignment of behaviors with long-term Group goals; support for internal mobility and career advancement to build long-term commitment.
text:
3.1.2.2 Employee skills policy
The policies presented in this paragraph aim to reinforce
the positive impacts and opportunities of upskilling employees.
The La Banque Postale Group training policy, implemented
by the Human Resources Department, aims to contribute
to the success of the Group’s Strategic Plan by implementing
skills development plans for employees working within or
on behalf  of the Group.
The training policy defines the rules relating to the
development of employees’ skills throughout their professional
career (starting a new role, support during transformations
to gain new skills and knowledge of the Company’s new
offers). The development of employee skills also includes
continuous training, and regulatory and mandatory training
(European and national  regulatory  banking standards,
GDPR, French  RGAA  law).
The skills development plan is created in collaboration
with La  Banque  Postale’s business lines and the human
resources teams that  support them.  It is  validated, shared
and managed with all Group departments.
The Human Resources Department therefore carries out
fundamental missions for the entire La  Banque  Postale
UES,  which include: recruiting and onboarding,  assessing
skills, managing career paths, promoting professional
development 
and developing potential, with the aim of
being attentive to all its employees. It articulates its
human resources policy around four principles:
•career  management  co-constructed by the company
and the employee;
•decompartmentalised pathways between La Banque Postale,
financial 
services, the  La  Poste Network and La Poste
Group;
•recruiting new talent;
•managerial development. [S1_1_01]  [S1_MDR_P_01_06]
2.

title: Employee Remuneration policy
heading: 2.3.1.2.3 Employee Remuneration policy
start_phrase: Remuneration policies aim to prevent and mitigate the negative impacts of the Group regarding a potential deterioration in remuneration levels, the number of jobs or the type of contract for employees.
summary:
- Overview: The excerpt outlines La Banque Postale Group’s social policies aimed at enhancing quality of life at work, safeguarding health and safety, developing employee skills, ensuring fair remuneration, and promoting diversity and inclusion across the Group and its subsidiaries.

- Quality of Work Life and Working Conditions (QWLWC):
  - Implemented by HR for La Banque Postale’s Economic and Social Unit (UES); aligned with French Labour Code and sector agreements.
  - Objectives: global QWLWC approach covering work content (workload regulation), prevention and health (physical/mental), work relations and work-life balance, and tackling information overload.
  - Method: multidisciplinary primary risk prevention—indicator-based analysis, co-building with stakeholders, broad involvement, continuous improvement, action monitoring.
  - Focus on good work relationships throughout careers; onboarding as a cultural alignment lever.
  - 2023 QWLWC agreement signed with three representative unions; published on intranet; annual commission monitors implementation.
  - CNP Assurances has a parallel QWLWC agreement and international D&I governance.

- Employee Skills Policy:
  - Training policy supports the Strategic Plan via skills development plans for all Group employees.
  - Covers onboarding, support during transformations, continuous learning, and mandatory/regulatory training (e.g., banking standards, GDPR, RGAA).
  - Skills plan co-built with business lines and HR; validated and shared across departments.
  - HR core missions: recruitment/onboarding, skills assessment, career path management, professional development, potential development.
  - Four HR principles: co-constructed career management; cross-entity mobility (La Banque Postale, financial services, La Poste Network, La Poste Group); talent recruitment; managerial development.

- Remuneration Policy:
  - Approved by Executive and Supervisory Boards; implemented by HR; based on performance recognition, fairness, transparency.
  - Aims: fair pay reflecting expertise, tenure, market and internal equity; gender pay equality; recognition of long-term individual/collective performance; alignment with long-term goals; career development to foster commitment.
  - Published on intranet; compliant with labor law and collective agreements.
  - Subsidiaries tailor policies to local/sector regulations.
  - CNP Assurances’ policy aligns with strategic, financial and non-financial objectives, ensures fairness and gender equality; each subsidiary drafts its own policy with HR oversight.
  - Louvre Banque Privée has remuneration and professional equality agreements.

- Health and Safety:
  - 2024 prevention plan validated by the Health, Safety and Working Conditions Commission (HSWCC):
    - Continue/adapt occupational risk assessments specific to La Banque Postale.
    - Analyze lost-time accidents using the “5 Whys” method.
    - Implement workstation adjustments recommended by occupational health.
    - Raise awareness of road safety risks.
  - QWLWC collective agreement integrated into UES development strategy; complements prior agreements (diversity, remote work).
  - Subsidiary measures: CNP’s QWLWC agreement; Louvre Banque Privée safety booklet; Louvre Banque Privée Immobilier Conseil DUERP.
  - Strengthened prevention via multidisciplinary impact assessments for transformation projects; three national HSWC committees held in 2023 plus monitoring of the “Réussir Ensemble” agreement.

- Diversity and Inclusion (D&I):
  - Policy renewed every three years via social agreement; implemented by HR for all UES employees; shared internally and externally.
  - Five pillars: Disability (RQTH recruitment and recognition), Generations (youth entry, older worker retention, intergenerational diversity), Parity (gender equality and governance parity, anti-sexism), LGBT+ inclusion, Social/Ethnic origins (fairness across the employee lifecycle).
  - Built with experts, charities, HR, and employees.
  - Covers all legally defined discrimination grounds (26 to date), including sex, gender, age, and disability.
text:
3.1.2.3 Employee Remuneration policy
Remuneration policies aim to prevent and mitigate the
negative impacts of the Group regarding a potential
deterioration in remuneration levels, the number of jobs
or the type of  contract for employees.
La Banque Postale Group’s remuneration policy is approved
by the Executive Board and the Supervisory Board and
implemented by the Human Resources Director, and is
based  on the values of  performance recognition, fairness
and transparency. It  meets the following targets:
•Ensure  that employees  receive  fair remuneration  for
their work, based on their expertise, length of service
and professional experience, taking  into  account market
benchmarks and the need for internal consistency;
•Respect gender equality in terms of remuneration;
•Recognise long-term individual and collective performance;
•Ensure that employee behaviours are consistent with
La Banque Postale Group’s  long-term targets; and
•Promote internal  professional development  and career
advancement to encourage long-term commitment
from employees.Please  see the glossary  on page 808 for definitions of the main CSR terms 2024 Universal  Registration Document     La Banque Postale 1692Sustainable performance
Social information
The remuneration policy  is published on the intranet and
accessible  to all employees. It complies strictly with
the regulatory framework applicable to its various business
segments, with  labour  legislation, collective bargaining
agreements and various Company agreements.
Each   subsidiary establishes its remuneration policy by
applying 
the guiding principles of the Group’s remuneration
policy, and taking into account local and sectoral regulations.
CNP 
Assurances'  remuneration policy aims to attract, retain,
motivate and recognise the contribution of employees  to
the Company’s development. It is consistent with the
strategic 
guidance and targets, performance and expected
financial  and  non-financial results.
This policy is implemented by general management, managed
operationally  by the Human  Resources  Department, and
supported  and deployed by all managers in each
CNP  Group entity.  It forms part of  a corporate  culture that
ensures  respect for fairness  within the company and
gender equality, in conjunction with the insurance market
and  the financial  sector.
The policy is governed by labour legislation, collective
bargaining agreements and various company agreements
and  thus  ensures  an adequate wage  for all employees.
Each  subsidiary drafts its own  remuneration policy, in
coordination with the CNP Assurances Human Resources
Department  and  taking into account  local regulations.
Louvre  Banque Privée also has a remuneration  policy and
a professional equality agreement to prevent negative
impacts  on its employees. [S1_1_01] [S1_MDR_P_01_06]
2.

title: Health and safety policies
heading: 2.3.1.2.4 Health and safety policies
start_phrase: The policies presented below aim to prevent and mitigate negative impacts on working conditions that could harm the physical or mental health of employees.
summary:
- Context: Excerpt from La Banque Postale’s 2024 Universal Registration Document (Sustainable performance – Social information).
- Remuneration policy:
  - Published on the intranet, accessible to all employees, and strictly compliant with applicable regulations, labor law, collective bargaining, and company agreements.
  - Group-wide guiding principles applied by subsidiaries, adapted to local/sectoral rules.
  - CNP Assurances’ policy aims to attract, retain, motivate, and recognize employees, aligned with strategic, financial, and non-financial objectives; implemented by management/HR and deployed by managers; ensures fairness, gender equality, and adequate wages.
  - Louvre Banque Privée has its own remuneration policy and a professional equality agreement to prevent negative impacts on employees.
- Health and safety:
  - Policies aim to prevent/mitigate risks to physical and mental health and ensure employee safety.
  - 2024 prevention plan (HR/HSWCC) focuses on: continuing LBP-specific risk assessments; analyzing lost-time accidents with the “5 Whys”; workstation adjustments via occupational health; road safety awareness.
  - A Quality of Work Life and Working Conditions (QWLWC) agreement signed for La Banque Postale UES, integrating into corporate strategy and complementing prior agreements (diversity, equality, remote work). Other subsidiaries maintain their own QWLWC/safety frameworks (e.g., CNP’s QWLWC agreement, Louvre Banque Privée’s safety booklet, DUERP for Louvre Banque Privée Immobilier Conseil).
  - Strengthened workplace prevention processes via multidisciplinary assessments of transformation projects, proactive change-risk management, and prevention plans; three national HSWC committees held in 2023 alongside “Réussir Ensemble” agreement monitoring.
- Diversity and inclusion:
  - Policy redefined every three years via a social agreement, implemented by HR and applicable across La Banque Postale UES.
  - Built with experts, charities, HR, and employees; communicated internally and externally.
  - Five pillars: disability (hiring and recognition), generations (youth entry and senior retention), parity (gender equality and balanced governance), LGBT+ inclusion, and social/ethnic origins (fairness across the employee lifecycle).
  - Covers all legally recognized discrimination grounds (26), including sex, gender, age, and disability.
text:
3.1.2.4 Health and  safety policies
The policies presented below aim  to prevent and mitigate
negative  impacts  on working  conditions  that  could harm
the physical or mental health  of employees.  They also
relate to employee  safety risks.
The 2024 annual prevention plan presented by the
Human 
Resources Department and validated by the Health,
Safety and  Working Conditions Commission  (HSWCC)
focuses on four areas:
•pursuing and adapting the occupational risk assessment
process  specif ic to La Banque  Postale ;
•analysing lost-time  accidents using the “5 Whys” technique;
•continuing  to make workstation  adjustments requested
by the occupational health office;
•raising  employee  awareness about  road  safety  risks.
In addition, a collective agreement on QWLWC was
signed by La Banque Postale UES and the social partners.
The purpose of this agreement is to implement an
ambitious 
QWLWC policy, which  is an integral  part of the
development  strategy of  the La Banque  Postale  Economic
and  Social Unit (UES).  Through this agreement, the
companies of  La  Banque  Postale ’s Economic and Social
Unit  wish to affirm and supplement the actions already
undertaken  under  previous  agreements (diversity and
professional  equality, working from home, etc.).The other La Banque Postale subsidiaries have their own
QWLWC  agreement. For example, CNP Assurances has a
QWLWC  agreement, Louvre  Banque  Privée has a safety
booklet 
and Louvre  Banque Privée Immobilier Conseil has
a Single Risk Assessment Document (DUERP).
The Prevention, Health and Safety in the Workplace
process was also strengthened with the introduction of
multidisciplinary  assessments of the impacts of  the
transformation projects. Therefore, the Group has been able
to 
proactively manage change-related risks and recommend
prevention plans to support employees. Operational
feedback has  also  been streamlined . Th erefore, three
national committees dedicated to the prevention of health,
safety and working conditions (HSWC) were held in 2023,
in addition to the committees monitoring the “Réussir
Ensemble
” (Succeeding Together) social agreement. [S1_1_09]
2.

title: Diversity and inclusion policies and commitments
heading: 2.3.1.2.5 Diversity and inclusion policies and commitments
start_phrase: The policies presented in this paragraph respond to the positive and negative impacts and risks related to diversity and inclusion.
summary:
- Scope and context: Excerpt from La Banque Postale’s 2024 Universal Registration Document (Sustainable performance – Social information), with references to CSR glossary and indicators.
- Remuneration policies: Group-wide, compliant with regulations, labor law, and collective agreements; published on the intranet and accessible to all employees. Subsidiaries set policies aligned with Group principles and local rules. CNP Assurances’ policy is tied to strategic goals and performance (financial and non-financial), implemented by management and HR, promoting fairness and gender equality. Louvre Banque Privée has a remuneration policy and a professional equality agreement.
- Health and safety (QWLWC) policies: Annual prevention plan validated by the HSWCC focusing on occupational risk assessment, “5 Whys” analysis of lost-time accidents, workstation adjustments, and road safety awareness. A QWLWC agreement was signed for La Banque Postale UES; other subsidiaries have their own instruments (CNP Assurances QWLWC agreement; Louvre Banque Privée safety booklet; Louvre Banque Privée Immobilier Conseil DUERP). Strengthened change management via multidisciplinary impact assessments and prevention plans; national HSWC committees held in 2023 alongside monitoring of the “Réussir Ensemble” agreement.
- Diversity and inclusion commitments: A triannual Diversity & Inclusion policy led by HR for La Banque Postale UES, covering all 26 legal discrimination grounds and built with experts, NGOs, and employees. Five pillars: disability, generations, gender parity, LGBT+, and social/ethnic origins; policy shared internally and externally.
- Disability policy: Under the sixth social agreement (27 March 2023), systematic recruitment of RQTH candidates on equal skills and incentives for RQTH declarations; applies across UES and banking functions, developed with AFMD and Entreprise pour la Cité. Two major, triannually renewed social agreements—Disability, and Diversity & Professional Equality—evidence long-term commitment.
- Subsidiary initiatives: CNP Assurances’ QWLWC agreement ensures equal treatment based on skills and performance; code of conduct on preventing discrimination/harassment; signatory of the Diversity Charter since 2006; Inclusion Committee (since 2021) to steer and monitor action plans and complaints mechanisms. Louvre Banque Privée has agreements on professional equality and quality of work life.
- Group-wide inclusion actions: Commitments include base agreements, a gender parity indicator for the mission-led company, partnerships with charities, and an Executive Committee–endorsed diversity strategy. Annual action plans cover gender parity (webinars, violence against women conference), pay streamlining with a new package, disability initiatives (Health & Disability Week, European Disability Employment Week, 10 disability officers, workstation adjustments, awareness web series), and broader diversity actions (webinars, managerial support for inclusion cases, mentoring, surveys on everyday sexism/LGBT+, sponsorship, executive advocacy). Over 30 events yearly and five D&I training courses (one mandatory) offered with La Poste Group.
- Reporting and whistleblowing: Established channels for victims or witnesses of discrimination, with processing and system governance referenced elsewhere in the document.
- Human rights policy: La Banque Postale Group aligns with La Poste Group’s Human Rights policy and the UN Global Compact, referencing the UDHR, UN Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights, ILO Declaration and core conventions, and OECD Guidelines, aiming to prevent and mitigate human rights risks, particularly within its own workforce.
