text:
3.2.3.1
Material IROs and links with strategy and
business model
Scope
La Banque Postale considers that all workers in the value
chain  may be  subject to material impacts, through the
financed  entities  or projects.  [S2_SBM_3_02]
As La  Banque  Postale Group’s financing activities are
mainly carried out by the subsidiaries CNP  Assurances,
LBP   AM and Louvre  Banque  Privée, the ESRS points will
mainly  be covered  through the  lens of these entities.Description of how impacts on workers in the value  
chain  result  from, and shape, the Company’s 
strategy and business model
The 
social and environmental targets enshrined in the
Group’s Articles of Association constitute a real
governance tool for La   Banque  Postale, taking into
account 
its direct and indirect societal and environmental
impacts, which are reflected in its  offer policy.
La Banque Postale has also defined topical commitments
in terms of biodiversity, climate and human rights, which
feed 
into its approach with regard to its own operations as
well as its Corporate and Investment Banking activities. It
also 
develops policies to control risks and principles of
intervention for sectors and activities identified as high-
risk in terms of exposure  to ESG issues.
La  Banque  Postale therefore takes into consideration
the actual and potential impacts on workers  in the
value chain of its portfolio companies. To do this, it
assesses companies and issuers using the Impact
Weighting Factor and manages ESG controversies (for
more information on the IWF, see focus point: The Impact
Weighting Factor  (IWF)).
These topics are taken into consideration but do not
directly 
shape La Banque Postale’s strategy and business
model.  [S2_SBM_3_11]
La  Banque  Postale does not identify any significant
opportunities arising from the impact on workers in the
value chain.
The risk of financial loss  related to a failure in the
assessment of the Group’s partners (financed activities), in
a context of transition  to a fairer and  more inclusive
society, in particular in the event of a failure in the working
conditions 
of the companies in the portfolio, is identified
as material for La Banque  Postale .
This risk arises from the fact that La  Banque   Postale’s
asset management activity is not limited to a single
geographic area and is  multi-sectoral.
This risk  is identified  as material in the risk map.  [S2_SBM_3_12]
Risks  of forced  labou r and child labour
The Group has  an indirect exposure to forced labour and
child labour in its financed activities, primarily  through its
asset management portfolios. By way of example, as a
management 
company, LBP AM invests, through various
instruments, 
in thousands of  companies, themselves
belonging to many sectors and geographies, which
present specific human rights risks. The risks of human
rights 
impacts related to investment  activities, including
risks related to workers  in the value chains of  the invested
companies, are therefore multiple and of variable
intensity,  the main risk being that an invested company
causes, contributes or  is linked to  a critical impact on
human rights. Nevertheless, in 2023, LBP  AM carried out
an 
initial mapping exercise of salient human rights risks
related 
to investment activities, based on the
recommendations of the OECD and the United Nations
on the application of the UNGP  and the OECD Guidelines.
This analysis was disclosed, specifying in particular the
methodology used and the results obtained, and is
available 
on the LBP  AM institutional website. The most
critical 
risk identified for workers in the downstream value
chain  is the risk of a violation of fundamental workers’
rights. 
[S2_SBM_3_04]204 La Banque  Postale      2024 Universal Registration  Document Please see the glossary on page 808 for definitions of  the main CSR terms2Sustainable performance
Social information
Material  impacts,  risks and opportunities
The main negative impacts identified in the double
materiality 
analysis are related to possible degraded working
conditions,  and situations  of forced  labour or  child labour
within companies in the credit/investment portfolio.
[S2_SBM_3_05]
The 
main positive impacts identified in the double materiality
analysis are related to the improvement of working
conditions,  diversity  and inclusion within the companies  in
the investment portfolio through minimum requirements,
training, encouraging the signing of charters etc. [S2_SBM_3_06]
The risk of financial loss related to a failure to assess the
Group’s partners (financed  activities), and in particular a
failure  in the working conditions of the companies in the
portfolio, was identified as material.
For LBP  AM, the risk related to invested companies’
human 
rights practices may result in an impact on these
companies (financial, legal,  reputational or operational)
that may  subsequently  have an impact on  the value  of the
investment. Conversely, good  value chain management
and incorporating human rights  into the Company’s
operational  policies and  procedures can reduce  ESG  risk,
or even increase the value of the  invested issuers and
companies.
Louvre  Banque Privée  could also suffer a reputational risk
(with regard to its customers) and a risk of a decline in the
valuation 
of shares in customer portfolios. This risk is moderate
because 
they are most often liquid securities, which
Louvre  Banque  Privée can  sell quickly in the event of an
identified breach. In addition, the investable scope (large
European  companies/listed companies) is less exposed to
the risk of breach than unlisted or non-European companies.
[S2_SBM_3_07]
In 2024, as part of its Responsible  Financing and Investment
Charter, La   Banque   Postale implemented a controversy
management  process. La  Banque   Postale is therefore
committed  to ensuring that  its business  customers  or
prospects are not subject to severe or repeated ESG
controversies. Specifically, La  Banque  Postale includes
human rights violations and  violations of  fundamental
rights,  including those relating to work, in its definition of
severe  ESG controversies. The UN Guiding Principles,
the  International  Labour Organization Conventions on
fundamental principles and rights at work and  the OECD
Guidelines for Multinational Enterprises  serve  as guiding
frameworks.  La  Banque  Postale uses this reference base
to identify  the  groups of workers  who  may be exposed to
a higher risk of harm. Therefore, La  Banque  Postale pays
particular  attention to child labour, forced labour, migrant
labour, 
work in conflict zones and precarious work. Human
rights  and workers’ rights are assured without direct
interaction  with the  at-risk  parties mentioned. [S2_SBM_3_08]
La Banque  Postale recognises the vulnerability of  certain
groups  of workers in the value chain and takes into
account  the impacts on  vulnerable workers. However,
La Banque  Postale has no  direct  impact  on the workers  in
the value chain of the companies in its portfolio. [S2_SBM_3_09]2.3.2.3.2

title: Applicable policies
heading: 2.3.2.3.2 Applicable policies
start_phrase: La Banque Postale’s Responsible Financing and Investment Charter aims, among other things, to minimise and prevent the negative impacts of degraded working conditions and cases of forced labour or child labour in portfolio companies.
summary:
- Focus area: Social information within La Banque Postale’s 2024 Universal Registration Document, centered on human rights and working conditions across credit and investment portfolios.
- Double materiality findings: 
  - Main negative impacts: degraded working conditions and risks of forced or child labor in portfolio companies.
  - Main positive impacts: improved working conditions, diversity, and inclusion via minimum requirements, training, and charters.
  - Material risks: financial loss from inadequate partner assessment; human rights issues potentially affecting investee value; moderate reputational/valuation risk for Louvre Banque Privée mitigated by liquid, large-cap European exposure.
- 2024 controversy management: A new process under the Responsible Financing and Investment Charter screens for severe or repeated ESG controversies, explicitly including human and labor rights, guided by UN Guiding Principles, ILO conventions, and OECD Guidelines. Priority risk groups include child, forced, migrant, conflict-zone, and precarious workers; the Group notes no direct interaction with these workers.
- Applicable policies and exclusions:
  - La Banque Postale: Responsible Financing and Investment Charter as the main tool for ESG controversy detection and management; exclusion list aligned with sustainable development, health, and well-being.
  - CNP Assurances: Country exclusions based on Freedom House and Transparency International; excludes UN Global Compact violators and companies tied to tobacco and prohibited/controversial weapons.
  - LBP AM: SFDR-aligned methodology for Article 8 and 9 products with minimum thresholds, “do no significant harm” checks on human rights, and standards-based exclusions across funds to prevent/mitigate negative human rights impacts.
  - Louvre Banque Privée: ESG Charter aligned with international standards, screening for serious controversies and violations of UN Global Compact/OECD Guidelines.
- Compliance and commitments: No reported non-compliance with UN Guiding Principles or ILO Declaration involving downstream workers. Group-level Human Rights policies (La Poste Group, CNP Assurances, LBP AM) reaffirm commitments; Louvre Banque Privée limits investments to France/Europe to reduce exposure.
- Dialogue mechanisms: No direct engagement with workers in financed value chains due to scale and diversity of holdings; a global worker interaction system is not currently feasible.
- Reporting and remediation: In line with OECD expectations, investors are directly linked to investee impacts and should influence companies to prevent/mitigate harms; responsibility to remedy lies with companies causing or contributing to impacts. LBP AM uses stewardship to support remedies. The Group relies on investee reporting and commitments and maintains whistleblowing protections that prevent reprisals against employees of financed entities.
text:
Applicable policies
La Banque Postale’s Responsible Financing and Investment
Charter 
aims, among other things, to minimise and prevent
the negative  impacts of degraded working conditions and
cases of forced labour or child labour in portfolio companies.
This Charter describes the management of ESG controversies
implemented by La  Banque  Postale, and serves as the
main 
tool for detecting negative  impacts in the event of
poor working conditions, violations of human rights and
workers’  rights throughout the value chain of companies
in the credit  and investment portfolio, for all business
sectors and regions.
In addition to dealing with controversies, La Banque Postale
uses an exclusion list to pay particular attention to activities
that 
are incompatible with the targets of sustainable
development, 
health and well-being for all. For more
information, 
see focus point: La Banque Postale's Financing
and Investment Charter.
CNP 
Assurances relies on the lists drawn up by Freedom
House and  Transparency International  to exclude more
than  100 countries posing serious problems with regard to
democracy,  human rights and corruption. In addition,
CNP  Assurances excludes companies that do not comply
with 
the fundamental principles of the United Nations
Global Compact, or  are involved in the production of
tobacco or controversial and prohibited weapons such as
cluster 
munitions and anti-personnel mines,  or chemical
or biological  weapons.
LBP AM is subject to the implementation of the European
Sustainable Finance Disclosure Regulation (SFDR). Human
Rights issues are integrated into asset selection through
minimum sustainable investment thresholds, established
for Article 8 and Article 9 products. In order to ensure that
an investment contributing to a sustainability target
within the meaning of SFDR does no significant  harm to
any socially sustainable investment target, LBP   AM has
established a sustainability methodology ensuring systematic
verification  of the issuer’s human rights practices, the
issuer’s exposure to risks of severe human  rights impacts,
and the issuer’s exposure to severe human rights or
environmental 
controversies.  LBP  AM may exclude
companies for which there is a risk related to  violations of
its ethical standards. This standards-based exclusion
policy is applied to all LBP AM open-ended funds, as well
as 
to all or some of the dedicated funds or funds under
discretionary  management according to the choice of
investors,  therefore preventing and mitigating the risks of
negative 
human rights impacts in connection  with its
investment activities.
The ESG Charter is the cornerstone of Louvre Banque Privée’s
human rights policy and reflects its adherence to
international  standards  in favour of a responsible  value
chain. Louvre  Banque  Privée is committed to promoting
respect 
for human rights throughout its downstream
value chain. This commitment is based on a proactive
approach aimed  at:
•identifying serious  controversies involving portfolio
companies;
•identifying companies in violation of the ten principles
of the United Nations Global Compact or the OECD
Guidelines  for Multinational Enterprises. [S2_MDR_P_01_06]
[S2_1_04]  [S2_1_05]  [S2_1_08]  [S2_2_05] [S2_4_05] [S2_4_08]  [S2_4_10]Please  see the glossary  on page 808 for definitions of the main CSR terms 2024 Universal  Registration Document     La Banque Postale 2052Sustainable performance
Social information
No case of non-compliance with the United Nations
Guiding  Principles on Business and Human Rights  or the
ILO Declaration involving  workers  in the  downstream
chain  has been reported  to date within  La Banque Postale
Group.  [S2_1_09]
Human  rights
La Poste Group has implemented a Human Rights policy
that formalises its commitments to protect, respect and
promote  human rights  in all of its activities  and  within  its
value chain, both  in France  and throughout the world.
This  policy therefore covers  workers in the downstream
value chain. In  addition, the Human Rights  policies of
CNP Assurances and LBP AM are detailed in Section 2.3.3.2.1
“Applicable policies”.  [S2_1_01]  [S2_1_02]  [S2_1_03]
Compliance with international standards
In December 2023, La  Banque Postale updated its Responsible
Financing and Investment Charter.  Through this Charter,
La  Banque  Postale has set up a process  for managing
serious and/or repeated controversies. The Charter specifies
that violations of human rights and fundamental rights
related  to work, in particular based on the benchmarks of
the United Nations Guiding Principles, the International
Labour  Organization  Conventions  on fundamental rights
at work and the OECD Guidelines for Multinational Enterprises,
are considered  serious  controversies.
La  Banque   Postale Group’s subsidiaries  are  also
implementing  policies :
•CNP  Assurances joined  the UN  Global Compact  in 2003,
and is committed to respecting  the Human and Citizen
Rights  defined in the Universal Declaration of Human
Rights ;
•LBP  AM  has a  human rights  risk  map  and  an exclusion
policy;
•Louvre Banque Privée invests exclusively in France and
Europe  in order  to reduce  risk exposure;
La Banque Postale uses this reference base to identify  the
groups of workers who may be exposed to a higher  risk of
harm. Therefore, La Banque Postale pays particular attention
to child labour, forced labour,  migrant labour,  work in
conflict zones and  precarious work.  [S2_1_05]  [S2_1_08]2.3.2.3.3

title: Dialogue mechanisms
heading: 2.3.2.3.3 Dialogue mechanisms
start_phrase: To date, La Banque Postale Group does not interact directly with workers in the value chain of its financed activities.
summary:

text:
Dialogue mechanisms
To 
date, La Banque Postale Group does not interact directly
with workers in the value chain  of its financed activities.
This is due to the diversity of investments made in thousands
of 
companies operating in various sectors and geographies.
Consequently, the human rights impacts related to these
investment  activities, including the risks for the workers of
the invested companies, differ in nature and intensity.
This complexity  does not make it possible, at this stage, to

title: Reporting and remediation process
heading: 2.3.2.3.4 Reporting and remediation process
start_phrase: The general approach to preventing negative impacts on workers in the value chain is mainly relevant to LBP AM.
summary:
- The document outlines La Banque Postale Group’s approach to human rights within its sustainable performance and social information disclosures for 2024.
- It reports no cases of non-compliance with the UN Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights or the ILO Declaration involving downstream workers.
- La Poste Group has a formal Human Rights policy covering its global value chain; subsidiary policies (CNP Assurances, LBP AM) complement this framework.
- In December 2023, La Banque Postale updated its Responsible Financing and Investment Charter, establishing a process to manage serious controversies, especially human and labor rights violations, aligned with UNGPs, ILO conventions, and OECD Guidelines.
- Subsidiary commitments include: CNP Assurances’ participation in the UN Global Compact since 2003; LBP AM’s human rights risk mapping and exclusion policy; Louvre Banque Privée’s focus on France/Europe to limit exposure.
- The Group identifies high-risk worker categories for enhanced vigilance: child labor, forced labor, migrant labor, conflict zones, and precarious work.
- Due to the breadth of holdings and geographies, the Group does not directly engage with workers in financed entities’ value chains; this complexity precludes a universal interaction system.
- Investors, including minority holders, may be directly linked to human rights impacts per OECD Guidelines; they are expected to integrate risks and incentivize prevention/mitigation, while remediation responsibility lies with the companies causing or contributing to harm.
- LBP AM uses its influence to support remedies when material impacts occur and relies on investee disclosures in the absence of direct worker dialogue.
- Protections exist against reprisals for employees of financed entities who use the Group’s whistleblowing channels.
- Group-wide actions include 2024 e-learning for all employees on fundamental human rights, forced labor, and child labor.
- CNP Assurances incorporates human rights via ESG ratings (LBP AM’s GREaT methodology), prioritizing working conditions and respect for human and trade union rights in asset selection.
- LBP AM integrates human rights into asset management through SRI ratings, controversy checks aligned with SFDR (Articles 8 and 9), exclusion policies, and active shareholder engagement guided by UN Global Compact, UNGPs, and OECD Guidelines.
- Louvre Banque Privée manages material risks/opportunities via ESG data providers to flag controversies and an internal ESG network for qualitative assessment.
- Monitoring effectiveness relies on LBP AM’s SRI governance: the GREaT Committee (steers engagement/exclusions, standards policy, watchlists, escalation) and the ESG Committee (weekly trend/risk monitoring, prioritizing enhanced due diligence and engagements).
- Proprietary SRI methodologies and decision tools integrate human rights risk assessment into issuer selection and ongoing monitoring.
text:
3.2.3.4 Reporting and remediation process
The general approach to preventing negative impacts on
workers in the  value  chain is  mainly relevant to LBP  AM.
However,  according to the OECD analysis(1), investors, even
those holding minority stakes, may be directly linked to
the negative human rights impacts caused by the invested
companies, due to their shareholding or management of
shares in said companies. In  other words, in the majority of
cases, the impacts of a  portfolio in terms of  human rights
are generally “direct links” with the operations, products or
services of the invested companies.
Consequently, within the meaning of the OECD Guidelines,
investors 
are expected to take  into account the risks
associated with the conduct of the  invested companies
throughout the investment process and to provide incentives
to the companies in which they invest to prevent or mitigate
negative impacts. The responsibility for remedying the
impacts lies with the companies that caused or contributed
to the negative impact.
LBP 
AM uses its sphere of “influence” with companies to
allow or support a remedy in the  event of an actual or
potential material impact, in accordance with its Human
Rights 
policy as  described in Section 2.3.3.2.1 “Applicable
policies”. [S2_3_01] [S2_4_07]
As 
a financial institution, La  Banque  Postale Group does
not 
interact directly with workers in its financed activities.
The 
relationship with these workers is therefore indirect,
via the entities receiving the financing. In the absence of
direct 
dialogue, La  Banque  Postale relies on the reports
and commitments of the financed entities to meet this
requirement. 
[S2_3_02] [S2_3_03] [S2_3_04] [S2_3_05]
In 
addition, policies are in place to prevent reprisals against
employees of financed entities who use the Group’s
channels to  raise their concerns or needs, and are detailed
in Section 2.4.1.3.5 “Independence and accessibility of the
whistleblowing system”.  [S2_3_06]

title: Action plans and resources
heading: 2.3.2.3.5 Action plans and resources
start_phrase: La Banque Postale Group as a whole implements ambitious and consistent policies to prevent, mitigate and remedy negative impacts on human rights, based on approaches adapted to its various entities.
summary:
- Focus: La Banque Postale Group’s human-rights due diligence within its financing and investment activities, including action plans, monitoring, incidents, resources, and targets (Social information, Sustainable performance).
- Group-wide actions: 2024 rollout of an e-learning module for all employees on human rights, including preventing forced and child labor.
- Subsidiary frameworks tailored to activities to prevent negative human-rights impacts in downstream value chains.
- CNP Assurances: Integrates human-rights considerations into asset selection via LBP AM’s GREaT ESG methodology, prioritizing working conditions and respect for fundamental rights.
- LBP AM: Human Rights policy aligned with SFDR and international standards; integrates human-rights risk into SRI analysis, applies controversy screening and exclusions, and conducts active shareholder engagement.
- Louvre Banque Privée: Applies strengthened qualitative ESG analysis, uses external ESG data to flag controversies, and leverages internal ESG expertise.
- Monitoring effectiveness: Governance via GREaT and ESG Committees; proprietary SRI rating methodologies embedded in investment decisions; use of SFDR Main Adverse Impact indicators, controversy monitoring, and a standards watchlist.
- 2024 results: Exclusion of three companies for severe workers’ rights violations in supply chains; written AGM questions to two companies after insufficient engagement progress; targeted engagement campaigns in personal care products and automotive sectors to mitigate severe supply-chain risks.
- Resources: Dedicated Sustainability Department team to manage controversies and engage clients to remediate detected negative impacts.
- Targets: No measurable targets yet for poor working conditions, forced labor, or child labor due to data/methodology gaps; ongoing monitoring of controversies with operational adjustments to the Responsible Financing and Investment Charter.
text:
3.2.3.5 Action plans  and  resources
Measures and actions  implemented
La  Banque  Postale Group as a whole implements
ambitious 
and consistent policies to prevent, mitigate and
remedy  negative impacts on human rights, based on
approaches  adapted to its various entities. These efforts,
although  complementary, are adapted  to the specificities
of the activities of each  of the subsidiaries.
For the entire La Banque Postale Group, a key cross-functional
initiative 
is employee awareness-raising. In order to minimise
and prevent the negative impacts  of degraded working
conditions, forced labour or child  labour in the portfolio
companies, 
La  Banque  Postale has designed and rolled
out in 2024  an e-learning training module dedicated to
human rights. This training, accessible to all employees,
aims to strengthen their  knowledge of fundamental
human rights and specific issues such as  how to combat
forced  labour  and  child labour.
La Banque Postale’s  subsidiaries have put in place a framework
that promotes the prevention of negative impacts  on the
human rights of workers in  the downstream  value chain,
which is adapted  to their activity.
CNP  Assurances
With  regard to the shares and bonds held directly by
CNP Assurances SA and its French subsidiaries, the selection
of assets takes  human rights matters into account by
looking  at the  ESG ratings  of companies.  The  ESG  rating of
companies and issuers is based on the GREaT methodology
developed 
by LBP AM. This approach also looks at sustainable
management of resources. Two  social criteria are prioritised:
•Working conditions: ensuring that employees, subcontractors
and  suppliers  work in good  health and safety conditions;
•Human  rights: ensuring that  trade union freedoms and
the fundamental human rights of employees, subcontractors
and suppliers  are respected.
LBP  AM
As a subsidiary  specialising in asset management, LBP AM
translates 
these commitments through targeted practices
and robust  methodologies.
LBP  AM’s Human Rights policy is in line with international
standards  and  European regulatory  requirements, such as
the SFDR,  and  is based  on several areas:
•integration  of human rights in asset management: risks
relating  to value  chain workers are integrated  into the
analysis, selection and  monitoring  of assets  using  SRI
rating  tools. These tools assess issuers on their ability to
prevent, mitigate and remedy severe human rights impacts.
•sustainability  analysis  methodology:  LBP   AM  applies a
methodology  that  systematically verifies that  issuers
respect human rights and are not associated with serious
controversies. This methodology is  aligned with the
minimum sustainable investment thresholds for products
classified in Article 8  and  Article  9 of the SFDR.•exclusion policy: LBP AM excludes companies associated
with serious violations of  fundamental ethical standards,
with 
an extended application to its open-ended funds
and, according to investors, to dedicated funds or mandates.
•shareholder 
engagement: LBP AM actively communicates
with 
invested companies to encourage them to strengthen
their human rights due diligence practices, in accordance
with the principles of the United Nations Global Compact,
the UNGP and the  OECD  Guidelines.
Louvre  Banque  Privée
For its part,  Louvre Banque  Privée adapts these commitments
to the specific nature of its activities, primarily by integrating
a 
strengthened qualitative analysis within its  operational
framework. Louvre  Banque  Privée relies on a framework
designed to manage the material  impacts, risks and
opportunities 
related to workers in the value chain.
This framework is based on:
•the use of ESG  data providers to identify serious controversies
and  human rights  violations.
•a team of  internal ESG contacts (for qualitative analysis).
[S2_MDR_A_01_12] [S2_4_01]
Monitoring  the effectiveness of actions
The 
exclusion and engagement actions provided for by
the LBP AM's Human Rights policy are primarily implemented
through two SRI  Committees:
•The 
GREaT Committee, which steers the cross-functional
deployment of engagement and exclusion policies and
decides on the implementation of the various components
of the  exclusion policy, in particular  decision-making
relating  to the LBP  AM’s Standards policy.  The GREaT
Committee monitors issuers on the standards and
exclusion watchlist and  may, in the event of positive or
negative 
changes, adopt escalation or de-escalation
measures with the issuer;
•The ESG Committee, which brings together all members
of the asset management, the SRI Solutions and the
fundamental analysis teams on a weekly basis during
which the following are carried out: awareness-raising
and monitoring of trends, risks, salient topics  and companies’
human rights development;
•Prioritising 
and  organising enhanced  due diligence  or
engagement, in accordance with the LBP AM's Human
Rights policy.
In addition to these committees, LBP AM relies on a set of
tools and procedures to monitor the effectiveness of its
actions. 
Among them, its proprietary SRI rating methodologies,
which make it possible to incorporate major human
rights risks into its analysis and selection of assets.
These 
methodologies are directly integrated into the
decision-making tools used by the management teams.
These tools make it possible to identify, select and monitor
companies 
and their ability to prevent, mitigate and
remedy the impacts and risks  of human rights impacts.Please  see the glossary  on page 808 for definitions of the main CSR terms 2024 Universal  Registration Document     La Banque Postale 2072Sustainable performance
Social information
Ratings  are included in the management of SRI funds
according to two contribution methodologies to stock
selection. 
These methods tend to disqualify the issuers most
exposed 
to high-impact human rights risks, and favour
those that  best  control  their exposure to these risks:
•Main Adverse Impacts: The SFDR Delegated Regulation
defines a list of indicators to measure the negative impacts
of an issuer  on environmental  and  social  sustainability
factors, known as “IAP indicators”. Among these, indicators
relate  to respect for Human Rights and fundamental
ethical  standards.
•Controversies  monitoring: Data related to data supplier
controversies  makes it possible to monitor issuers, in
particular  their  ability  to prevent and remedy impacts.
•Standards  watchlist:  The standards  watchlist primarily
includes issuers analysed by the GREaT Committee and
marked for monitoring.  This list allows for continuous
monitoring of the issuer and the measures adopted by
the GREaT Committee, as well as their effectiveness,
particularly  in the event of engagement with the
Company.  [S2_4_04]
Severe  human  rights  incidents
As part  of the implementation of its standards-based exclusion
policy, in 2024, LBP AM excluded three companies due to
serious  violations of the fundamental rights of workers in
the supply  chains of  the companies  studied.
As part of  the implementation of its engagement policy,
LBP   AM submitted written questions to the General
Meetings  of two companies, following engagement that
did not sufficiently demonstrate that effective changes
had  been  made  to the  policies and practices  of the  targetcompanies. In both cases, some of the issues were related
to the respect  of fundamental workers’ rights, particularly
in 
supply chains. Following a  serious controversy affecting
a group of companies in the personal care products
sector, LBP AM launched an engagement campaign with
the invested companies covered by this human rights risk.
Several 
individual issuers were  also  subject to more
robust engagement campaigns during 2024, in particular
companies in the automotive and automotive components
sector, to reduce the  risk of severe  human rights impacts
on supply chains. [S2_4_11]
Resources allocated
Remedying La   Banque   Postale 's negative impacts  linked
to the activities of its portfolio companies involves dialogue
with 
customers. If a negative impact is detected through
the controversy management process, La  Banque  Postale
may  ask the business customer to remedy it quickly.
La Banque Postale provides a dedicated team within the
Sustainability 
Department to put its controversy management
process into operation. 
[S2_4_12]
2.

title: Targets
heading: 2.3.2.3.6 Targets
start_phrase: La Banque Postale has not defined a measurable target related to the negative impacts of poor working conditions, forced labour or child labour within the portfolio companies.
summary:
- Explains how ESG ratings are used in SRI fund selection to address human rights risks via: SFDR Principal Adverse Impact (PAI) indicators, controversies monitoring, and a standards watchlist overseen by the GREaT Committee for ongoing issuer monitoring and engagement effectiveness.
- Details 2024 actions on severe human rights issues: LBP AM excluded three companies for serious supply‑chain labor rights violations; submitted AGM questions to two companies after insufficient progress; launched engagement following a major personal care sector controversy; intensified engagements with automotive and components firms to curb severe supply‑chain human rights risks.
- Describes controversy management and resources: dialogue with business customers to seek rapid remediation when negative impacts are detected; a dedicated Sustainability Department team operates the controversy process.
- Notes absence of quantitative targets on poor working conditions, forced labor, or child labor in portfolios due to methodological and data gaps; ongoing monitoring of controversies and adjustments to the Responsible Financing and Investment Charter as needed.
- Defines scope of potentially affected communities: people near La Banque Postale’s regional network and downstream communities (including indigenous peoples) linked to financed/invested companies.
- Outlines material negative impacts from exposure to high‑risk sectors (conflict zones, privacy/freedom of expression breaches, environmental pollution, health and human rights harms) across diversified portfolios of La Banque Postale, CNP Assurances, LBP AM, and Louvre Banque Privée; highlights heightened vulnerability of certain groups; mitigation through responsible investment strategies.
- Highlights positive community impacts: alignment with Caisse des Dépôts priorities (economic development, territorial cohesion/housing, social cohesion, ecological transition); regional presence ensuring banking access, including in underserved areas; financing for local authorities and associations; societal programs such as L’Envol, solidarity team building, and Déclic.
- States financial materiality conclusion: affected communities topic deemed non‑material with no significant risks or opportunities identified, including for specific groups.
- Summarizes policy framework: Responsible Financing and Investment Charter excludes financing of sensitive sectors and entities with serious/repeated ESG controversies and avoids capital contributions to countries that do not respect fundamental rights and international standards to protect affected communities.
text:
3.2.3.6 Targets
La  Banque  Postale has not defined a measurable target
related 
to the negative impacts of poor working conditions,
forced labour or child labour within the portfolio companies.
This would require adapted methodologies, and access to
high-quality data, which are not currently available.
Nevertheless,  La  Banque  Postale monitors  the handling
of  controversies,  and then adapts the operational
implementation  of the Responsible Financing and
Investment Charter where necessary. [S2_MDR_T_01_13]208 La Banque  Postale      2024 Universal Registration  Document Please see the glossary on page 808 for definitions of  the main CSR terms2Sustainable performance

title: Material IROs and links with strategy and business model
heading: 2.3.3.1 Material IROs and links with strategy and business model
start_phrase: The communities likely to be affected by significant impacts related to the activity of the Group and its subsidiaries or projects financed through investment or credit activities are presented in the information published under the ESRS 2 heading.
summary:
- Scope: Identifies communities potentially affected by La Banque Postale Group’s own operations (people around its extensive regional network and societal initiatives) and by financed activities (downstream communities, including indigenous peoples, impacted by portfolio companies), aligned with ESRS 2/S3.

- Material negative impacts: Linked to investments in high-risk sectors (conflict-related operations/materials, privacy and freedom of expression breaches, environmental pollution, health and Human Rights harms). Exposure spans La Banque Postale, CNP Assurances, LBP AM, and Louvre Banque Privée due to diversified, multi-sector, multi-geography portfolios. Particularly vulnerable groups include indigenous peoples, women, children, displaced persons, and populations in conflict or high-risk areas. Mitigation via responsible investment strategies.

- Positive impacts: Strategy aligned with Caisse des Dépôts priorities—economic development and sovereignty, territorial cohesion and housing, social cohesion, and ecological transition. The Group’s regional network enhances banking access in rural/underserved areas; financing supports local authorities and associations for infrastructure renovation, local services, ecological/social initiatives, and inclusion/solidarity projects. Societal programs (e.g., L’Envol for youth from low-income backgrounds) and employee engagement initiatives (solidarity team building, Déclic) reinforce positive community impact.

- Risks and opportunities: The “affected communities” topic is non-material from a financial standpoint; no significant risks or opportunities identified for the Group or for specific groups.

- Commitments/policies for negatively affected communities: Acknowledges potential adverse impacts from financed activities in critical-risk sectors. The Responsible Financing and Investment Charter guides lending and investment, excluding financing of sensitive sectors or entities involved in serious/repeated ESG controversies, and prohibiting capital contributions to countries that do not respect fundamental rights and international standards—aimed at protecting affected communities.
text:
3.3.1 Material  IROs  and links 
with  strategy  and business model
Scope
The communities  likely to be affected by significant impacts
related to the  activity  of the  Group and  its subsidiaries or
projects financed through investment or credit activities
are presented in the information published under the
ESRS  2 heading.  [S3_SBM-3_01]
The communities likely to be affected by significant
impacts  are:
•for its own operations, people close to the network, as
part  of La  Banque  Postale Group’s extensive regional
network  and  those covered by societal initiatives;
•for the financed activities,  the communities, including
indigenous peoples, downstream of La Banque Postale
Group’s  value chain, which could be affected  by the
activity of the companies  in the investment portfolio.
[S3_SBM_3_02] [S3_SBM_3_03]
Material impacts,  risks and opportunities
Negative  impacts
The material negative impacts are related to investments
in 
sectors with critical levels of risk, in particular in connection
with operations or materials from conflict zones, risks of
invasion 
of privacy and freedom of expression, environmental
pollution, as well as impacts on  health  and Human Rights.
These  impacts cover La Banque Postale, CNP Assurances,
LBP   AM and Louvre  Banque   Privée, which  have multi-
sectoral investment strategies that are diversified in terms
of 
geographic area. The associated portfolios may therefore
include  companies  with activities  in these  high-risk
sectors.  [S3_SBM_3_04]
Local  and indigenous communities exposed to these
sectors  are particularly vulnerable, especially in the agri-
food,  metals and mining industries, as well as energy  and
utilities (water, gas, renewable energies).  The impacts are
all the more severe for populations with limited access to
remedies, 
such as  indigenous populations, women, children,
displaced populations or those living in conflict or high-
risk areas.
In order to prevent and minimise these negative impacts,
La  Banque  Postale, CNP   Assurances, LBP  AM and
Louvre Banque Privée have adopted responsible investment
strategies.  [S3_SBM_3 _07]
Positive  impacts
La Banque Postale Group’s strategic priorities are aligned
with  those  of the  Caisse  des  Dépôts Group to which it
belongs.  Caisse des  Dépôts Group is a  major public
developer of the French regions and a long-standing financier
of the local public sector. It has three main targets:
economic  development & sovereignty (companies of  all
sizes,  infrastructure),  territorial  cohesion  and  habitat, social
cohesion and  ecological  transformation.La  Banque  Postale’s activities have  positive impacts on
communities. The Group’s extensive network ensures a
presence 
in the regions, providing banking access to
citizens, including in rural or underserved areas.
La Banque Postale’s financing activities also help support
the activities  of local authorities and associations through
dedicated offers. La  Banque  Postale thus participates in
the development of local projects,  such as the renovation
of public  infrastructure, the development  of local services,
ecological  and social initiatives and associative actions in
favour of  inclusion  and  solidarity.
Lastly, societal sponsorship also generates positive impacts.
For example, the L'Envol program, run by La Banque Postale,
supports the education of young people from low-income
backgrounds. In addition, initiatives such as solidarity team
building or the Déclic project aim to raise employee
awareness, engage them in societal projects, and reinforce
the Group’s  impact. For more  information on
La  Banque  Postale Group’s actions and positive impacts,
refer to Section 2.3.3.3 “Commitments to affected
communities  to generate a positive impact”. [S3_SBM_3_05]
Risks and  opportunities
The topic related  to the affected communities is non-
material in La Banque Postale Group's financial materiality
analysis. Indeed, no significant risks or opportunities for
La Banque Postale have been identified in relation to the
affected communities. 
[S3_SBM_3_06]
No significant risk or opportunity was identified for a
specific  group. [S3_SBM 3_08]
2.

title: Commitments to communities negatively affected by financed activities
heading: 2.3.3.2 Commitments to communities negatively affected by financed activities
start_phrase: This section reviews the negative impacts on the financed activities, particularly in relation to investments in sectors with critical levels of risk: operations and materials from conflict zones, breaches of privacy and freedom of expression, environmental pollution, impacts on health, Human Rights, etc.
summary:
- Scope and framework: ESRS S3 coverage of communities affected by La Banque Postale Group’s own operations and by financed activities across its value chain, including indigenous peoples; references to ESRS 2 disclosures.
- Who is affected: People near the Group’s extensive regional banking network and beneficiaries of societal initiatives (own operations), and communities downstream of investment/credit activities (financed activities).
- Material negative impacts: Potential harms linked to investments in high‑risk sectors and contexts—conflict zones, privacy and freedom of expression risks, environmental pollution, health impacts, and Human Rights issues—across diversified portfolios of La Banque Postale, CNP Assurances, LBP AM, and Louvre Banque Privée. Vulnerable groups include local and indigenous communities, women, children, displaced persons, and populations in conflict or high‑risk areas; sectors named include agri‑food, metals/mining, and energy/utilities.
- Mitigation approach: Adoption of responsible investment strategies to prevent and minimize adverse impacts, including application of a Responsible Financing and Investment Charter that excludes financing of sensitive sectors, companies with serious or repeated ESG controversies, and capital contributions to countries not respecting fundamental rights and international standards.
- Positive impacts: Alignment with Caisse des Dépôts Group priorities (economic development and sovereignty, territorial cohesion and habitat, social cohesion, ecological transformation). The Group’s regional presence promotes banking access in rural/underserved areas; financing supports local authorities and associations for infrastructure renovation, local services, and ecological/social initiatives. Societal sponsorships (e.g., L’Envol for education, solidarity team building, Déclic) enhance inclusion, solidarity, and employee engagement.
- Risks and opportunities: The topic is non‑material from a financial perspective; no significant risks or opportunities identified for the Group or specific groups related to affected communities.
- Forward reference: Further detail on positive impact commitments is provided in Section 2.3.3.3.

title: Applicable policies
heading: 2.3.3.2.1 Applicable policies
start_phrase: La Banque Postale’s Responsible Financing and Investment Charter sets out the fundamental principles that guide the Bank’s lending and investment decisions.
summary:
- Focus: La Banque Postale Group’s commitments and practices regarding communities affected by its operations and, especially, by financed activities, within the Group’s CSR framework (ESRS S3).
- Scope of affected communities: 
  - Own operations: people near the Group’s extensive regional network and beneficiaries of societal initiatives.
  - Financed activities: downstream communities, including indigenous peoples, potentially affected by portfolio companies.
- Material negative impacts: 
  - Linked to investments in high‑risk sectors (conflict-zone links, privacy/freedom of expression breaches, environmental pollution, health and Human Rights issues).
  - Vulnerable groups highlighted (indigenous peoples, women, children, displaced populations, those in conflict/high‑risk areas).
  - Entities concerned: La Banque Postale, CNP Assurances, LBP AM, Louvre Banque Privée; mitigation via responsible investment strategies.
- Positive impacts:
  - Regional presence ensuring access to banking, including rural/underserved areas.
  - Financing supports local authorities/associations (public infrastructure renovation, local services, ecological/social initiatives, inclusion and solidarity).
  - Societal sponsorship and employee engagement (e.g., L’Envol education program, solidarity team building, Déclic).
- Financial materiality: Affected communities topic deemed non‑material for financial risks/opportunities; no specific group-level risks/opportunities identified.
- Policies and standards:
  - Responsible Financing and Investment Charter: exclusions for sensitive sectors and serious ESG controversies; no capital to countries violating fundamental rights.
  - LBP AM Human Rights Policy; CNP Assurances due diligence with impact mapping across own activities, suppliers, and investments.
  - Alignment with UN Global Compact, UN Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights, ILO Conventions, OECD Guidelines; no 2024 non‑compliance identified.
- Targets: No specific targets set to manage negative impacts on affected communities (no direct interaction claimed); controversies handling used to monitor Charter implementation.
- Dialogue mechanisms:
  - Regular engagement with local authorities via La Poste’s local presence and specialized public-sector business centers to identify needs and build trust.
  - Investor stewardship: LBP AM engages portfolio companies to address human rights issues; breadth of holdings limits systematic, direct community interaction.
- Remediation/influence approach:
  - Use “sphere of influence” to:
    - Assess company responses to halt/remedy negative impacts.
    - Set expectations, support corrective actions, and monitor measures.
  - Companies are expected to create action plans, remedy impacts they cause/contribute to, and actively consult affected stakeholders, demonstrating integration of their views.
text:
3.3.2.1 Applicable policies
Responsible Financing and Investment Charter
La Banque Postale’s Responsible Financing and Investment
Charter 
sets out  the fundamental principles that guide
the Bank’s lending and investment decisions. By excluding
the financing of companies involved in sensitive sectors or
in 
serious or repeated controversies  on environmental,
social  and governance issues, it aims to protect affected
communities from the negative impacts of these activities.
In addition, it excludes the contribution of capital to countries
where fundamental rights and international standards are
not respected. For more  information,  see focus point:

CNP  Assurances  Human Rights  policy
As part of its due diligence process, CNP  Assurances has
set up a mapping  of the  impacts in terms of infringement

Alignment with  relevant  internationally

the 
United Nations Guiding Principles, the ILO Conventions
and the OECD  Guidelines  as a reference base.
The LBP AM Group is  committed to respecting internationally

title: Targets
heading: 2.3.3.2.2 Targets
start_phrase: La Banque Postale has not established targets to manage the material negative impacts of the communities affected by the financed activities.
summary:
- Extract from La Banque Postale’s 2024 Universal Registration Document (CSR/Sustainable performance – Social information) focused on human rights governance in financing and investment.
- LBP AM Human Rights Policy referenced (with detailed mechanisms in Section 2.3.4.3); CNP Assurances describes a due-diligence mapping of human-rights, health/safety, and environmental impacts across own operations, suppliers, and investments, with control systems.
- Strong alignment with international standards: UN Global Compact, UN Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights, ILO conventions, and OECD Guidelines; commitment to comply with applicable laws and France’s international agreements.
- 2024 outcome: no identified non-compliance with UNGPs, ILO fundamental principles, or OECD Guidelines affecting communities.
- Targets: no specific targets set for managing material negative impacts on affected communities due to lack of direct interaction; instead, controversies are monitored and addressed under the Responsible Financing and Investment Charter.
- Dialogue mechanisms: ongoing, localized engagement with authorities via La Poste’s network to identify regional needs (public facilities, energy renovation, local economy) and build trust; in investments, stakeholder dialogue is conducted through LBP AM’s stewardship, acknowledging limits to systematic, direct engagement with all potentially affected communities given investment breadth.
- Remediation and influence approach: LBP AM uses its “sphere of influence” to engage companies identified via standards-based reviews or ESG Committee decisions to mitigate and remedy human-rights impacts. Objectives include assessing company responses, clarifying expectations, monitoring measures, and supporting remediation. Engaged companies are expected to develop action plans, cease/mitigate and remedy impacts they cause or contribute to, and actively consult affected stakeholders, demonstrating integration of their views.

title: Dialogue mechanisms
heading: 2.3.3.2.3 Dialogue mechanisms
start_phrase: La Banque Postale maintains regular dialogue with local authorities to better understand their challenges and adapt its solutions.
summary:
- Focus on La Banque Postale Group’s human rights approach within its Sustainable Performance/Social Information section, including LBP AM and CNP Assurances.
- Due diligence and risk mapping: identification and control of potential infringements on human rights, fundamental freedoms, health/safety, and the environment across own operations, suppliers, and investments.
- Alignment with international standards: UN Global Compact, UN Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights, ILO Conventions, and OECD Guidelines; no cases of non-compliance identified in 2024.
- Targets: no specific targets set for managing negative impacts on affected communities due to lack of direct interaction; reliance on controversy handling and the Responsible Financing and Investment Charter.
- Stakeholder dialogue: ongoing engagement with local authorities via La Poste’s on-the-ground network; responsible investment strategy leverages LBP AM’s influence over invested companies; no systematic direct interaction with all potentially affected communities due to investment breadth.
- Engagement and remediation approach: use of investor “sphere of influence” to push companies to stop, mitigate, and remedy human rights impacts; expectations include action plans, stakeholder consultation, avoiding immediate relationship severance when impacts are remediable, and strengthening due diligence; effectiveness tracked through engagement outcomes.
- Grievance mechanisms: expectation that portfolio companies implement culturally appropriate whistleblowing channels, with sector-specific guidance (e.g., oil and gas); monitoring via engagements and an annual report; consultation with external stakeholders; policies to prevent reprisals for whistleblowers; LBP relies on financed entities’ reporting given its indirect relationship with communities.
- Controversy monitoring and exclusions: pre-investment and ongoing checks for ESG controversies; severe/repeated human rights violations trigger exclusion from future investments and potential restriction of financing relationships.
- CNP Assurances’ ESG integration: application of Ostrum AM’s GREaT methodology in equity and bond selection, assessing social pillars such as working conditions and respect for human rights.
text:
Dialogue mechanisms
La  Banque  Postale  maintains regular dialogue with local
authorities 
to better understand their  challenges and
adapt its  solutions. The La Poste network is on the ground
daily to reinforce this dialogue . The managers of the
dedicated local public sector business centres and the
local 
La Poste managers often play a bridging role between
local authorities and  La Banque  Postale , providing:
•rapid identification of the specific needs of the regions,
whether in terms of investment in public facilities, energy
renovation projects or support for local economic activity;
•a 
close relationship which is essential  to establishing
lasting trust with local elected representatives and
economic players.
La  Banque  Postale Group incorporates dialogue  with
stakeholders into its  responsible investment strategy,
drawing on the influence exerted by LBP  AM on the
invested companies. This approach makes it possible to
address human rights issues and promote corrective
actions when negative impacts are identified. However,
due to the range of investments made – through various
instruments and in  thousands  of companies operating  in
various sectors and regions  – at this stage, there is no
systematic and direct interaction with all communities
potentially affected by these activities. [S3_2_08]
General  approach and remediation procedures:  
influence with financed entities
LBP 
AM uses its “sphere of influence” with the companies
that have been examined within the framework  of the
standards-based 
policy and for which it has been determined
that engagement would be the best lever for mitigating
and 
remedying the negative impacts related to the investment
activities, 
as well as companies that have been subject to
a review and an engagement decision by the ESG Committee.
There are multiple targets:
•assess the company’s response to stopping and remedying
the negative  human rights  impact;
•clarify  LBP  AM’s expectations in terms of stopping
and   remedying imp acts,  and monitor the measures
implemented  by the company  in this  respect;
•support the company in the process of stopping and
remedying the  impacts.
In addition, the companies covered by engagement
processes are  expected to:
•develop  an action plan  to mitigate and/or put  an end to
the negative impacts that they have caused, to which
they have contributed or to which they are directly
linked through a commercial  relationship;
•strive to remedy the negative human rights impacts
that they  may have  caused or to which they may have
contributed;
•actively consult affected stakeholders, or any relevant
stakeholders,  and have the  ability to demonstrate that
their action plan has been developed taking into
account these stakeholders’ views, concerns and needs;210 La Banque  Postale      2024 Universal Registration  Document Please see the glossary on page 808 for definitions of  the main CSR terms2Sustainable performance
Social information
•not immediately  sever a business relationship in the
event of a  remediable negative impact, but instead seek
to work with that contact towards mitigating the impact;
•strengthen  their due diligence measures to prevent this
impact  from  recurring.
LBP  AM assesses  the effectiveness of these approaches by
monitoring the results of  engagement campaigns and
measuring  the progress of the companies involved  in the
areas identified.  [S3_3_10]
Channels for reporting concerns
LBP   AM expects  the invested companies to put in place
suitable, effective and culturally appropriate whistleblowing
systems to  enable stakeholders,  including affected
communities, to report their concerns. These requirements
are integrated into the engagement policies and monitored
as part  of the interactions  with  the companies  in question.
For example,  LBP  AM  has  included guidelines in its  oil and
gas sector policy  requiring companies to set up specific
alert mechanisms  for affected  local communities. [S3_3_11]
Encouraging  channels in business  relationships
LBP   AM  encourages  invested companies to  establish  or
improve  their alert and remediation mechanisms by
prioritizing at-risk sectors. These expectations are discussed
during  direct engagements in which LBP  AM assesses
the implementation of due diligence by  companies and
their ability to meet the expectations of local communities.
[S3_3_12]
Monitoring and evaluation of channel effectiveness
LBP AM monitors issues raised by engagement campaigns
and stakeholder  feedback  through:
•analysis of the responses of the invested companies to
the engagement  process  and the actions implemented
to remedy  the identified  impacts;
•the publication of an annual engagement report detailing
the progress  made and  the best  practices  identified.
External  stakeholders,  including representatives  of local
communities and sector experts,  are regularly consulted
to ensure that the mechanisms  in place effectively meet
users ’ expectations. [S3_3_13]
As a financial  institution, La   Banque  Postale does not
interact directly with the communities affected by the
projects  or activities financed. The relationship with  these
communities is mainly indirect, via  the entities receiving
the financing.  In  the  absence  of  direct  dialogue,
La Banque Postale relies on the reports and commitments
of the financed  entities  to meet  this requirement. [S3_3_14]
In addition, policies are in place to prevent reprisals against
people  who use the channels to raise their concerns or
needs, and are detailed in the Section 2.4.1.3.5 “Independence
and  accessibility  of the whistleblowing system”.  [S3_3_15]2.3.3.2.4

title: Action plans and resources
heading: 2.3.3.2.4 Action plans and resources
start_phrase: According to the OECD, investors may be linked to the negative impacts on Human Rights caused by the invested companies.
summary:
- Focus: La Banque Postale Group’s social responsibility approach to affected communities, with emphasis on human rights due diligence, grievance mechanisms, engagement and exclusion policies in investment, and positive local impacts via financing and sponsorship.

- Expectations for investee companies:
  - Prefer engagement and remediation over immediate relationship termination; strengthen due diligence to prevent recurrence.
  - Establish accessible, culturally appropriate whistleblowing and grievance channels; sector-specific guidance (e.g., oil and gas) for local community alerts.
  - Demonstrate effective remediation aligned with UN Guiding Principles and OECD Guidelines, especially in sensitive/conflict areas.

- Monitoring and evaluation:
  - Track responses and corrective actions from engagement campaigns; publish annual engagement reports.
  - Consult external stakeholders (local communities, experts) to test channel effectiveness.
  - Non-retaliation and independence of whistleblowing systems are reinforced.

- Investor responsibility and action:
  - Recognizes OECD view that investors are “directly linked” to impacts; uses influence to prevent/mitigate, while remediation lies with companies.
  - When material impacts are found, LBP AM consults local experts/affected communities, promotes action plans, strengthens company policies, and monitors remedies.

- Controversy screening and exclusions:
  - Pre- and post-investment checks for ESG controversies under a Responsible Financing and Investment Charter; serious/repeated controversies can trigger exclusion or relationship surveillance.
  - CNP Assurances uses Ostrum AM’s GREaT ESG methodology, including social pillars on working conditions and human rights.

- Governance, tools, and methodologies:
  - Two SRI committees drive policy: GREaT Committee (engagement and exclusions) and ESG Committee (trend/risk monitoring, awareness).
  - Exclusion decisions consider severity, company linkage, preventive/remedial measures, and likelihood of future violations.
  - Human rights integrated into investment analysis and SFDR “do no significant harm” checks; formal exclusion and engagement policies; active bilateral/collective dialogues.
  - Participation in sector initiatives: Coalition for Ethical AI, Ranking Digital Rights, Access to Medicine Foundation, ChemSec.

- Operating posture:
  - As a financial institution/asset manager, the Group does not directly engage communities affected by financed activities but relies on investee reporting and leverages influence to uphold due diligence and remediation.

- Resources and 2024 outcomes:
  - Dedicated SRI Solutions team (10 experts, including a human rights lead), SRI rating tools, and internal guidance on risk mapping and salient issues.
  - No serious human rights incidents concerning affected communities reported in 2024.

- Positive impact commitments:
  - Through sponsorship, a nationwide branch network, and financing of local authorities/associations, the Group supports regional development and social value creation.
  - CLDB-led initiatives include:
    - Local Finance Steering Committee (advisory/observatory role).
    - Strong partnership with the social and solidarity economy; advisors support 4,000 major associations.
    - “Advance on subsidy” cash-flow solution for associations.
    - Green/social financing solutions (e.g., responsible real estate, access to essential services) with accessible social loans.
    - “Donation collection” offer to boost online fundraising; 100+ partnerships with leading NGOs/foundations.
  - Goal: support associations in a just and sustainable transition.
text:
Action  plans  and resources
Actions implemented
According  to the  OECD,  investors may  be linked to the
negative impacts on Human Rights caused by the
invested companies. These  impacts  are generally “direct
links” rather than causes or contributions. Investors are
therefore  expected to consider the risks associated with
the invested companies during the investment process,
and  use their influence to  encourage these companies to
prevent or mitigate negative impacts. The responsibility
for remediation therefore lies  with the responsible
companies; however, the Group engages directly with
these  entities to  influence them.
Controversy monitoring
As part of its Responsible Financing and Investment
Charter, 
La  Banque  Postale SA undertakes to verify,
before 
investing in or financing a company, that the
company 
is not involved  in an ESG controversy, based on
an exclusion list validated by the Controversies and
Exclusion Committee. This Charter specifies that violations
of human rights  and fundamental rights related to work,
in particular under the United Nations Guiding Principles,
the International Labour Organization  Conventions on
fundamental rights at work, and the OECD Guidelines for
Multinational 
Enterprises, are considered serious controversies.
Controversies of this type that may potentially be detected
concerning the companies in the portfolio can vary greatly
in scope and nature, given La Banque Postale’s exposure
to a multiplicity of sectors  and  geographical positions.
In addition, as part of the monitoring of financing and
investments, 
La  Banque  Postale undertakes to regularly
check 
for potential  controversies. In  the event of serious
and/or  repeated controversies, the company in question
may  be excluded from future investments and existing
investments. For financing activities related to existing
customers,  La  Banque  Postale may decide to no longer
carry out new transactions with the customer  in question
and place its commercial  relations with that customer
under surveillance.
With regard to the shares and bonds held directly by
CNP Assurances SA and its French subsidiaries, the selection
of 
assets takes into account Human Rights issues through
the ESG ratings of companies carried  out by the Ostrum
AM teams. The ESG rating of companies and issuers is
based  on the GREaT methodology, enabling a pragmatic
and  differentiating analysis of companies with regard to
sustainable development issues (see focus point: The GREaT
methodology). This methodology measures commitment,
responsibility, opportunities and risks for companies based
on four pillars, including the sustainable management of
resources. 
This pillar is studied according to four criteria,
two of which are social:
•working conditions: ensuring that employees,
subcontractors and suppliers work in good health and
safety conditions;
•human rights: ensuring that trade union freedoms and
the fundamental human rights of employees,
subcontractors and suppliers are respected.Please  see the glossary  on page 808 for definitions of the main CSR terms 2024 Universal  Registration Document     La Banque Postale 2112Sustainable performance
Social information
Implementation  of the LBP AM Human  Rights Policy
When  an actual material impact is identified, LBP  AM
implements specific 
measures to support or enable
remedies. Thus, when material impacts are identified,
LBP  AM consults local experts, representatives of affected
communities  or specific stakeholders to assess the need
for repairs. For example, as part of an engagement
campaign  related to operations in conflict areas, LBP AM
worked  with regional experts and directly  affected people
to identify  reparation  expectations.
LBP   AM uses  its influence to encourage the companies
involved  to put in place effective mechanisms to repair
the damage caused. This includes: the implementation of
action  plans to address negative impacts, developed in
consultation  with  the affected parties, the strengthening
of company policies and practices to prevent the recurrence
of impacts, and the monitoring of  the steps taken by
companies to ensure that the  remedy is effective and
aligned  with  the identified  needs.
This  approach is part of LBP  AM’s  proactive influence
approach to  identify,  mitigate and  remedy negative
Human  Rights  impacts based on the integration of
Human  Rights in the analysis, selection and monitoring of
assets, the implementation of an exclusion  policy and
increased engagement  with at-risk  companies.  For more
information  on this approach, see paragraph 2.3.2.2.4
“Human  Rights”.
In addition to these commitments,  LBP AM participates in
a set of initiatives directly  related  to the  risks of Human
Rights  impacts of the companies’ products and services
on their customers and end-users. Among its initiatives
are the Coalition for Ethical AI, the  investor initiative in
collaboration  with  Ranking Digital Rights , the  initiative led
by the Access to Medicine Foundation, and the at-risk
chemicals investor initiative  organised  by ChemSec.
[S3_MDR_A_01_12] [S3_1_05]  [S3_4_01] [S3_4_02]
Monitoring the effectiveness of actions
The exclusion and engagement actions provided for by
the 
LBP AM's Human Rights policy are primarily implemented
through two SRI Committees:
•the GREaT Committee  (see focus point: The GREaT
methodology
), which steers the cross-functional deployment
of engagement  and exclusion policies;
•the ESG Committee, which brings together all members
of 
the asset management, SRI Solutions and fundamental
analysis teams on a weekly  basis, during which the
following 
are carried out: awareness-raising and monitoring
of trends, risks, salient topics and companies’ Human
Rights  development.  [S3_4_04]
LBP   AM  constantly  monitors  the invested  companies in
order  to identify specific actual or potential negative
impacts  on the affected communities. LBP  AM therefore
identifies and may exclude issuers presenting critical risks
of serious and/or repeated violations, and/or those subject
to serious, proven and  repeated controversies of the
principles of the UN Global  Compact, the Guiding Principleson Business and Human Rights or the OECD Guidelines
on Multinational Enterprises. This monitoring is carried
out 
by the GREaT Committee, which bases its decisions
on an assessment of:
•the severity of the impact or risks of the impact on people,
the environment or the principles of good governance;
•the link between the impact and the  company analysed
(cause, contribution,  direct link);
•prevention, cessation and remediation measures
implemented  by the company;
•the likelihood of future violations of standards by the
company.
The 
final decision adopted by the GREaT Committee must
aim, as far as possible, to reduce and mitigate the risks of
future violations of the  standards. [S3_4_05]
LBP  AM has put in place a structured approach to
prevent, mitigate and remedy specific material impacts
on affected communities, in line with international standards
such as the United Nations Guiding Principles, the OECD
Guiding  Principles and the Ten Principles of  the United
Nations Global  Compact . This  approach includes:
•integration of Human Rights issues into investment
processes: 
Human Rights are integrated into the analysis,
selection and monitoring of financial assets via  an
investment sustainability analysis  methodology which
incorporates human  rights and fundamental  freedoms.
In order to ensure that an investment contributing to a
sustainability target within the meaning of SFDR does
not 
cause significant harm to any socially sustainable
investment target, LBP AM has established a sustainability
methodology ensuring systematic verification  of the
issuer’s human rights practices, the issuer’s exposure to
risks of severe human rights impacts, and the issuer’s
exposure  to severe H uman Rights or environmental
controversies.  Human Rights are also taken into
account in the GREaT methodology rolled out by
LBP AM (see focus point: The GREaT  methodology);
•the implementation of an exclusion policy related to
violations 
of human rights and fundamental ethical
standards: LBP  AM may exclude companies for which
there 
is a risk that they cause, contribute or are linked to
particularly serious violations of  their  fundamental
ethical standards;
•the implementation of an engagement policy  focused
on the prevention, mitigation and remedy of negative
human rights impacts: LBP AM undertakes to conduct
active engagement with the invested companies to
encourage  and support them in the implementation of
Human Rights due diligence and managing their impact
on people. It therefore conducts regular and consistent
bilateral 
or collective dialogue  with companies. It aims
in particular to strengthen understanding of Human
Rights 
issues, to warn of systemic risks that companies
may  face and to promote compliance with the ten
principles 
of the United Nations Global Compact, the
UNGP and the OECD Guidelines.  [S3_4_06]212 La Banque  Postale      2024 Universal Registration  Document Please see the glossary on page 808 for definitions of  the main CSR terms2Sustainable performance
Social information
As an asset management company, LBP  AM does not
interact  directly with the communities affected by the
activities  of the companies in which it invests. However, it
is committed to using its sphere of  influence with the
invested companies to support the remediation of significant
negative  human rights impacts, in accordance with the
OECD 
Guidelines and the United Nations Guiding Principles
on Business  and  Human  Rights  (UNGP).
As explained  above, LBP AM  requires  invested companies
to consult affected stakeholders in an appropriate and
effective manner in order to understand their needs
and expectations,  set up whistleblowing and complaints
systems  which are accessible and culturally appropriate to
enable communities to report impacts, and demonstrate
that  recourse mechanisms are aligned with international
standards,  including the UN Guiding Principles and the
OECD  Guidelines.
In particular,  LBP  AM has  required  companies  operating
in sensitive areas to implement mechanisms adapted to
the local communities  affected. As part of engagement
campaigns related to  operations in conflict areas, LBP AM
asked  the  companies involved to actively consult the
affected parties and demonstrate the effectiveness of
their  recourse  mechanisms.  [S3_4_07]  [S3_4_10]
Resources allocated
LBP   AM  devotes  significant and  structured resources to
integrating Human Rights issues, particularly those involving
affected 
communities,  into  its  investment  activities.
This  commitment is based on clear processes, dedicated
teams  and well-defined governance  aimed at preventing,
mitigating  and  remedying potential  negative impacts.
•Dedicated  team  and  specialis ed expertise:
•the Human Rights policy is developed and implemented
by the SRI  Solutions team, composed of ten experts,
including a lead expert specifically in charge of Human
Rights.  This  team  works  in coordination with the
members  of the  management, fundamental  analysis
and commercial teams, as well  as with the Risk
Department  and  CSR  managers.
•Tools  and  methodologies:
•LBP AM uses SRI rating tools incorporating salient human
rights  issues  to analyse,  select and monitor assets,
•guides  relating to risk mapping and the salient issues
identified  are made available to employees to help
them better  understand  Human  Rights  risks  and
incorporate them into their investment decisions. [S3_4_12]
No cases of serious Human Rights incidents concerning
the affected  communities  were  reported  in 2024 . [S3_4_11]2.3.3.3

title: Commitments to affected communities to generate a positive impact
heading: 2.3.3.3 Commitments to affected communities to generate a positive impact
start_phrase: This section reviews the positive impact of the La Banque Postale Group in connection with its societal sponsorship actions, its regional network and the financing of local authorities.
summary:
- Focus area: Sustainable performance/Social information from La Banque Postale’s 2024 Universal Registration Document, with CSR term definitions referenced.
- LBP AM’s human rights approach as an asset manager:
  - Uses investor influence to promote remediation of significant human rights impacts, aligned with OECD Guidelines and UNGP.
  - Expects portfolio companies to consult affected stakeholders, implement accessible and culturally appropriate whistleblowing/complaints systems, and align grievance mechanisms with international standards.
  - Heightened expectations for companies in sensitive/conflict areas, including proof of effective recourse mechanisms.
- Governance and resources for human rights integration:
  - Dedicated SRI Solutions team (10 experts, including a human rights lead) coordinating across investment, risk, and CSR functions.
  - SRI rating tools incorporate salient human rights risks; internal guides support risk mapping and investment decision-making.
  - Reported no serious human rights incidents concerning affected communities in 2024.
- Positive impact commitments toward affected communities:
  - Through financing activities: strong role in funding local authorities and associations to drive regional development and social value.
  - Through own operations: societal sponsorship and extensive regional network to support local communities.
- Financing and support for local authorities, associations, and the local economy (via CLDB):
