title: Actions implemented to generate positive impacts
heading: 2.3.4.5.2 Actions implemented to generate positive impacts
start_phrase: La Banque Postale Group is committed to generating positive impacts for its customers by placing their needs at the heart of its priorities.
summary:
- Focus of the section: actions implemented to generate positive impacts for customers as part of La Banque Postale Group’s CSR/social commitments—quality service, universal accessibility to banking/insurance, and customer protection/financial security.
- Universal banking accessibility mission: as State-appointed custodian, guarantees non-discriminatory access to essential services centered on the Livret A (universal eligibility, €1.50 cash transactions in post offices, payment of essential bills and welfare transfers, free associated services). Serves about 1.2 million people excluded from traditional banking.
- Accessible products and clearer information: simplification of contractual documents to improve customer understanding.
- Inclusive banking and insurance:
  - Simplicité low-cost account option for 1.7 million customers in financial difficulty, including an annual fee cap of €1,500 on incident-related charges.
  - CNP Assurances: 14 inclusive insurance products covering 828,000 policyholders by end-2024; affordable funeral cover with ATD Fourth World (up to €2,500); microinsurance in Latin America (illness, death, property damage) and solutions in Italy enabling low-income retirees to access consumer credit.
  - Plain-language governance at CNP since 2024; 24% of management letters revised; multichannel distribution via post offices and lottery points in France and Brazil to reach remote areas.
- Credit inclusion:
  - Youth-focused loans (e.g., “€1/day” driving licence, student/apprentice loans).
  - Personal microloans via partners (CCAS, Restos du Cœur) for social reintegration.
  - Professional microloans for very small businesses/micro‑entrepreneurs to tackle unemployment and exclusion.
  - Temporary workers’ personal loan; Django three-instalment solution using open banking analytics.
  - Home loans without personal contribution and social home loans to widen access to home ownership.
- Protection of vulnerable customers:
  - L’Appui free banking/budget support (330,000+ people helped since 2013).
  - Educational tools (BGV, Dilemma) and staff training to detect/respond to vulnerability.
  - Pooled long‑term care contracts by CNP (no medical screening; population-based pricing; €100–€500 monthly payments) for broad accessibility.
  - Targeted services: Youth Pass (Wizbii) with 10 non‑financial services for ages 15–29; support for protected adults; digital inclusion via We Tech Care; “right to be forgotten” for cancer survivors; Family Help guarantee; accessible ATMs; life insurance death benefits paid within 30 days of complete file receipt.
- Regional proximity: 7,000+ retail outlets ensure geographic accessibility, including rural and priority neighborhoods; CNP distributes via post offices/lottery points in France and the Correios postal network in Brazil.
- Structured assistance for customers in financial difficulty: early detection (including 400 specially trained online advisors), right‑to‑an‑account services, fee reductions, microloans, solidarity offers, over‑indebtedness support, personalized guidance and referrals to relevant organizations.
- Enabling a just transition:
  - Systematic ESG integration through a mandatory product design checklist (updated 2021) covering customer experience and civic ambition for the just transition; products scoring >50/100 labeled “community-friendly.”
  - 2024 results: 30% of reviewed offers labeled (20% Retail Banking, 25% CLDB, 100% Transaction Banking); target 80% sustainable products by 2025; monitoring via annual citizen‑certified offers, independently assured.
  - Impact products: Créa‑Sol financing for social entrepreneurs; Green Vehicle/Green Works loans; Avance Rénovation (PAR); impact real estate loan; impact bank card that channels spending to energy renovation and biodiversity preservation.
- Governance and outcomes: no severe human rights incidents involving consumers/end‑users in 2024; consumer/end‑user targets managed via mission‑led indicators (e.g., NPS for financially vulnerable customers, access metrics) and CNP’s purpose metrics (e.g., number of inclusive products), plus customer satisfaction indicators like CES.
text:
3.4.5.2 Actions  implemented to generate 
positive impacts
La  Banque  Postale Group is committed to generating
positive 
impacts for its customers by placing their  needs at
the heart of its priorities. La  Banque  Postale acts to offer
quality  customer service, guarantee banking accessibility
and  insurance  services  for all,  as well  as to  ensure the
protection and  financial security  of its customers.
Provide  access  to bancassurance services  to all
Guaranteeing  access to bancassurance services for all is at
the heart  of the  La  Banque   Postale  Group’s DNA. This  is
reflected in its banking accessibility mission, as well as the
design 
of accessible bancassurance  products and services,
in order to meet the needs of as many people as possible.
La  Banque  Postale also implements specific actions for
vulnerable people and ensures its local proximity, a factor
of trust  with  its customers.  [S4_4_03]
Accessible banking mission
La Banque  Postale, the custodian of the banking accessibility
mission 
entrusted by the State, guarantees universal and
non-discriminatory access to  essential  banking services
for vulnerable  populations.
The Livret A savings account is at the heart of this mission,
offering 
an accessible and free product to all natural persons
who request it, based on  the principle of universality.
La Banque  Postale must comply  with  specific obligations,
such  as:
•any natural person must be able to open a Livret A savings
account. In practice, the specific focus is on households
with 
low incomes or in a precarious situation and certain
eligible legal  persons;
•the option to make withdrawals and deposits from €1.50,
available  in all authorised  post offices;
•authorised  transfers for welfare benefits and deductions
for low-cost housing, taxes, and essential bills (water, gas,
electricity, telecommunications);
•additional  free services  (transfers to the  current account
of the holder or their legal representative, cheques
and   withdrawal cards which can be used within the
La Banque  Postale network).
This mission guarantees access to  banking services for
1.2 million 
customers excluded from traditional banking
services, and therefore  contributes to their social and
financial inclusion.
Access to products  and services
La  Banque  Postale is first and foremost  committed to
guaranteeing access to products and services that provide
basic  banking services and finance essential needs, while
meeting the specific needs of the most vulnerable populations.
In addition, work has been carried out to simplify the
contractual  documents in order to ensure a better
understanding  of the offers  by customers.
Banking  and insurance  products
La Banque Postale has a specific offer, the Simplicité low-
cost account option, designed for the 1.7 million customers
experiencing 
financial difficulties, which limits the costs of
banking incidents and is linked to monitoring indicators
(e.g.  cap of €1,500  on annual  fees).CNP   Assurances, as a player in inclusive insurance, offers
accessible 
solutions to vulnerable populations. By way of
illustration, in 2024, CNP  Assurances had 14 products
which improve access to insurance for vulnerable groups.
At the end of 2024, 828,000 policyholders were covered by
these  products.
In partnership with ATD Fourth World, CNP  Assurances
offers  an affordable funeral insurance solution for people
in 
vulnerable  situations, covering up to €2,500 in costs. In
Latin America, where  the  illness  or death  of a loved one
can exclude families already experiencing financial
difficulties, microinsurance  packages have been  created
to protect low-income families against financial risks
related to illness, death or certain types of property
damage. In Italy, insurance  provides  low-income  retirees
with access to  consumer credit, without changing the
duration of the credit, and limiting repayments to 20% of
the monthly pension.
CNP   Assurances  is also  committed  to making  insurance
more  understandable and accessible to its customers.
Since  the beginning of 2024, a dedicated governance has
overseen 
the use of clear language in contractual,
management and commercial documents. In 2024, 24%
of 
management letters sent were reviewed to use plain
language.
The 
distribution of insurance products is facilitated through
various channels, such as post offices in France and
lottery  points in Brazil, making  services accessible even in
remote areas.
Credit
La Banque Postale offers  various consumer  loans:
•loans adapted to  young people, such as the “one-euro-
a-day driving licence loan” or the Student and Apprentice
Loans, to promote the  financial independence of young
people;
•personal microloans, offered in partnership with associations
such  as the CCAS and Restos du  Cœur, to finance
projects promoting social reintegration;
•professional microloans intended for small businesses,
craftspeople,  traders or  micro-entrepreneurs  who  do
not have  access to traditional financing. It is a means of
combating unemployment  and social exclusion that
allows business creators to sustain their activity and
encourages project leaders  to get  started;
•the temporary personal loan, adapted to the  needs of
temporary workers;
•financing  solution in three instalments with the Django
application,  based on open  banking analytics.
In addition, La Banque Postale offers several types of home
loans, such as home loans without personal  contribution,
to promote access to home ownership for vulnerable or
low-income 
households, or social home loans to facilitate
access home ownership for low-income families.
Protecting vulnerable  customers
As a socially responsible bank, La Banque Postale is committed
to protecting all of its customers, including  the most
vulnerable, through specific  systems  and  services.Please  see the glossary  on page 808 for definitions of the main CSR terms 2024 Universal  Registration Document     La Banque Postale 2232Sustainable performance
Social information
La Banque Postale and CNP Assurances are implementing
specific measures to protect customers in vulnerable situations:
•L'Appui,  a free  banking and budget support service that
has supported more than 330,000 people since 2013.
Advisors  analyse the situation of customers and propose
appropriate  solutions, such as  microloans or reduced
bank  fees;
•educational  tools such as “BGV” (High Speed Budget) or
the “Dilemma” game to raise awareness of budget
management;
•employee  training,  with  increased  awareness to detect
and  respond  effectively  to situations  of vulnerability ;
•for several years now, CNP Assurances has offered pooled
long-term  care contracts. The peculiarity of these so-
called  pay-as-you-go contracts is  their  maximum
accessibility, as they are included in the health
insurance  contracts offered to employees by our partner
mutual  insurance providers. This  system covers the
long-term  care risk, without medical screening, for all
members  of Group who  are  policyholders (only  risks
that  have already occurred are excluded). Pricing is
based  on the  entire population covered and on wide
age brackets, so that premiums are affordable and
within  reach  of as many people  as possible.  This type  of
scheme therefore guarantees a basic level of protection
against loss  of autonomy, with  monthly  payments
ranging  from  €100 to  €500.In addition,  there  are special services for  specific  groups:
•the Youth Pass (Wizbii), a platform offering 10 non-financial
services 
to 15-29 year olds, such as job searches, financial
assistance and  support  for academic  success;
•advice for protected adults, with a specific inter-bank
payment offer;
•We Tech Care, a digital inclusion plan to support customers
unfamiliar  with  digital tools;
•the right to be forgotten for cancer victims and the Family
Help guarantee to support relatives of sick children, two
initiatives 
by CNP  Assurances, which is committed to
pushing  the boundaries of insurability;
•accessibility for people with disabilities by providing
automated teller machines adapted for people  with
reduced mobility  and  the visually impaired.
Finally, in accordance  with the regulations relating to the
payment of death lump sums, CNP Assurances undertakes
to 
pay the capital of a life insurance  contract to the
various designated beneficiaries in the event of death
within 
a maximum  period of 30 days from receipt  of the
complete file.
Regional proximity for access to services
La  Banque  Postale Group is committed to ensuring that
its 
services are close to  its customers, even in  the most
isolated areas. Therefore,  its dense regional network  allows
everyone to easily access essential banking and insurance
services, regardless of  their location.

With  more than  7,000 retail outlets, La  Banque  Postale
guarantees geographical accessibility,  including  in rural
areas and priority neighbourhoods, thus offering a genuine
regional network.
CNP  Assurances also acts to make its  products accessible,
in particular for vulnerable populations. In France, the
distribution  of products  in post offices and lottery points
has been set up, facilitating access for people far from
traditional  circuits. In Latin America, life and health
microinsurance  is distributed through the Correios postal
network  in Brazil.  [S4_4_03]Enabling customers to play a role in the just transition
La 
Banque Postale enables its customers to actively contribute
to the just transition by  developing and promoting products
that take into account  ESG or positive impact criteria.
ESG assessment of offers
Committed  to the just transition, La Banque Postale takes
ESG criteria into account in  the design of its product  and
service offerings.
The ESG checklist: responsible products “by design”
In order to ensure the systematic integration of ESG
criteria 
in the design of its products, La  Banque  Postale
introduced  an ESG checklist in 2008, revised in 2021 to
align  with  new  CSR challenges.
The ESG checklist assesses offers and products in terms
of their contribution to the customer experience and
satisfaction,  as well as  to the just  transition. It is
mandatory  at Product  Review  Committees.
This checklist, developed in collaboration with Utopies and
WWF France, is based on two major pillars: on the one
hand, leadership in the customer experience and satisfaction,
which includes clarity of  offers, customer satisfaction
(service and journey), traceability and improvement of
the user journey; on the other hand, the civic ambition
for the just  transition, which aims to reduce inequalities,
encourage virtuous ecosystems and  promote customer
citizenship and responsibility.The ESG checklist assesses  each product on a basis of
100 
points. Products that achieve a score of more than
50 points are labelled “community-friendly”. In 2024,
30% 
of the offers examined by the committee obtained
this label, broken down as  follows: 20% for Retail
Banking, 
25% for CLDB and 100% for the Transaction
Banking 
scope. The target is to reach 80% of sustainable
products by 2025.
In 2024, throughout the design phase of the impact
card offer, the  checklist was used to identify and
improve the environmental aspects related to the offer.
To ensure the effectiveness of these actions, La Banque Postale
monitors  an annual  indicator of the proportion of new
citizen-certified offers. The results are published each
year 
in the mission-led company report and certified by
an independent third party.
Presentation  of impact offers
In addition to banking accessibility and the consideration
of ESG criteria, La  Banque  Postale is developing impact
financial products  aligned  with its just transition mission.
La  Banque  Postale offers a range of loans to small
professionals,  such as the Créa-Sol program, which offers
financing adapted to social entrepreneurs, making it possible
to support  local  projects with a sustainable impact.
Loans  are  also  granted  to retail customers,  such as the
Green  Vehicle and Green Works personal loan, to support
green  projects,  including  home energy improvements
and  electric vehicle purchases.  The Avance Rénovation
(PAR) 
loan finances energy efficiency work, and the impact
real estate loan is designed to finance acquisition or
renovation projects that meet strict environmental criteria.
Lastly,  La Banque  Postale offers  an impact banking offer.
For example, the impact bank card makes it possible  to
contribute to the energy renovation of the French real
estate  portfolio, particularly thermal  strainers, while taking
part  in the preservation  of biodiversity.  [S4_4_03]
No cases of severe Human Rights incidents concerning
consumers  and  end-users were reported  in 2024.  [S4_4_11]2.3.4.6 Consumer  and end-user targets

title: Targets
heading: 2.3.4.6.1 Targets
start_phrase: The Group’s targets related to consumers and end-users are managed through La Banque Postale’s mission-led company indicators (for example, the NPS of customers experiencing financial difficulties) and CNP Assurances’ company purpose (for example, the number of products improving access to insurance for vulnerable groups).
summary:
- Scope and context: Extract from La Banque Postale’s 2024 Universal Registration Document (Sustainable performance – Social information) outlining how the Group advances accessibility, customer protection, and the just transition through ESG-integrated products and impact finance.

- Geographic and social accessibility:
  - Over 7,000 retail outlets ensure nationwide access, including rural areas and priority neighborhoods.
  - CNP Assurances broadens access for vulnerable populations: distribution via post offices and lottery points in France; life and health microinsurance via Brazil’s Correios network in Latin America.

- Enabling customer participation in the just transition:
  - Development and promotion of products incorporating ESG or positive-impact criteria.

- ESG assessment of offers (ESG checklist):
  - Checklist launched in 2008, revised in 2021; mandatory in Product Review Committees; co-developed with Utopies and WWF France.
  - Two pillars: customer experience/satisfaction (clarity, satisfaction, traceability, journey) and civic ambition for the just transition (reduce inequalities, build virtuous ecosystems, foster citizenship/responsibility).
  - Scoring out of 100; >50 points earns “community-friendly” label.
  - 2024 labeling outcomes: 30% of examined offers labeled (20% Retail Banking, 25% CLDB, 100% Transaction Banking); target is 80% sustainable products by 2025.
  - Applied during impact card design to enhance environmental performance.
  - Annual indicator of new “citizen-certified” offers published in the mission-led company report and third-party assured.

- Impact product suite:
  - Small professionals: Créa-Sol program for social entrepreneurs and local sustainable projects.
  - Retail customers: Green Vehicle and Green Works loans; Avance Rénovation (PAR) for energy efficiency; impact real estate loan tied to stringent environmental criteria.
  - Impact banking: impact card contributing to energy renovation (including thermal strainer remediation) and biodiversity preservation.

- Customer protection and incidents:
  - No severe human rights incidents involving consumers/end-users reported in 2024.

- Targets and performance management:
  - Group targets anchored in La Banque Postale’s mission-led indicators (e.g., NPS for financially vulnerable customers) and CNP Assurances’ company purpose (e.g., number of products improving access for vulnerable groups).
  - Use of performance insights to adjust commercial targets and advisor guidance for community-based financing.
  - Customer metrics used by CNP: CES (effort), NPS (recommendation/loyalty), CSAT (satisfaction).

- Negative impact monitoring:
  - Trialing indicators for potential negative impacts (e.g., cybersecurity, information/security of consumers), not disclosed for confidentiality.

- Stakeholder involvement:
  - Indirect involvement of consumers/end-users via mission-led status and public-service role, with the State guiding activities in the general interest.

- Alignment with international standards:
  - Integration of UN Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights, ILO standards, and UN SDGs.

- Additional indicators and recent results:
  - Proportion of new offers identified as sustainable via the ESG checklist declined from 39% (2023) to 30% (2024); target 80%.
  - Banking and insurance inclusion metrics (2023 → 2024 → 2025 target):
    - Sustainable new offers (ESG checklist): 39% → 30% → 80%.
    - Change in NPS among financially vulnerable customers: 3 → 9 → (target not specified here).
    - CNP products/partnerships improving access for vulnerable populations: 9 → 14 → 15.
text:
3.4.6.1 Targets
The Group’s targets related to consumers and end-users
are managed through La  Banque   Postale’s mission-led
company 
indicators (for example, the NPS of customers
experiencing 
financial difficulties) and CNP  Assurances’
company purpose (for example, the number of products
improving access to insurance for  vulnerable groups).
By managing these targets, the Group can identify its
performance  progress in terms of customer satisfaction,
service accessibility and customer protection.
For 
example,  the  Bank’s performance in providing
community-based financing allows better support and
guidance for business advisors on supporting their customers,
and more specifically in adjusting commercial targets for
this purpose.  
CNP  Assurances has a number of indicators  which reflect
customer satisfaction:
•the Customer Effort Score (CES) measures the effort
made by customers to obtain a response to their request;Please  see the glossary  on page 808 for definitions of the main CSR terms 2024 Universal  Registration Document     La Banque Postale 2252Sustainable performance
Social information
•the Net Promoter  Score (NPS) allows the Company to
measure the likelihood that its customers will recommend
its products or services to others, thus providing a direct
indication of customer loyalty to the brand;
•finally, the Customer Satisfaction Score (CSAT) measures
the level of  customer satisfaction with the products and
services offered, providing an overview of perceived
perfo rmance.
The target s for  La Banque Postale’s  mission-led company
indicators and CNP   Assurances ’ company purpose are
presented  in Section 2.3.4.7 “Additional indicators specific
to the entity”.  [S4_MDR_T_01_12] [S4_5_04]
La Banque Postale is trialling some indicators  for potential
negative impacts such as cybersecurity impacts, or impacts
related  to the  information or security of consumers and
end-users. It does not wish to disclose these  indicators for
confiden tiality  reasons. [S4_MDR_T_13_14]

title: Personal data protection indicators
heading: 2.3.4.7.3 Personal data protection indicators
start_phrase: The percentage of employees trained in GDPR includes all employees recorded in the workforce of the relevant entities at the end of the calendar year who have completed the training during the last two years.
summary:
- Focus on social inclusion and accessibility of banking and insurance services:
  - Customer NPS for people experiencing financial difficulties improved from 2023 to 2024 but did not meet the annually updated target; results influenced by the economic environment; an ambitious support plan is being implemented.
  - Products improving access to insurance for vulnerable populations are close to the 2025 target.
  - L’Appui, La Banque Postale’s support program for customers in financial difficulty, significantly increased its reach (42,209 people in 2024 vs. 33,595 in 2023 and 30,121 in 2022), reflecting tougher economic conditions.
  - Inclusion metrics:
    - Consumer loans ≤ €1,500 stable at 5.7% in 2024.
    - Home loan borrowers earning <2x minimum wage rose to 19.4% (from 17.1% in 2023).
    - Livret A accounts with balances <€100 increased slightly to 46.9%.
    - Simplicité account users grew to 418,840, indicating continued foundational banking access for vulnerable customers, with some upgrading to broader packages.

- Personal data protection (GDPR) training:
  - Training validity is two years; coverage increased across entities in 2024:
    - La Banque Postale SA: 98.1%.
    - CNP Assurances SA: 90.7%.
    - La Poste employees working for LBP: 88.7%.

- Accessibility for people with disabilities:
  - La Poste maintains nationwide physical accessibility of branches and ATMs.
  - 98% of ATMs accessible to people with reduced mobility; 100% accessible to blind and visually impaired.

4.1.1 Corporate culture
La Poste Group’s  values, shared by La  Banque  Postale,
guide 
the Group  on a  day-to-day basis. They include
accessibility,  fairness,  consideration,  proximity,  openness
and a  sense of  service. They lead  to the  fight  against
exclusion by promoting banking accessibility and inclusion,
proximity and regional development, thanks to an accessible
and responsible offer, and to reinforcing the relationship
of trust  with  customers.  The code  of conduct, which sets
out the Group’s rules of good  conduct, fully reflects these
values.
As a bancassurance provider and a mission-led company
since  2022, La Banque Postale includes this commitment
in its Articles  of Association  and in  all of  its activities
(additional  information is available in Section 2.16.1 “The
impact-awareness culture at the heart of the mission-led
company” ). [G1_1_01]
As a player  in a highly  regulated  sector, it complies with
the most rigorous ethical  and regulatory standards.
The  Code of conduct, prefaced by the Chairman of the
Executive Board, is widely distributed and is a reference
for all  employees.  They  confirm their  understanding using
the “Confirmodoc” tool, an automated process guaranteeing
the adoption of the ethical principles. This document is
appended to the Internal Regulations and is given to each
new  employee, as well as being available on the
La  Banque  Postale intranet. It is regularly  reviewed, and
submitted to the Supervisory Board for  approval.CNP  Assurances, a subsidiary  of La Banque  Postale, has its
own business conduct policies, which are formalised in its
own code of conduct. Its  company purpose, enshrined in
its Articles of Association, is worded as follows: “As a
responsible  insurer and investor,  driven by the community
values of our Group,  we work with our partners  to create
an inclusive and sustainable society, providing solutions to
as many people as possible to protect and support them
on their chosen  paths.” These commitments reflect the
responsibility of CNP Assurances in its business segment,
while being consistent with the Group’s values. A secure
whistleblowing platform is also available to report any
breaches of  the values and  principles. [G1_MDR_P_01_06]

start_phrase:
La Poste Group’s values, shared by La Banque Postale,
guide

summary:
- Accessibility of services
  - Commitment to physically accessible banking via post offices and ATMs.
  - 98% of ATMs accessible to people with reduced mobility; 100% accessible to the blind/visually impaired.
  - Customer assistance in French Sign Language via Deafi, with 6,044 deaf/hearing‑impaired customers assisted in 2024.

- Ethical and responsible business conduct
  - Corporate culture anchored in accessibility, fairness, proximity, and service; mission-led company status since 2022.
  - Group-wide Code of Conduct, periodic reviews, Confirmodoc acknowledgement tool; CNP Assurances maintains its own code and secure whistleblowing channel.
  - No political financial or in-kind contributions in 2024; lobbying overseen by Chief Risk & Compliance Officer and General Secretariat.
  - Key advocacy topics in 2024: Basel 3 (CRR3/CRD6), CMDI, Retail Investment Strategy, FiDA, digital euro/legal tender, PSD3/PSR, AI Act, SFDR review, CS3D, Solvency II review; national focus on inheritance banking fees.
  - Compliance with transparency rules: registrations in EU Transparency Register and France’s HATVP.
  - Public administration involvement: APE representative on Supervisory Board; Government Commissioner attends boards/committees in advisory capacity.
  - Participation in industry bodies (FBF, AMAFI, ASF, AFG, France Assureurs).

- Anti-corruption governance and performance
  - Governance bodies (Supervisory Board, Risk Committee, Executive Board) oversee the anti-corruption framework, risk mapping, controls, and reporting.
  - Policies aligned with Sapin II and UN Global Compact; zero-tolerance stance, internal whistleblowing accessible to all employees and third parties.
  - Annual corruption risk mapping; accounting controls; tailored training across entities and geographies.
  - 2024 results: zero convictions and zero fines for corruption/bribery.
  - Ongoing enhancements: strengthened controls, procedures on whistleblowing and conflicts of interest, third‑party assessments, accounting controls; sponsorship policy formalization and beneficiary assessment tool rollout.

- Whistleblowing system
  - Group platform (third-party hosted) accessible to employees and external stakeholders; Ethics Officer oversight; independence of investigations with a three‑level validation process.
  - CNP Integrity Line available 24/7 with response within three months post-acknowledgment (extendable for complex cases).
  - Strong protections for whistleblowers (confidentiality, anti-retaliation) under Sapin II and EU Directive 2019/1937; unitary control of alerts reported to governance from 2024.

- Employee awareness and training
  - Induction and recurring training on ethics, AML/CFT, conflicts of interest, data confidentiality, and systems use.
  - New 2024 training module on ethics, anti-corruption, and influence peddling; widespread deployment across employees and those acting on behalf of the bank.
  - High completion rates: 99% completion of ethics/anti-corruption e‑learning among target population by end‑2024; 98.7% AML/CFT training (LBP SA scope); 99% of roles classified as “at‑risk” (LBP SA scope) covered.
  - Entity-specific programs (CNP, LBP AM, La Financière de l’Échiquier) and ESG/culture training for Supervisory Board members.

- Supplier relations and responsible purchasing
  - Supplier dependency management with a 25% alert threshold; monitoring, diversification support, and orderly exit planning.
  - Commitment to timely supplier payments: RFAR charter signatory; Group responsible purchasing policy; risk mapping and action plan oversight.
  - Monthly dashboards since 2021; SME officer and SME-specific tracking added in 2025; internal Supplier Relations Mediator (no 2024 referrals).
  - 2024 payment metrics: average payment term 51.6 days; invoices paid on time—SMEs 81.2%, ISEs 84%, large corporates 80.5%, unspecified 69.8%; no legal proceedings for late payments.
  - Integration of ESG criteria in procurement: EcoVadis assessments at CNP; AFNOR sectoral CSR criteria (typically ~10% weighting); ISO 20400-aligned approach; equal treatment and transparent selection; contract clauses on ethics, ESG compliance, audit rights, and termination for non‑compliance.

- EU Green Taxonomy (GAR) disclosure
  - Presentation of assets included in the Green Asset Ratio calculation across loans, debt securities, and equity instruments for financials, non-financials, households, and local governments.
  - Breakdown by environmental objectives (climate change mitigation/adaptation, water & marine resources) and instrument types (including use‑of‑proceeds, enabling, transitional).
  - Highlights of household exposures (notably residential real estate and renovation loans) and taxonomy‑eligible/aligned portions across portfolios.

Governance information
In 2024, La  Banque  Postale and CNP  Assurances SA
presented their positions to  public authorities, either
directly  or by contributing to market lobbying, on several
European issues that  have been  the subject of proposals
for regulations  or directives:
•transposition of the Basel 3 agreement (CRR3 regulation
and  CRD6 directive): defend the  ability of banks to
finance the economy, in  particular  local authorities and
strategic  investments;
•revision of texts on bank crisis management and deposit
insurance  (CMDI):  protect equal treatment between
credit institutions, with regard to the conditions of
access  to resolution tools and the requirements for
holding  instruments eligible for resolution;
•Retail  Investment Strategy (RIS):  preserve the feedback
mechanism  for advice  that is accessible to all, and
guarantee the  proportionality of  governance,  products
and tests with  the customer,  and benchmarks as non-
public  oversight tools;
•proposal  for a  regulation on access to financial data
(FiDA): clarify the scope, strengthen the security and
sequencing  of the opening up of data,  due diligence
points concerning consumer protection, the risk of
demutualisation  and  European  sovereignty;
•digital euro and legal tender of the euro: prevent risks to
financial  stability, have a holding ceiling consistent with
cash  usage,  specify the remuneration model and
distribution  methods;
•payments (proposal for a PSD3 directive and PSR regulation):
better  manage reimbursement criteria in the event of
identity  theft;
•Artificial Intelligence Act: precisely define AI and its associated
statistical techniques, and define  an appropriate scope
of high-risk AI, prepare codes  of conduct and guidelines
for the  Commission,  develop  harmonised technical
standards;
•draft  revision of the  Sustainable Finance Disclosure
Regulation  (SFDR): simplify  disclosure  requirements,
clarify key concepts and adjust categories according to
management  strategies,  ensure  consistency  with the
Taxonomy Regulation,  consistency  with the Corporate
Sustainability Reporting Directive (CSRD),  in particular
on sector-specific standards for  insurance and financial
reporting  standards  (XBRL);
•Corporate Sustainability  Due Diligence Directive (CS3D):
implement  La Poste  Group's system and risk analysis
methodology  and contribute to its due diligence plan,
to ensure that parent companies and initiating companies
comply with the French Due  Diligence  law;
•revision  of the Solvency II Directive: consider climate
issues  (integration of climate risks in the ORSA), simplify
reporting,  support low risk  profile  criteria.
In France, La Banque Postale’s direct or indirect lobbying
mainly 
focused on the proposed law on inheritance banking
fees, in order to ensure the consistency of the planned
threshold  for free payments and the classification of
complex inheritances with  considerable human resources
used. [G1_5_09]Compliance  with  transparency  rules
La Banque Postale complies with the rules of transparency.
It is registered in the European Transparency Register
under number 667676145713-34 and in the  French directory
of 
interest representatives of the High Authority for

CNP   Assurances Holding is registered in the European

CNP   Assurances SA is also registered in the French
directory of interest representatives of the High Authority
for Transparency in  Public Life (HATVP). [G1_5_10]
Supervisory  Board members 
from  the public  administration
The Head of the audit and accounting division of the French
State  Investment  Agency (Agence des Participations  de
l’Etat – APE) at the French Ministry of the Economy,

Board of La  Banque  Postale SA as a

In addition, pursuant to the provisions of Article 15 of

Participation in organisations  representing

La  Banque  Postale SA is a member of the French Banking

firm, it is a member of the French Financial

LBP CF and LBP LF are members of the ASF (French

LBP AM is registered with the Paris Trade and Companies

authority. LBP  AM and La Financière de
l’Échiquier are members of the French Asset Management

CNP Assurances is a member of France Assureurs (French
Insurance Federation), which represents the insurance
industry in France before national, European and international
public authorities, institutions and administrative and
market authorities. [G1_5_12]
2.4.1.3 Business conduct commitments
2.4.1.3.1 Role of governance bodies  
in business conduct
The 
governance bodies ensure the implementation of an
effective  anti-corruption system, which is managed by the
Compliance Department.
Specifically, 
the Supervisory Board promotes and implements
the code of conduct aimed, in particular, at preventing,
detecting 
and managing conflicts of interest as well as
acts of corruption and influence peddling within the Company.
The 
Risk Committee examines the corruption  risk
management strategy, the structure of the anti-corruption
system, and the monitoring of actions within the Group,Please  see the glossary  on page 808 for definitions of the main CSR terms 2024 Universal  Registration Document     La Banque Postale 2292Sustainable performance
Governance information
receiving  regular reports on the deployment, corrective
actions  and  assessments  of the system. The Executive
Board,  which is responsible for implementing measures to
prevent  and detect corruption, meets every two months
as part of an internal control body that addresses issues
related  to  the  Group’s  anti-corruption compliance.
The information shared during the  meetings of this body
includes a  report  on alerts and significant  information
feedback  and their processing, action plans and their
monitoring  as well  as an assessment of the effectiveness
of the system  as a whole.  [G1_3_03]
2.4.1.3.2 Prevention and detection  of corruption 
and bribery
La Banque Postale, a subsid iary of La Poste Group and a
signatory of the United Nations Global Compact since 2003,
applies a strict anti-corruption  and influence peddling
policy,  in accordance with the French Sapin II law and
international  standards. This policy is based on La Poste
Group ’s principles: “Everyone’s concerned  – Everyone’s
vigilant – Zero -tolerance”.
All Group entities deploy a code of conduct that defines
ethical  expectations and a zero- tolerance policy in terms
of corruption. This code is accompanied by an internal
whistleblowing  system  accessible  to all employees.
The  secure and confidential reporting system makes it
possible  to report  facts or situations at risk anonymously
or by name. Each entity is responsible  for adapting this
system  to its  specific needs.
A corruption risk map is  implemented within each entity
to identify  and  prioritise  risks,  and is regularly updated . It is
presented annually  to the Supervisory  Board.
Accounting  controls are implemented to ensure that the
books, records and accounts are not used to conceal acts
of corruption or influence peddling. In the event of an
anomaly, the findings are analysed by  the dedicated
teams and, if necessary, brought to the  attention of the
Ethics  Officer  and  the Executive Board.
La  Banque  Postale Group is  strengthening this  system
with  training actions adapted to the level of employee
exposure. All entities are covered and deploy an ad hoc
system . CNP   Assurances,  for e xample, places  particular
emphasis  on raising awareness among teams about gifts,
invitations, facilitation payments and conflicts of interest.
LBP  AM focuses on the training of exposed managers and
staff, while La Financière de l’Échiquier extends its
programme  to  its  international  offices  located  in
Switzerland,  Spain, Germany and  Italy. Each organisation
ensures  that the systems are  applied operationally, incompliance with local and international  regulations.
The  systems, validated by the governing bodies,  aim to
provide employees with the necessary  tools to identify
situations of corruption or influence peddling in their
activities. 
[G1_3_01]
La Banque Postale  informs its workforce of the existence
of these policies via the code of conduct, appended to the
Internal 
Rules, which is provided to new employees and
available 
on the La Banque Postale intranet. Communication
and awareness-raising actions are carried out periodically,
particularly 
for Group employees. In addition, a new tool,
Confirmodoc, 
was introduced in 2024 to ensure that the
code 
of conduct is made fully available to La Banque Postale
employees or those acting for and on behalf of
La Banque Postale. [G1_3_05]
2.4.1.3.3 Business conduct indicators
No convictions for corruption, payments or bribery were
recorded  in 2024
2.4.1.3.4 Actions related  to the fight against 
corruption  and bribery
Corruption risk mapping makes it possible to define action
plans to mitigate the major or critical  risks identified.
In 2023 and 2024, the main actions implemented concern
the strengthening of control systems, the  development of
policies and procedures  related  to the whistleblowing
system,  conflicts of  interest and the promotion of the
whistleblowing  system.
Other action  plans are still being defined. They relate  in
particular to the  extension of the control system, in
particular to human resources or conflicts of interest, the
dissemination of procedures to assess third parties and
the strengthening  of anti-corruption accounting controls.
In September 2024, a new plan was  launched to formalise
a sponsorship policy, roll out  a beneficiary assessment tool
and enhance the conflict of interest declaration completed
by managers.
All initiatives  aim to strengthen the fight against corruption,
with completion expected by 2025. [G1_MDR_A_01_12] [G1_4_03]

2.4.1.3.5 Independence and accessibility of the whistleblowing system
Presentation  of the whistleblowing system
The whistleblowing system for processing reports was set
up by La Poste and rolled out to La Banque Postale Group.
This 
common platform is accessible to all La Banque Postale
entities. 
Each corporate entity is responsible for processing
the alerts received within its scope. The Group Ethics
Officer has an overview of all reports within the Group scope.
This 
system reflects the Bank’s commitment to maintaining
ethical  and rigorous governance  while benefiting from
La Poste  Group ’s shared infrastructure.
It enables any person concerned to report behavio ur
contrary  to the  Group’s values  or reprehensible acts, in
accordance  with the Sapin II law and the requirements of
the duty of vigilance. It is  accessible to internal employees
(employees, interns and work-study students) and to third
parties  (specifically service providers or suppliers).
This  system is  based on  a secure platform  hosted by  a
third-party provider, the Whistleblowing Centre, guaranteeing
the confidentiality of exchanges and the protection of
whistle blowers.  The access procedures are detailed in the
Group’s  code of  conduct, available  in internal and public
versions.  Training  and  awareness-raising  campaigns  are
regularly organised for  Group employees to ensure  a clear
understanding of the system  and encourage its use.At CNP Assurances, in addition to the Group system, this
system  takes the form of the CNP Integrity Line online
whistleblowing  platform, which is available 24 hours a day
to 
any third party in the Group, wherever they are located.
Each  alert filed  via this platform  is subject to  a report,
which is sent  immediately to the  Managing Director
when the seriousness of the events warrants it. Once the
investigation of the file is completed, a response is provided
to the whistleblower  within a reasonable period of time
not exceeding three months after the acknowledgment of
receipt, 
provided that all the necessary information has
been provided. In the event  of a complex alert requiring
in-depth investigations, this period may be extended. [G1_1_02]
Processing of alerts and independence of investigators
Reports  received via  the platform are entrusted to the
Investigations  Department, which reports  to the Fraud
Management  Department. Following analysis, a report
may  lead to  an investigation by an independent team.
Interviews may be organised with the employees implicated
or witnesses of the facts. At the end of the investigation, a
confidential 
report is prepared. This independent department
is responsible for conducting target and rigorous surveys.
[G1_1_08]
A three-level process guarantees the integrity of the
investigations:  the investigators  collect and analys e
the  reported facts; a contact or deputy manager verifies
the results obtained; finally, the  head of the department
validates the conclusions.

Governance information
The interviews conducted as part of the surveys respect
the principles of confidentiality and fairness. At the end of
each  investigation, a confidential report is drafted and
sent  to the  competent departments, which is managed in
accordance with La  Banque   Postale’s ethical standards.
[G1_3_02]
In addition,  from  2024, a  unit check of alerts recorded on
the platform is set up by the Ethics Officer, who reports on
these aspects to  the governance and to the Supervisory
Board of La Banque  Postale. [G1_3_03]
Protection  of whistle blowers
Whistle blowers  benefit from  comprehensive  protection
against retaliation, in accordance with  the Sapin II law.
Their  identity,  as well  as that  of the  persons concerned or
third parties mentioned in the alerts, is strictly confidential.
La  Banque   Postale Group’s commitment  to compliance
with  the provisions of the law on the protection of
whistle blowers  is formally expressed  through a “procedure
for collecting and processing La  Banque  Postale reports”
available  to all employees.
No disciplinary,  discriminatory or punitive action, such  as
dismissal  or demotion,  may be taken against those who
have used the system to raise concerns. In addition,
La  Banque  Postale has introduced specific policies to
protect  these  individuals, guaranteeing  them a  safe
environment  free from pressure.
Therefore, the “Reporting User  Guide” specifies the
provisions  put in place to protect whistleblowers from any
reprisals  that may be taken against them following the
processing of the report . These  provisions relate to:
•guaranteeing  the confidentiality of the report, the facts
reported  and all the  information collected, as well as the
identity  of the originator of the report, the persons
targeted  and  any third  parties  mentioned;
•protecting  whistle blowers against  reprisals, in particular
disciplinary or discriminatory measures (direct or indirect):
“The good faith of the whistleblower exempts  them from
any disciplinary sanction, even if the facts subsequently
appear inaccurate or would not result  in any action”;
•prohibiting  any obstruction  of whistle blowers by  any
measure  whatsoever. Anyone who obstructs  would be
subject  to sanctions.
In the event of  a report in  good faith, no  sanction may be
applied, even if the reported facts are not  proven or do not
give rise  to action.  Finally, any  attempt to obstruct the
process or unauthorised disclosure of confidential information
is subject to sanctions. These measures reflect the Group’s
commitment to an ethical and protective framework. [G1_1_05]
La Banque Postale Group is subject to Directive 2019/1937
and  has associated policies and  procedures in place to
protect  whistle-blowers.  [G1_1_12]2.4.1.3.6 Raising employee  awareness 
of business conduct
La  Banque  Postale Group employees receive training on
ethics 
matters when they first join the Group and then
throughout their careers, through regular training
campaigns on the rules of good conduct. Upon arrival,
new  employees receive an induction booklet and a copy
of 
the code of conduct. Training sessions are carried out
regularly  and awareness-raising and  communication
initiatives are implemented on these topics. For example,
the employees of Louvre Banque Privée and CNP Assurances
deploy mandatory and regulatory training (Anti-Money
Laundering and Countering the Financing of Terrorism
(AML-CFT), etc.) which is regularly monitored. Mandatory
training at CNP  Assurances must be  carried out at least
every two years, and the completion rate is monitored  by
the Compliance Department in conjunction with the
Human Resources Department. [G1_1_10]
These 
awareness-raising and  training actions are essential
because  all functions of the Company, with the exception
of 
executive assistants and general services, regardless of
the hierarchical level, are considered to be highly exposed
to 
the risks of corruption and bribery, including members
of governing bodies.  [G1_1_11]
Employees of La Banque Postale Group and its entities are
made 
aware of ethics, professional conduct and the fight
against corruption as soon as they join and throughout
their 
careers. Training covers the key principles and rules
in 
operation at the  Group and  La  Poste , i.e. respect for
customer 
needs, banking secrecy and data confidentiality,
prevention of conflicts of interest, and compliance with
rules on using information systems. In 2024, the e-
learning 
course on ethics  and anti-corruption was
deployed for all employees of La Banque Postale Group as
well  as the people working for and on behalf of
La  Banque  Postale. Some 99% of this  target population
had completed the programme by 31 December 2024.
A new training course entitled “Regulations: adopting the
rules and procedures on ethics, anti-corruption and
influence peddling” was launched in April 2024. Lasting
1  hour and 15  minutes, it replaced the two previous
training  sessions “Regulations: ethics  and anti-corruption”
and “Regulations: anti-corruption for the most exposed
employees”.
The training  covers the  following topics:
•anti-corruption, definition  and challenges, corruption
and influence peddling:  differentiation and  scenarios;
•anti-corruption system: enforcement, confidentiality
and  professional  secrecy:  identifying and managing
conflicts of interest, whistleblower rights.
The e-learning course on ethics and anti-corruption is
intended  for the employees of La  Banque  Postale Group
as well as the people working under the name of and on
behalf of La  Banque  Postale. It allows all employees and
managers to understand how  ethics, anti-corruption and
influence peddling  works in reality,  by being trained  to the
highest level. As of 31 December 2024, 94%  of the target
trainees were  compliant  with  these  regulations.232 La Banque  Postale      2024 Universal Registration  Document Please see the glossary on page 808 for definitions of  the main CSR terms2Sustainable performance
Governance information
Awareness-raising and  communication  operations run
hand  in hand  with training as such. Ethics and
anti‑corruption  officers relay these  actions across their
respective  areas. La  Banque Postale’s Head of Ethics also
sits on  various  bodies (managerial  communities,  Executive
Committees,  special  audit  training,  subsidiaries).
At CNP  Assurances, anti-corruption training has been
mandatory  and has been included in a compliance
training  program since 2019.  This training programme
consists  of two  modules: a first instilling an anti-corruption
and  influence peddling culture, and a second on
managing  corruption risks related  to activities, including
the purchasing  component.
LBP  AM employees receive training on the French Sapin II
law, while La Financière de l’Échiquier employees receive
initial  training,  and special training  every five years. [G1_3_06]Since  2022, a programme consisting of several modules
spread throughout the year has been offered to Supervisory
Board 
members, including specific ESG training. Other
training 
courses are also provided, in particular on corporate
culture. [G1_3_08]
All La Banque Postale SA employees, with the exception of
executive assistants and general services, are considered
to be in at-risk roles. As a result, they are required to complete
anti-money laundering and financing of terrorism training
every two years.
2.4.1.4
Commitments to suppliers
2.4.1.4.1 Supplier  dependency  management
In order to  guarantee a balanced relationship with its
suppliers, La  Banque Postale takes  great  care to avoid any
situation  in which  its suppliers  are dependent on it.
In terms of a “dependency rate”, La  Banque  Postale  has
set 25% as the alert threshold, above which it sets up a
special  monitoring system to raise supplier awareness of
this situation. This rate was  set to avoid abuse of a
dominant position. La  Banque  Postale  is therefore trying
to find  a fair balance  between this rate  and  ensuring that
its contracts  are open  to SMEs.
Buyers  are made responsible for these situations of
dependency at all stages of the purchasing process, in
particular with  the  application of anti-corruption
commitments/pillars, the AFNOR sectoral  analysis and  the
regulatory and  financial  risk documentary analysis.
Various  actions can be  taken when the dependency rate is
high:
•dependency  warning mail: email sent to inform the
supplier and ask them to diversify, particularly if
La Banque Postale knows that orders are one-off or that
the contract  will not be renewed;
•supplier  tracking with regular reviews to monitor the
situation;
•supporting  and searching for other potential customers
for the supplier.
Finally, if the relationship has to be terminated, it is planned
according  to a schedule defined  with the supplier (the
period  of notice  being prorated according to the duration
of the relationship). [G1_2_02]2.4.1.4.2 Management  of supplier payment terms
Since  2022,  La Banque Postale has been a signatory of the
Supplier Relations and Responsible Purchasing charter
with 
several La Poste Group entities. The Group undertakes
to comply with ten commitments, including the guarantee
of a responsible financial  relationship with  its suppliers.
As part of the  signing of the Supplier Relations and Responsible
Purchasing 
Charter (RFAR) and its certification in
September 2023, CNP  Assurances has undertaken to
implement 
a progress approach in its relations with suppliers
by introducing  a culture of dialogue  and  mediation.
In 2024, La Poste Group formalised its Responsible Purchasing
policy, which applies to La Banque Postale, based, among
other  things, on La  Banque  Postale’s commitment to
prevent  late payments, particularly with regard to micro-
enterprises and SMEs (small and medium-sized enterprises).
[G1_2_01]
The 
Purchasing Department takes into account the risks it
incurs 
in various aspects in its relationship with its
suppliers:  with respect to the Company itself, with respect
to 
non-compliant suppliers, as well as in the context  of
consultations for the outsourcing of services. In line with
its 
responsible purchasing approach for 2023-2025, a
three-year improvement plan has been set out, making
compliance 
with payment deadlines a priority for the
Group. The risk of non-compliance with supplier payment
deadlines  is also included in La  Banque  Postale’s risk
mapping,  with a follow-up of the action plan presented
every 
six months to the Finance and Strategy
Department’s Risk and  Compliance Committee.

Since  2021, a monthly  dashboard has been  set up to
manage  supplier payment terms.  This monitoring makes
it possible to address potential sources of delay, manage
billing disputes and raise supplier  awareness of the risks  of
late shipments. The  subject  has also been included in  the
individual  target s of Purchasing Department employees.
La  Banque  Postale pays particular attention to its
suppliers,  which are small  and medium-sized enterprises
(SMEs).  An SME  officer  has  been appointed to manage the
improvement  of payment terms for SMEs. Moreover, in
February 2025, La Banque Postale’s Purchasing Department
supplemented  its payment time  dashboard with an
indicator  specific to SMEs. It  will be integrated from March
2025 with  monthly  monitoring.
In addition, as part of the RFAR certification process,  since
2023 La Banque Postale has appointed an internal “Supplier
Relations” Mediator, who reports  to the Responsible
Purchasing  Committee (ARCOM) three times a year with
any supplier referrals and complaints. No referrals were
reported  by the Mediator  in 2024.  [G1_2_02]
2.4.1.4.3 Payment  practices with respect 
to supp liers
La  Banque  Postale has chosen to calculate the average
invoice  payment time in relation to the number of
invoices. Indeed, this method is more representative of
the situation  of small  companies  (particularly  SMEs)  than
an average in relation to the invoice amount. The average
payment  period  remained  stable  between  2023 and 2024.
The Group's standard  payment terms (in number of days)
by major  supplier category  are as  follows:
•suppliers  at 10 days: mainly the charity sector and
administrations, which account for less than 1% of invoices;
•suppliers at 20 days: mainly the production and distribution
of electricity, gas, steam and air conditioning  and the
collection, treatment and distribution of water and the
collection  and treatment of wastewater, which account
for less than  1% of invoices;
•suppliers  at 30  days: mainly  the social and medical
sectors,  which  account for  around  15% of invoices;
•suppliers  at 45 days: mainly the temporary employment
sector,  which account s for  around  15% of invoices;
•suppliers  at 60 days:  this covers all other categories of
purchases,  which account for around 70% of invoices.
[G1_6_02]Invoices  paid  on time to ISEs improved  by 2 points  and
those paid to unspecified category companies were up by
4.8 points compared to 2023. The percentage of invoices
paid outside the payment  deadline is  explained  by:
•the supplier's failure to comply with invoicing procedures
(non-compliant  invoices, invoices sent too late, wrong
issue date, etc.);
•the specifier's failure to comply with procedures (not
receiving invoices  on time);
•technical  errors (inability to formalise and  effectively
monitor proven disputes in La  Poste’s IS): therefore,
these  invoices are not cancelled out when calculating
payment terms.
In addition, suppliers without  a specified category account
for 6.5% of  the total number of invoices.
No legal  proceedings were recorded for 2024. This information
was confirmed by La Banque  Postale ’s Mediator.
Methodological  information 
and background information
The average payment period represents the average number
of 
days required to settle supplier invoices. The date of
issue of the invoice corresponds to the date of the document.
The 
average payment  period is calculated using the following
formula:
∑(payment date - issue date)

Louvre 
Banque  Privée, Louvre  Banque  Privée IC and Ma
French Bank.
For 
2024, the results are calculated over 11 months (from
January 
to November) supplemented  by an  extrapolation
for the 12th month based on the average  of the first 11 months.

For the CNP   Assurances SA scope, the average payment

The percentage of invoices paid on time is broken down
according to the  categories of supplier companies:
•Small  and  Medium-sized  Enterprises  (SMEs);
•Intermediate-Sized Enterprises (ISEs);
•large  corporates;
•company  category  unspecified.
Each invoice is checked to identify whether the payment
was made in accordance with the contractual commitment.
The ratio between the number of invoices passing this
check and the total number of invoices is then calculated.
The 
scope of analysis covered is the scope of La Banque Postale
SA and five of its main subsidiaries. The subsidiaries selected
are: LBP  AM, La  Banque  Postale Consumer Finance,
Louvre   Banque  Privée, Louvre  Banque   Privée IC and Ma
French 
Bank. This scope represents approximately 80% of
the number of invoices issued  within the scope of analysis
of the average  payment  period (1).
For 2024, the results are calculated over 11 months (from
January  to November)  supplemented  by an  extrapolation
for the 12th  month based on the average of the first 11 months.
[G1_6_05]
2.4.1.4.4 Integration of ESG criteria in the selection 
and monitoring of suppliers
CNP   Assurances France has formed a partnership with
Ecovadis,  which carries  out an assessment of its main
suppliers on environmental, social and ethical issues. Its
foreign  subsidiaries (Argentina, Brazil and Italy) deploy
policies  in this  area, with procedures specific to their
geography.
La  Banque  Postale must ensure that social, societal and
environmental  criteria relating to  the service being
purchased  are  included  in the  consultation  requirements
and  during the supplier selection process. Each product/
service purchasing segment is screened against specific,
tailored CSR criteria. Depending on the purchasing category,
environmental 
and social concerns usually represent 10% of
the 
overall weighting when assessing tenders. This approach
is 
based on an AFNOR sectoral mapping methodology. The
choice 
of supplier is governed by internal rules, in particular
to 
guarantee equal treatment, and is validated by the
Purchasing Manager and the specifying business line.
La 
Banque Postale also ensures that the requirements of the
specifications remain accessible to VSEs and SMEs.In 
addition,  the Responsible Purchasing Charter promotes
the definition  of responsible purchasing  (sustainable
procurement) according to international standard ISO 204001,
a 
benchmark standard on this subject,  as “procurement
that has the most positive environmental, social and
economic  impacts possible over the entire life cycle”.
The 
Group’s approach is to look for suppliers who offer
services and products that meet these requirements, in a
partnership approach with all stakeholders.
The choice of supplier is also governed by internal rules
and  justified in a document “Presentation report” which is
validated 
by the Purchasing Manager and the specifying
business 
line. The operating methods also define supplier
notifications before and  during  calls  for tenders.
La  Banque  Postale is not  subject to public procurement
and  is therefore free to weight its coefficients. But as  a
subsidiary of La  Poste, it has written all the appropriate
procedures  to show its commitment to equal treatment.
All buyers  are made aware of equal treatment: in  fact, the
choice of supplier is traced in the presentation report, a
mandatory document accompanying any new contract.
Once all bidders have submitted their bids, a multi-criteria
analysis of supplier bids is carried out, to guide the choice of
the 
supplier who will be selected to carry out the
outsourced service. As specified above, this multi-criteria
grid includes social and environmental criteria. Given the
financial 
value of the project, the criticality and sensitivity of
the 
service, the recommended choice will be submitted for
approval to the governance bodies specified above.
The progress of the entire tender  process is reported  in a
presentation report prepared jointly by the buyer and the
business 
line specifier in charge of the project, and approved
by 
their respective line manager(s). Purchasing employees
and 
specifiers are trained in this process, which is described
in the Purchasing Manual and the purchasing procedure.
When entering into the contract, the “Responsible and
Ethical Purchasing Charter between La  Banque  Postale
and  its suppliers” and the “code of conduct” are included
in the appendices to the contract, and  must therefore be
accepted by the supplier for each new contract.
La Banque Postale regularly includes new paragraphs in its
contract templates and General Purchasing Conditions (GPCs)
concerning compliance with regulations and environmental
and social issues, the possibility of audits and its ability to
terminate 
the relationship in the event of non-compliance.

summary:
- Context: Extract from La Banque Postale’s 2024 Universal Registration Document, “Sustainable performance – Notes to the sustainability report,” focused on European Green Taxonomy disclosures and the Green Asset Ratio (GAR).

- GAR methodology and scope:
  - Detailed templates showing assets included in the GAR numerator and denominator and those excluded from the numerator but in the denominator.
  - Coverage spans loans and advances, debt securities, equity instruments (banking book), and specific household products (mortgages, renovation, motor vehicle loans) plus local governments.
  - Environmental objectives reported: climate change mitigation (CCM), climate change adaptation (CCA), water and marine resources (WMR), circular economy (CE), pollution prevention and control (PRP), and biodiversity and ecosystems (BIO), with sub‑categories for use‑of‑proceeds, transitional, and enabling activities.
  - Accounting categories: amortised cost, FVOCI, FVPL (designated/mandatory), investments in subsidiaries/JVs/associates, and repossessed real estate.

- Two calculation bases and timeframes:
  - GAR disclosures presented “Based on turnover” and “Based on CapEx.”
  - Comparative data for the reporting date (T) and prior period (T‑1).

- Key quantitative structure (illustrative figures for T):
  - Total assets: ~€321.3bn; total GAR assets: ~€180.1bn; GAR‑covered assets (numerator/denominator): ~€148.1bn.
  - By counterparty within GAR‑covered assets: financial undertakings (~€24.3bn), non‑financial undertakings (~€30.1bn), households (~€83.6bn; taxonomy‑relevant ~€78.4bn, largely mortgages).
  - Assets excluded from numerator but in denominator include SMEs and non‑NFRD entities, non‑EU counterparties, derivatives, interbank on‑demand, cash, and other assets.
  - Assets not covered for GAR: central governments/supranationals, central bank exposures, and trading book.

- Off‑balance sheet disclosures:
  - Financial guarantees and assets under management (AUM) with taxonomy‑eligible and aligned breakdowns across the six objectives, including separate views for debt securities and equities; shown for T and T‑1.

- Sector (GAR) information:
  - Banking book exposures mapped to 4‑digit NACE sectors, indicating gross and “environmentally sustainable” amounts (primarily for CCM) for NFRD‑subject corporates and SMEs/others.
  - Examples include electricity (D35), construction (F41–F43), vehicle manufacturing (C29), waste (E38), and selected manufacturing and trade sectors; sectors lacking sufficient granularity are grouped on a final row.

- Methodological notes and caveats:
  - Institutions with non‑EU subsidiaries must provide best‑effort separate GARs for non‑EU exposures using estimates/proxies and explain assumptions/limitations.
  - Motor vehicle loans are included only if originated after the disclosure’s application date.

- High‑level takeaways:
  - Taxonomy‑relevant exposure is dominated by retail mortgages; reported taxonomy‑aligned volumes concentrate in climate objectives, with comparatively limited amounts for water, circular economy, pollution, and biodiversity.
  - Use‑of‑proceeds green instruments are identified separately.

title: GAR sector information
heading: 2.5.1.2 GAR sector information
start_phrase: This table shows banking book exposures to sectors covered by the European Green Taxonomy, with the counterparty’s economic activity or the activity concerned by the project financed by the Bank identified by the relevant NACE code.
summary:
- The excerpt is from La Banque Postale’s 2024 Universal Registration Document (Sustainable performance – Notes to the sustainability report) and presents EU Taxonomy Green Asset Ratio (GAR) disclosures.

- It provides detailed GAR sector information for the banking book at NACE 4‑digit level, shown:
  - Based on turnover and, separately, based on CapEx.
  - Split between non‑financial corporates subject to the NFRD and SMEs/other non‑financial corporates not subject to the NFRD.
  - By environmental objectives: climate change mitigation (CCM), climate change adaptation (CCA), water and marine resources (WMR), circular economy (CE), pollution prevention and control (PRP), and biodiversity and ecosystems (BIO).
  - For each sector: gross carrying amounts in € millions and the share “of which environmentally sustainable (CCM).”

- The sectoral breakdown highlights significant exposures (and, where available, CCM‑sustainable portions) across:
  - Electricity, gas, steam and air conditioning (D35.*) with notable CCM‑sustainable amounts.
  - Real estate activities (L68.*), including large volumes in L68.2.0.
  - Construction (F41–F43), transport and storage (H49–H53), air transport (H51), wholesale trade (G46), retail trade (G47), information and communications (J61), and professional/technical services (M70–M71).
  - Waste collection, treatment and disposal (E38.*).
  - An “Other” row aggregates exposures where the required NACE granularity is not available.

- Methodology notes clarify:
  - Counterparty assignment is based solely on the immediate counterparty’s principal activity (relevant NACE code).
  - For exposures incurred jointly by multiple obligors, classification reflects the obligor most relevant/determinant for granting the exposure.
  - Information is disclosed at the required level of disaggregation; where granularity is unavailable, amounts appear in the final “Other” line.

- The CapEx‑based view generally mirrors the turnover‑based view but shows different “of which environmentally sustainable (CCM)” amounts for several sectors, notably:
  - Higher CCM‑sustainable amounts in electricity (D35.*), real estate (L68.2.0), and waste activities (E38.3.2).

- GAR Technical Reserves KPI (based on turnover) summarizes the ratio of Taxonomy‑aligned assets to covered assets, with breakdowns by counterparty/instrument:
  - Shows the proportion of total covered assets that fund Taxonomy‑relevant sectors (eligible) and those that are Taxonomy‑aligned, across CCM, CCA, and WMR.
  - Indicates components “of which” use‑of‑proceeds, transitional, and enabling (largely negligible in the presented data).
  - Illustrates contributions from financial undertakings (including credit institutions and insurance), non‑financial undertakings, households, and local governments.
  - Notable household details: loans collateralised by residential property are fully covered (100%), with an indicated c. 11.8% CCM share; building renovation and motor vehicle loans show small CCM shares (~0.1%).

- Overall, most reported sustainability alignment appears under climate change mitigation (CCM), with limited amounts disclosed for other environmental objectives in the presented tables.

- A glossary on page 808 is referenced for definitions of key CSR terms.

title: GAR Technical Reserves
heading: 2.5.1.3 GAR Technical Reserves
start_phrase: Based on the information presented in Section 2.5.1.1, the B ank indicates in these tables the ratio of Taxonomy-aligned assets to covered assets.
summary:
- Context: Extract from La Banque Postale’s 2024 Universal Registration Document (Sustainable performance – Notes to the sustainability report), detailing EU Taxonomy Green Asset Ratio (GAR) disclosures.
- Scope covered:
  - 2.5.1.3 GAR Technical Reserves: KPIs based on turnover and on CapEx, for the current year (T) and prior year (T‑1).
  - 2.5.1.4 GAR Flow: turnover‑based KPIs on flows of eligible assets during the period.
  - References to the CSR glossary and methodological notes (templates, coverage, replication for turnover and CapEx).

- What is disclosed and how:
  - Proportions of covered assets that are Taxonomy‑eligible and Taxonomy‑aligned across environmental objectives: climate change mitigation (CCM), climate change adaptation (CCA), water and marine resources (WMR), circular economy (CE), pollution prevention and control (PRP), and biodiversity and ecosystems (BIO).
  - Breakdowns by portfolio segment and instrument: financial undertakings (credit institutions, other financial corporations, insurance undertakings), non‑financial undertakings, households, local governments; loans and advances, debt securities including Use‑of‑Proceeds (UoP/green bonds), equity; with retail detail for mortgages, renovation loans, and motor vehicle loans.
  - “Of which” flags for Use‑of‑Proceeds, transitional, and enabling activities.
  - Proportion of total assets covered by the GAR.

- Headline results (Technical Reserves):
  - Based on turnover:
    - T: total eligible GAR assets 51.4% of covered assets; Taxonomy‑aligned 5.7% in total, largely CCM (about 5.0%), with marginal CCA and WMR (~0.1% each).
    - T‑1: total eligible 54.7%; aligned 5.5% (mostly CCM ~5.2%; negligible for other objectives).
  - Based on CapEx:
    - T: total eligible 51.7%; aligned 6.0% (primarily CCM ~5.0%; small CCA and WMR ~0.1% each).
    - T‑1: total eligible 53.7%; aligned 5.7%.
  - Observations: eligibility is concentrated in households (notably residential mortgages) and non‑financial undertakings; equity exposures are negligible; enabling and transitional shares are largely nil.

- Headline results (GAR Flow – turnover):
  - T: flows of eligible assets represent 18.5%; flows that are Taxonomy‑aligned 1.7% overall, mostly CCM with small contributions from CCA and WMR.
  - Flow breakdowns mirror stock metrics, with a notable role for UoP/green bonds in non‑financial undertakings and consistent contributions from household mortgage flows.

- Methodological notes:
  - KPIs are calculated from the covered assets template using prescribed formulas; templates are replicated for turnover and CapEx.
  - Credit institutions may additionally present the proportion of assets funding Taxonomy‑relevant sectors that are environmentally sustainable (Taxonomy‑aligned) to enrich the KPI.
  - Glossary reference provided for CSR terms.

title: GAR Flow
heading: 2.5.1.4 GAR Flow
start_phrase: •This template discloses the GAR KPIs on the technical reserves of loans, calculated based on the data disclosed in template 1 on covered assets, and by applying the formulas proposed in this template.
summary:
- Context: Extract from La Banque Postale’s 2024 Universal Registration Document (Sustainable performance – Notes to the sustainability report) detailing EU Taxonomy disclosures and Green Asset Ratio (GAR) flow KPIs.
- Scope and methodology: Presents GAR flow metrics calculated both on a turnover basis and a CapEx basis, using prescribed templates and formulas derived from “template 1” (covered assets). Breakdowns follow EU Taxonomy environmental objectives and sub-classifications (use‑of‑proceeds, transitional, enabling). A glossary reference is provided.
- Environmental objectives covered: Climate change mitigation (CCM), climate change adaptation (CCA), water and marine resources (WMR), with placeholders for circular economy (CE), pollution prevention (PRP), and biodiversity and ecosystems (BIO) largely unfilled.
- On-balance-sheet GAR Flow (turnover basis):
  - Total GAR assets: about 18.5% taxonomy‑eligible; taxonomy‑aligned shares are low (around 1.7% in aggregate across objectives).
  - By counterparty/instrument:
    - Financial undertakings/credit institutions: mid‑20% eligibility; near‑zero alignment.
    - Non‑financial undertakings: ~17.6% eligibility; alignment primarily in CCM (~3.9%); higher eligibility/alignment seen in debt securities including use‑of‑proceeds.
    - Households: mortgages 100% taxonomy‑eligible with ~5.4% aligned (CCM); overall household line shows ~92% eligibility and ~4.9% aligned; building renovation and vehicle loans show eligibility but no aligned share reported.
- On-balance-sheet GAR Flow (CapEx basis):
  - Total GAR assets: about 18.5% taxonomy‑eligible; taxonomy‑aligned modestly higher than turnover basis (~1.9%).
  - Patterns mirror turnover basis with slightly higher eligibility/alignment for some non‑financial debt securities (use‑of‑proceeds) and similar low alignment for financial counterparties; households/mortgages again 100% eligible with ~5.4% aligned (CCM).
- Off-balance-sheet exposures:
  - Templates disclose KPIs for financial guarantees (FinGuar KPI) and assets under management (AuM KPI), on both turnover and CapEx bases.
  - Turnover basis: indicative figures show FinGuar ~2.7% eligible; AuM ~13.5% eligible with ~1.4% aligned to CCM (small shares in other objectives).
  - CapEx basis: FinGuar ~5.46% eligible; AuM ~15.94% eligible with alignment primarily to CCM; alignment shares across use‑of‑proceeds/transitional/enabling are minimal or zero.
- Notes: Institutions are to replicate these templates for both turnover and CapEx; results are computed from covered‑assets data using the prescribed formulas.

heading: 2.5.1.5 Off-balance sheet exposures
start_phrase: The following tables show off-balance sheet exposures calculated on the basis of data published in the table on covered assets.
summary:
The excerpt from La Banque Postale’s 2024 Universal Registration Document (Sustainable performance – Notes to the sustainability report) presents EU Taxonomy-related disclosures focused on off-balance sheet exposures and exposures to nuclear and fossil gas activities. It details:
- KPIs for off-balance sheet exposures—financial guarantees and assets under management—calculated from “covered assets” (Template 1), with results shown on two bases (turnover and CapEx). Metrics report the proportion of total eligible off-balance sheet assets that fund Taxonomy-relevant sectors, distinguishing Taxonomy-eligible vs. Taxonomy-aligned activities.
- Breakdowns by environmental objectives: climate change mitigation (CCM), climate change adaptation (CCA), water and marine resources (WMR), circular economy (CE), pollution prevention and control (PRP), and biodiversity and ecosystems (BIO), including “of which” categories for use-of-proceeds, transitional, and enabling activities, plus aggregate totals across all objectives. The templates are intended to be replicated for technical reserves and flow KPIs.
- A qualitative disclosure (Template 1) on nuclear and fossil gas-related activities, stating the bank’s exposures arise via general purpose financing to companies in these sectors, whose main counterparties are committed to SBTi-aligned low-carbon pathways. In line with Delegated Regulation (EU) 2022/1214, it flags that quantitative Taxonomy-alignment indicators are also required. The checklist confirms exposures across nuclear R&D/innovative generation, construction and operation of new and existing nuclear installations, and fossil gas electricity and heat generation (construction, refurbishment, and operation).
