title: Nuclear and fossil gas-related activities [Template 1]
heading: 2.5.1.6.1 Nuclear and fossil gas -related activities [Template 1]
start_phrase: La Banque Postale is exposed to gas and nuclear activities through general purpose financing to companies in these sectors.
summary:
- Context: Extract from La Banque Postale’s 2024 Universal Registration Document, “Sustainable performance – Notes to the sustainability report,” section 2.5.1.6 on nuclear and fossil gas-related activities, with references to CSR glossary (p. 808) and EU Delegated Regulations 2022/1214 and 2021/2139.

- Qualitative disclosure (Template 1):
  - The Bank has exposures to nuclear and fossil gas activities via general purpose financing.
  - All listed activity types are marked “YES,” covering:
    - Nuclear: R&D/innovation in nuclear generation; construction and safe operation of new installations; safe operation and upgrades of existing installations.
    - Fossil gas: Construction/operation of electricity generation; combined heat and power; heat/cooling generation using fossil gaseous fuels.
  - Main counterparties are committed to Science Based Targets initiative (SBTi) low‑carbon pathways.

- Quantitative Taxonomy alignment for GAR denominator (Template 2):
  - Based on turnover:
    - Section 4.28 activities: €108m (0.1%) total; €96m (0.1%) under climate change mitigation (CCM); no climate change adaptation (CCA).
    - Sections 4.26, 4.27, 4.29, 4.30, 4.31: €0.
    - Other Taxonomy-aligned activities (not 4.26–4.31): €10,158m (5.6%); CCM €10,170m (5.6%); CCA €1m (0.0%).
    - Total applicable KPI denominator: €180,087m (100%).
  - Based on CapEx:
    - Section 4.27: €16m (0.0%) total; €14m (0.0%) CCM.
    - Section 4.28: €97m (0.1%) total; €78m (0.0%) CCM.
    - Sections 4.26, 4.29, 4.30, 4.31: €0.
    - Other Taxonomy-aligned activities (not 4.26–4.31): €10,716m (6.0%); CCM €10,738m (6.0%); CCA €1m (0.0%).
    - Total applicable KPI denominator: €180,087m (100%).

- Key takeaway: The Bank’s EU Taxonomy-aligned exposures to nuclear and fossil gas activities constitute a very small share (~0.1%) of the GAR denominator, while “other” aligned activities represent around 5.6% (turnover basis) to 6.0% (CapEx basis).

summary:
- Context and scope: Extract from La Banque Postale’s 2024 Universal Registration Document (Sustainable performance – Notes to the sustainability report), presenting EU Taxonomy-aligned economic activities for the Green Asset Ratio (GAR) using Delegated Regulation (EU) 2021/2139, Annexes I and II, Sections 4.26–4.31 (nuclear and gas). Data are shown per regulatory templates for the GAR denominator (Template 2) and numerator (Template 3), split by turnover and CapEx, and by climate objectives: climate change mitigation (CCM) and adaptation (CCA).
- Denominator (Template 2):
  - Total applicable KPI (turnover and CapEx): €180,087m (100%).
  - Nuclear/gas sections:
    - Turnover: 0 for 4.26, 4.27, 4.29, 4.30, 4.31; €108m (0.1%) in 4.28 (mainly CCM: €96m, 0.1%).
    - CapEx: 0 for 4.26, 4.29, 4.30, 4.31; €16m (0.0%) in 4.27 (CCM €14m), €97m (0.1%) in 4.28 (CCM €78m).
  - Other Taxonomy-aligned activities (outside 4.26–4.31):
    - Turnover: €10,158m (5.6%).
    - CapEx: €10,716m (6.0%).
  - Indicative aligned share of denominator: ≈€10.27bn (~5.7%) on turnover basis; ≈€10.83bn (~6.0%) on CapEx basis.
  - Climate objective split: almost entirely CCM; CCA negligible (€1m, ~0.0%).
- Numerator (Template 3):
  - Total Taxonomy-aligned activities:
    - Turnover: €10,267m (100%).
    - CapEx: €10,831m (100%).
  - Nuclear/gas sections:
    - Turnover: €108m (1.1%) in 4.28 (CCM €96m); 0 in 4.26, 4.27, 4.29, 4.30, 4.31.
    - CapEx: €16m (0.2%) in 4.27 (CCM €14m); €97m (0.9%) in 4.28 (CCM €78m); 0 in other sections.
  - Other Taxonomy-aligned activities (outside 4.26–4.31):
    - Turnover: €10,158m (98.9%).
    - CapEx: €10,716m (98.9%).
  - Climate objective split: overwhelmingly CCM; CCA is minimal (€1m, ~0.0%).
- Key takeaway: The Bank’s Taxonomy alignment is driven almost entirely by activities outside the nuclear/gas sections (4.26–4.31), with negligible exposure to those transitional activities; alignment is predominantly for climate change mitigation, with adaptation immaterial. A glossary of CSR terms is referenced on page 808.

summary:
- Source and scope: Extract from La Banque Postale’s 2024 Universal Registration Document (Sustainable performance – Notes to the sustainability report), covering EU Taxonomy disclosures for the Green Asset Ratio (GAR).
- What’s reported: Amounts and proportions of Taxonomy-aligned activities in the GAR numerator (Template 3) and Taxonomy-eligible but not aligned activities in the GAR denominator (Template 4), with splits by:
  - Turnover and CapEx bases
  - Climate objectives: climate change mitigation (CCM) and climate change adaptation (CCA)
  - Specific EU Taxonomy sections 4.26–4.31 (nuclear and gas) and “other” activities
- Key results – Taxonomy-aligned (numerator):
  - Based on turnover: €10,267m aligned (100% of numerator); 98.9% in “other aligned activities,” 1.1% in Section 4.28; zero in 4.26, 4.27, 4.29–4.31. Strongly mitigation-driven (€10,266m CCM; €1m CCA).
  - Based on CapEx: €10,831m aligned (100% of numerator); 98.9% “other aligned,” with small amounts in 4.27 (€16m) and 4.28 (€97m); none in 4.26, 4.29–4.31. Predominantly mitigation (€10,830m CCM; €1m CCA).
- Key results – Eligible but not aligned (denominator, turnover basis):
  - Total €82,217m (45.7% of denominator), largely “other eligible but not aligned” (€82,191m; 45.6%).
  - Minimal amounts in nuclear/gas-related sections: 4.28 (€2m), 4.29 (€22m), 4.30 (€2m); none in 4.26, 4.27, 4.31; negligible CCA.
- Overall takeaways: Nuclear and gas activities contribute negligibly to both aligned and eligible-not-aligned amounts; almost all aligned exposure is in other Taxonomy activities and is overwhelmingly mitigation-focused. A glossary reference for CSR terms is provided (page 808).

start_phrase: This table presents the amounts and proportions of the GAR’s denominator represented by Taxonomy-eligible but not Taxonomy-aligned activities referred to in Sections 4.26 to 4.31 (nuclear and gas) of Annexes I and II of Delegated Regulation (EU) 2021/2139.
summary:
- Context: Excerpt from La Banque Postale’s 2024 Universal Registration Document, Notes to the sustainability report, covering EU Taxonomy disclosures tied to the Green Asset Ratio (GAR) denominator. References Delegated Regulation (EU) 2021/2139, Annexes I–II, Sections 4.26–4.31 (nuclear and gas). Points readers to the CSR glossary (p. 808).
- Template 4 (Taxonomy-eligible but not Taxonomy-aligned activities):
  - Presented on both turnover and CapEx bases, split by climate objectives: climate change mitigation (CCM), climate change adaptation (CCA), and combined (CCM+CCA).
  - Turnover-based total: €82,217m (45.7%) eligible but not aligned; overwhelmingly CCM (€82,214m; 45.7%), with negligible CCA (€4m; 0.0%).
  - CapEx-based total: €82,337m (45.7%); CCM €82,316m (45.7%); CCA €22m (0.0%).
  - Minimal exposure from nuclear/gas-specific sections (4.26–4.31), with small amounts in 4.28–4.30 and zeros or dashes elsewhere; the bulk sits in “other Taxonomy-eligible but not aligned” activities (row 7).
- Template 5 (Taxonomy-non-eligible activities):
  - Quantifies GAR denominator portions that are non-eligible under the same nuclear/gas sections.
  - Turnover-based total: €87,603m (48.6%), largely from “other non-eligible activities” (row 7: €87,587m; 48.6%); nuclear/gas sections contribute only marginal amounts (e.g., rows 2–3: €3m, €14m).
  - CapEx-based total: €86,919m (48.3%), similarly dominated by “other non-eligible” (€86,829m; 48.2%); minor amounts in rows 2–3 (€81m, €9m).
- Overall takeaways:
  - The GAR denominator is comprised mainly of “other” categories rather than nuclear/gas-specific sections.
  - Eligible-but-not-aligned exposures are about 45.7% on both bases and are almost entirely tied to mitigation; adaptation is de minimis.
  - Non-eligible activities account for roughly 48.3–48.6% of the denominator on CapEx/turnover bases.

title: Taxonomy-non-eligible activities [Template 5]
heading: 2.5.1.6.5 Taxonomy-non-eligible activities [Template 5]
start_phrase: This table presents the amounts and proportions of the GAR’s denominator covered by Template 1 activities that are Taxonomy-non-eligible in accordance with Sections 4.26 to 4.31 (nuclear and gas) of Annexes I and II of Delegated Regulation (EU) 2021/2139.
summary:
- Context: Extract from La Banque Postale’s 2024 Universal Registration Document (Sustainable performance – Notes to the sustainability report), covering EU Taxonomy disclosures, notably non-eligible activities and KPIs by business segment.
- Taxonomy-non-eligible activities (Template 5, GAR denominator):
  - Basis: EU Delegated Regulation (EU) 2021/2139, Annexes I–II, Sections 4.26–4.31 (nuclear and gas).
  - Turnover-based denominator:
    - Minimal amounts under gas/nuclear sections (e.g., €3m and €14m with 0.0% each due to rounding).
    - “Other” Taxonomy-non-eligible activities: €87,587m (48.6%).
    - Total Taxonomy-non-eligible: €87,603m (48.6%).
  - CapEx-based denominator:
    - Minimal amounts under gas/nuclear sections (e.g., €81m and €9m with 0.0% each).
    - “Other” Taxonomy-non-eligible activities: €86,829m (48.2%).
    - Total Taxonomy-non-eligible: €86,919m (48.3%).
- New disclosure scope (FAQs Nov 2024): Financial institutions must publish Taxonomy KPIs across all business segments, including asset management, insurance, and investment, beyond core banking. La Banque Postale provides segment KPIs for material businesses.
- Asset management (LBP AM):
  - Portfolio Taxonomy alignment ratio at 31 Dec 2024: 3.0%.
  - Contribution breakdown: 0.6% from debt securities; 2.4% from equity instruments.
- Insurance business (CNP Assurances within Group via equity-accounted shares):
  - Combined Taxonomy KPI (per EC Communication C/2024/6691):
    - Turnover-based alignment: 3.0%.
    - CapEx-based alignment: 4.1%.
- Underwriting indicators (non-life, adaptation objective):
  - Taxonomy-aligned non-life gross written premiums / total non-life GWP: 0.7% at end-2024.
  - Methodology: Eligible premiums must meet technical screening for substantial contribution to climate change adaptation, DNSH, and minimum safeguards; compliance supported by procedures to manage adverse impacts. In France, aligned premiums largely reflect natural disaster coverage in motor and homeowner policies.
- Investment indicators (insurance portfolios):
  - Aim to measure the share of CNP’s investments aligned with the Taxonomy for climate change adaptation and mitigation (turnover and CapEx bases), demonstrating capital reallocation toward sustainable activities.
- Cross-references: Further details in LBP AM’s off-balance sheet exposures section and CNP Assurances’ CSRD report; glossary reference for CSR terms.

title: Focus on asset management
heading: 2.5.1.7.1 Focus on asset management
start_phrase: As part of the Taxonomy reporting, the asset managemen t subsidiary of La Banque Postale LBP AM carries out an alignment analysis of its portfolios.
summary:
- Context: Extract from La Banque Postale’s 2024 Universal Registration Document (sustainability report notes) detailing EU Taxonomy Article 8 disclosures expanded by Nov 2024 FAQs to cover all business segments (asset management, insurance, investment) beyond core banking.
- Scope and approach: Group publishes Taxonomy-aligned key performance indicators (KPIs) for its material segments, with methodologies aligned to EU technical screening criteria, DNSH, and minimum safeguards.
- Asset management (LBP AM): Portfolio alignment analysis conducted; overall Taxonomy alignment ratio at 31 Dec 2024 is 3.0% (0.6% from debt securities; 2.4% from equity instruments). Results referenced in the off-balance sheet exposures section.
- Insurance business (CNP Assurances):
  - Consolidation: Included in Group indicators via equity-accounted subsidiaries, with additional insurance-specific KPIs.
  - Combined KPI per EC communication C/2024/6691: 3.0% turnover-based alignment and 4.1% CapEx-based alignment.
  - Underwriting indicators: Measure contribution to climate change adaptation via non-life business; at 31 Dec 2024, Taxonomy-aligned non-life gross written premiums are 0.7% of total non-life GWP for CNP Assurances Holding and its subsidiaries. Methodology: eligibility plus alignment to technical criteria, DNSH, and minimum safeguards; in France, aligned premiums largely reflect natural disaster cover in motor and homeowner policies.
  - Investment indicators: Assess the share of investments aligned with Taxonomy for climate mitigation and adaptation, measured via turnover and capital expenditure, evidencing reallocation of capital toward sustainable activities.
- References: Further methodological and result details available in CNP Assurances’ CSRD report; glossary of CSR terms noted on page 808.

start_phrase: Underwriting KPIs measure CNP’s participation in the adaptation target through its non-life insurance business.
summary:
- Section of La Banque Postale’s 2024 Universal Registration Document detailing sustainability report notes on EU Taxonomy indicators by business segment, in line with November 2024 FAQs requiring KPIs for banking, asset management, insurance, and investment activities.
- Asset management: LBP AM’s portfolio alignment analysis shows 3.0% Taxonomy alignment at 31 Dec 2024 (0.6% debt securities, 2.4% equity); detailed results referenced in Section 6.8.9.3.6 (off-balance sheet exposures).
- Insurance business (via equity-accounted subsidiaries): additional, insurance-specific KPIs presented for:

title: Investment indicators
heading: 2.5.1.7.2.2 Investment indicators
start_phrase: The investment KPIs aim to measure the proportion of CNP Assurances’ investments allocated to economic activities compliant with the Taxonomy on the targets of climate change adaptation and mitigation in terms ofturnover and capital expenditure.
summary:
- Scope and context: Extract from La Banque Postale’s 2024 Universal Registration Document detailing sustainability reporting notes, with a focus on EU Taxonomy indicators across business segments per November 2024 FAQs requiring KPIs for banking, asset management, insurance, and investment.
- Asset management (LBP AM): Portfolio Taxonomy alignment at 3.0% as of 31 Dec 2024 (0.6% debt securities, 2.4% equity); detailed results referenced in off-balance sheet exposures.
- Insurance business (CNP Assurances):
  - Combined Taxonomy KPIs per EC Communication C/2024/6691: 3.0% (turnover-based) and 4.1% (CapEx-based).
  - Underwriting KPIs (adaptation target): Taxonomy-aligned non-life gross written premiums at 0.7%; methodology based on substantial contribution criteria, DNSH, and minimum safeguards; in France, alignment mainly via natural disaster cover in motor and homeowner policies.
  - Investment KPIs (euro and unit-linked portfolios):
    - 3.3% of technical reserves investments in Taxonomy-aligned activities (turnover approach) excluding sovereign bonds.
    - 4.5% alignment using investment outlay basis, as a share of technical reserves investments excluding sovereigns.
    - Methodology highlights: exclude sovereign bonds (green/sustainable bonds not treated differently), apply non-financial issuer turnover/CapEx shares to equities/bonds for eligibility/alignment, financial sector holdings treated as invalid at end-2024 due to lack of KPIs on all six environmental targets; property and forest holdings classified as eligible/aligned/non-aligned per Taxonomy criteria.
  - Repeated references to CNP Assurances’ CSRD report for detailed methodology and results.
- Cross-reference tables (ESRS coverage):
  - ESRS 2 General disclosures: reporting scope, methods, changes, incorporation by reference; governance roles, skills, oversight, incentives, due diligence, and internal control; business model, stakeholders, material IROs, strategy resilience, and IRO identification/assessment processes.
  - ESRS E1 Climate change: transition plan, material climate IROs, policies, actions/resources, targets, energy consumption/mix, GHG emissions (Scopes 1–3), carbon credits, internal carbon pricing, anticipated financial effects, and European Green Taxonomy section references.
  - Table maps each disclosure requirement to specific paragraphs/sections demonstrating coverage.

summary:
- The excerpt is a cross-reference table from La Banque Postale’s 2024 Universal Registration Document (Sustainable performance – Section 2.6) that maps European Sustainability Reporting Standards (ESRS) disclosure requirements to the specific report paragraphs where each topic is addressed.
- ESRS 2 (General disclosures) coverage includes: reporting scope; calculation methods and changes vs. prior statements; disclosures by reference; governance roles, skills and oversight of sustainability; integration of sustainability into remuneration; due diligence; risk management and internal controls over sustainability reporting; strategy, business model and value chain; stakeholder interests; material impacts, risks and opportunities (IROs) and resilience; methodology to identify/assess IROs, risk/opportunity management, and data sources; and a list/annex of disclosure requirements covered.
- ESRS E1 (Climate change) coverage includes: transition plan aligned with a Paris-compatible low‑carbon pathway; material climate-related IROs and links with strategy and the business model; climate IRO assessment process; mitigation and adaptation policies; decarbonization levers, actions and resources; climate targets; energy consumption and mix; Scope 1, 2, 3 and total GHG emissions; GHG removals and mitigation projects via carbon credits; internal carbon pricing; anticipated financial effects of climate-related physical and transition risks; and governance links to incentives.
- The table also references the European Green Taxonomy section.
- Notes clarify that only material disclosure requirements are listed and some data points are detailed in other paragraphs; a glossary of CSR terms is available on page 808.

title: Cross-reference tables
heading: 2.6 Cross-reference tables
start_phrase: (1) Only material disclosure requirements are indicated in this table.
summary:
- Presents cross-reference tables mapping La Banque Postale’s sustainability disclosures to the European Sustainability Reporting Standards (ESRS) and to specific sections of the 2024 Universal Registration Document.
- Covers ESRS 2 (general disclosures) including reporting scope, methodologies, changes year over year, incorporation by reference, governance roles and skills, remuneration alignment, due diligence, and internal control over sustainability reporting; strategy, business model, stakeholder interests, material impacts/risks/opportunities (IRO), and IRO identification processes.
- Details ESRS E1–E5 environmental topics:
  - E1 Climate change: transition plan aligned with Paris Agreement, climate IROs, policies, actions/resources, targets, energy use/mix, Scopes 1–3 and total GHG, carbon credits and removals, internal carbon price, financial effects of climate risks, and EU Green Taxonomy.
  - E2 Pollution: IRO assessment, policies, action plans, and targets.
  - E3 Water and marine resources: IRO assessment, policies, actions, targets.
  - E4 Biodiversity and ecosystems: transition plan, IROs, policies, actions, targets.
  - E5 Circular economy: resource-use and circularity IROs, policies, actions, objectives, and metrics (including outgoing resources and waste).
- Covers ESRS S1–S4 social topics:
  - S1 Own workforce: policies, social dialogue, grievance/remediation, action plans, targets; workforce characteristics, diversity, adequate wages/social protection, disability inclusion, training, health and safety, work-life balance, pay gaps, and severe human rights incidents.
  - S2 Workers in the value chain: policies, engagement, grievance/remediation, actions/resources, objectives across upstream/downstream segments, including child/forced labor risks.
  - S3 Affected communities: policies, engagement, remediation, action plans, positive-impact commitments, and targets.
  - S4 Consumers and end-users: policies, engagement, remediation, actions/resources, and targets.
- Covers ESRS G1 Business conduct: governance roles/skills, corporate culture, commitments on business conduct, supplier management and payment practices, anti-corruption/bribery prevention, incident reporting, and lobbying transparency.
- Provides extensive linkage of ESRS data points to other EU legislation and frameworks, including SFDR, CRR/Pillar III ESG disclosures, the EU Benchmark Regulation, and the European Climate Law, specifying where metrics such as board diversity/independence, fossil fuel involvement, climate targets, energy use, GHG emissions and intensities, physical/transition risk exposures, labor and human rights metrics, waste, and water appear.
- Notes that only material disclosure requirements are listed in the cross-reference tables; some data points are detailed elsewhere in the document.
- Introduces the Risk factors – Pillar III disclosures section on ESG risks:
  - Defines ESG risks as the negative impact of environmental, social, and governance factors on financial performance/solvency, affecting counterparties and assets, and transmitting through traditional risk categories.
  - Outlines the evolving regulatory framework: ECB (2020) supervisory expectations, EBA (2021) report, EU Green Taxonomy with first-time Green Asset Ratio (GAR) calculation at 31 Dec 2023 (annual for taxonomy, semiannual for Pillar III), and Implementing Regulation (EU) 2022/2453 governing semiannual qualitative and quantitative ESG risk disclosures (transition and physical risks).
  - References French regulations on business ethics (duty of care, Sapin II) and corporate governance codes.
  - Points to related sections with quantitative indicators and methodologies (e.g., Sections 6.8.7–6.8.10 and 6.1).

Environmental, social and governance (ESG) risks
6.8
Environmental, social and governance (ESG) risks
6.8.1 Definition  of ESG risks
6.8.1.1 General definitions
ESG  factors include all environmental, social and
governance  issues that may have a negative or positive
impact  on the  financial performance or solvency of a
company, entity, sovereign or individual.
From a regulatory standpoint, ESG risks correspond to the
negative  impact  of  ESG  factors on  the  financial
performance  or solvency of a financial institution  due to
the current or prospective  effects of these factors on the
institution’s  counterparties or assets. The ESG risks
represent  the risks  of losses generated by climate and
environmental events, social  and societal developments or
governance  failures affecting La  Banque   Postale’s
internal  operations  or its businesses.
ESG risk management is based on a national and European
regulatory 
framework that is in the process of being
developed. The European Central Bank (ECB) guide,
published in November 2020, sets out the supervisory
expectations for the management and reporting of climate
and environmental risks. It is supported by the European
Banking  Authority  (EBA)  Report on  ESG Risk
Management  and  Supervision dated June 2021.
In addition to these regulations,  there are  two main
reporting requirements:
•the European Green Taxonomy Regulation (EU) 2020/852
of 18 June 2020, which is designed to facilitate sustainable
investment by defining a common classification system for
sustainable economic activities. The related transparency
requirements and environmental targets are set out in a
series 
of delegated regulations. In accordance with the
regulatory requirements, La Banque Postale has, for the firsttime, calculated its Green Asset Ratio (GAR) at 31 December
2023. This exercise will be done  annually under the
regulatory requirements of the taxonomy and half-
yearly 
under the Pillar III ESG requirements (see Section
6.8.9  “Inputs in the calculation of the green asset ratio”);
•implementing Regulation (EU)  2022/2453 published in the
Official Journal of the European Union on 19 December 2022,
which describes the Pillar III disclosure requirements for
ESG 
risk. La  Banque  Postale underwent this regulatory
exercise for the first time on 31 December 2022.
This 
exercise has  since been repeated every six months,
with the publication of this qualitative report accompanied
by a quantitative exercise covering physical risk and
transition risk. The results of this exercise  are presented
in this chapter (see Sections 6.8.7 “Indicators of potential
climate 
change transition risk”, 6.8.8 “Indicators of
potential climate  change physical  risk”  and 6.8.10  “Other
climate change mitigation measures not covered by the
European Green Taxonomy”).
In 
addition to European regulations, French regulations
also cover social and governance issues. This mainly
concerns business ethics regulations (duty of care, Sapin II
law, etc.
) and the code of governance of listed companies,
published in 2020 by the French Association of Private
Companies.
ESG 
risk may be identified as a risk category in its own
right 
or as a factor affecting traditional risk categories
(credit 
risk, market risk, operational risk, liquidity risk, etc.)
through 
different transmission channels, as shown  in the
dedicated paragraph in Section 6.1 “Summary of risks”. The
chains of transmission should  therefore be differentiated
according to the asset class concerned.

title: Certification of consolidated sustainability information and control of the disclosure
heading: 2.7 Certification of consolidated sustainability information and control of the disclosure
summary:
- Scope and purpose
  - Extract from La Banque Postale’s 2024 Universal Registration Document, Pillar III disclosures on Environmental, Social and Governance (ESG) risks.
  - Explains definitions, regulatory context, governance, identification, measurement, management and reporting of ESG risks, plus required Pillar III templates and EU Taxonomy KPIs.

- Regulatory framework and definitions
  - ESG risks defined as the potential negative impact of environmental, social, and governance factors on financial performance/solvency.
  - Key references: ECB 2020 climate and environmental risk guide; EBA 2021 report on ESG risk management; EU Green Taxonomy Regulation (EU) 2020/852; Implementing Regulation (EU) 2022/2453 on ESG Pillar III disclosures.
  - French requirements on ethics and governance (duty of care, Sapin II, governance code).
  - Double materiality principle (outside-in financial materiality and inside-out impact materiality).

- ESG risk typology
  - Environmental: climate risk (physical acute/chronic and transition) and nature risk (dependencies/impacts per TNFD; systemic risks such as ecosystem collapse, contagion).
  - Social and societal: impacts from employment, health and safety, inclusion, data protection; risks from regulatory/market changes.
  - Governance: failures in governance practices and integration of E/S factors; reputational risks and strategy execution failures.
  - ESG as a standalone category and as a driver across traditional risk types (credit, market, operational, liquidity).

- Governance and organization
  - Mission-led company since 2022; ESG embedded in Articles of Association and strategic planning.
  - Oversight by Supervisory and Executive Boards; Sustainability Department reporting to the Executive Board; Group Risk Department (ESG Risk unit) sets framework and second line monitoring; Group Compliance oversees compliance/reputational dimensions.
  - Training for employees (climate modules, Climate Fresk); subsidiaries align frameworks; group steering committees.

- Risk identification, assessment and mapping
  - Integration of ESG in lending and product design (pre-deal climate analysis, sector exclusions, support for renewables).
  - Climate risk assessed across short, medium, long horizons; links to credit, market, liquidity, operational, strategic risks with mitigation frameworks.
  - Annual ESG risk map with environmental (physical/transition climate and nature), social/societal, and governance risk families; tracking indicators (e.g., flood exposure, SBTi alignment, fossil fuel exposure, HR and customer protection metrics).
  - Criticality of ESG risk rated “major”; biodiversity added in 2023.

- Measurement and monitoring
  - ESG embedded in Risk Appetite Framework (non-financial ratings, reputational risk).
  - Physical risk indicators: exposure of LBP buildings to 1-in-100-year flood; exposure of real estate book to flooding (2.6% of residential book at risk; concentration in Île-de-France).
  - Transition risk indicators:
    - Alignment with SBTi pathways (annual gap tracking).
    - Financed emissions (PCAF-based): ~10,920 ktCO2 for corporate and real estate books (c.74% coverage) at 30 June 2024; Pillar III table shows 2.97 MtCO2e as of 31 Dec 2024 for covered scope.
    - Sector exposures and near-zero net exposure to fossil fuels (0.005% of corporate book in Q4 2024); coal/oil & gas phase-out policies.
    - EU Taxonomy Green Asset Ratio (GAR) 2024: 5.7% mandatory (stock, turnover view), plus 2.3% voluntary = 8.0% total; data and interpretation caveats noted.
  - Social/societal indicators: customer satisfaction 7.5/10; gender equality index ≥91/100 across entities.
  - Governance indicators: 50% women on Supervisory Board (2024); 39% of offers labeled “socially responsible” in 2023; target 80% by 2025.

- Time horizons, provisions, and stress testing
  - ESG Risk Management Policy covers short/medium/long-term impacts; sector policies for coal and oil & gas (exit by 2030), aviation financing principles (2022), and deforestation (2023).
  - 2024 provisions: transition risk on corporates (carbon price impacts) and physical flood risk on retail mortgages (recoveries).
  - Participation in ACPR (2020/21) and ECB (2022) climate stress tests; internal stress testing based on NGFS scenarios over 1–3 years with intent to extend >10 years in 2025; market and operational risk scenarios (e.g., Seine flood, greenwashing).

- Business model integration and incentives
  - Commitments: PRB, Finance for Biodiversity Pledge, SBTi-approved portfolio pathways with targets for Scope 1–2–3 reductions, 100% renewable electricity, and temperature alignment for portfolios by 2025.
  - ESG integrated in credit approval and client reviews (transition plans, IWF scores); Disputes and Exclusions Committee for counterparties.
  - Remuneration: ≥40% of individual variable pay tied to non-financial targets since 2022; profit-sharing includes ESG ratings metric (25% weight); budget for gender pay equity.

- Products, tools, and client support
  - ESG checklist mandatory in product approvals; eco-design approach.
  - Impact Weighting Factor included in impact mortgages and specialized financings; Carbo app for client carbon footprinting/offsets.
  - Retail: extensive home energy renovation financing (e.g., Prêt Avance Rénovation), impact consumer finance, solidarity savings.
  - Corporate/public sector: green and impact loans; SRI offering via LBP AM (GREaT methodology).

- Monitoring and reporting model
  - Three lines of defence with ESG in Internal Audit scope.
  - Internal dashboards to GRMC; regulatory disclosures; reliance on external data; ESG data platform underway.

- Pillar III ESG templates and key results
  - Credit quality by sector and financed emissions (Template 1):
    - Method to identify firms excluded from EU Paris-Aligned Benchmark (via NACE + GOGEL/GCEL, minus SBTi-aligned renewables); exposure €411m; sustainable exposures €498m.
    - Financed emissions in table: 2.97 MtCO2e (incl. 2.24 Mt Scope 3) as of 31 Dec 2024.
  - Energy efficiency of real estate collateral (Template 2):
    - €85.3bn loans; EP score distribution; EPC labels; majority without EPC label; mix of obtained/estimated data; stability vs 2023.
  - Sectoral low-carbon pathways (Template 3): alignment metrics and distance to IEA NZ2050 2030 milestones for autos, air transport, cement.
  - Exposure to top 20 global emitters (Template 4): €43m (0.14% of covered assets), mostly green-aligned exposure; decreased since June 2024.
  - Physical risk exposures (Template 5): 5.9% of total exposures sensitive to physical risks (12.3% corporates; 4.7% residential RE; 0.1% commercial RE); sector/maturity breakdown.
  - EU Taxonomy KPIs:
    - GAR stock 5.7% (turnover) and 6.0% (CapEx); flow 1.7%; households (mortgages and renovations) dominate aligned assets.
    - Voluntary GAR +2.3% (stock); off-balance sheet alignment for assets under management; inclusion of CNP Assurances via equity method.
    - Detailed numerator/denominator composition and sector splits (Templates 6–9).
  - Other climate mitigation not covered by Taxonomy (Template 10): ~€11bn of green-targeted assets (green/sustainability bonds, renewable energy loans, Eco-PTZ and other green retail loans, RT 2012/RE 2020 housing) outside mandatory GAR.

climate 
change has been directly linked to human activity and
the massive use of fossil fuels (coal, oil and gas), which are
highly emissive.
The main consequences of climate change as currently
observed are droughts, floods, water shortages, fires,
melting ice caps,  rising sea levels, storms and declining
biodiversity.
Climate  change leads  to structural  changes, which in turn
affect economic activities and the financial system:
•physical  climate risk  corresponds  to the financial
effects  of climate change  (increased occurrence of
extreme  weather  events  and  gradual climate change).
The effects may be direct (loss of productivity, damage to
physical
 assets) or indirect (impact on supply chains).
Physical  risk may be  described  as:
•acute  when it results from extreme events (drought,
floods, storms),  or
•chronic when it results from gradual changes (rising
temperatures, rising sea levels, water stress, biodiversity
loss,  land  use  change,  habitat destruction, resource
scarcity);
•transition  climate  risk  corresponds to the direct or
indirect  financial loss that may be incurred by
La  Banque  Postale as it  transitions to a low-carbon
business 
model (abrupt change in the climate-related
regulatory framework, technological advances, market
developments).
A common indicator of climate risk is the emergence of
stranded  assets in portfolios. Stranded assets are assets
that  may decrease  in value or generate a lower-than-
expected return at some time prior to the end of their
economic 
life due to regulatory, technological or market
developments that  are in turn  linked  to the occurrence of a
physical or transition climate risk.
La Banque Postale has identified several asset  classes that
may become stranded assets in the medium to long
term:
•loans  and investments already in La  Banque  Postale’s
portfolios 
that are not aligned with current sector
policies;
•financing of projects or counterparties whose activity is
significantly 
threatened by the occurrence of a physical or
transition risk.
6.8.1.2.1.2
Nature risk
According to the Taskforce on Nature-related Financial
Disclosures  (TNFD) (1), nature can be defined through a
construct  of four  realms: Land, Ocean, Freshwater and
Atmosphere. It consists of two elements. The first concerns
environmental 
assets, i.e. living and non-living natural areas(forests, wetlands, agricultural areas, etc.) that are at the
origin of the ecosystem services that provide benefits to
businesses. The second concerns biodiversity, which is an
essential 
feature of nature. Biodiversity is key to
maintaining the quality, resilience  and quantity of
ecosystem assets and providing the ecosystem services
on which businesses and  society  depend.
Nature risks are the potential  threats to  an organisation
that result from its dependence and impact on nature.
They are analysed according to the double materiality
principle, distinguishing between:
•dependency  risk: an organisation may be more or less
dependent 
on one  or more ecosystem services for the
operation of its business processes. Any deterioration of
these 
ecosystem services would expose the organisation to
risk. These risks may be linked to a physical risk;
•impact  risk: an organisation’s  activity may cause
changes in the state of natural capital. These changes
may  be positive or negative  and direct, indirect or
cumulative.  They  may  be linked to a transition risk.
In the case of biodiversity, the following systemic risks exist
alongside the physical and transition risks:
•risk of ecosystem collapse: risk of a critical natural
system ceasing to function (tipping point reached,
causing 
ecosystem collapse  at the geographical or
sector  level);
•global risk: risk associated with the fundamental
impacts  of nature loss on the levels of transition risk and
physical risk in one or more portfolios;
•contagion risk: risk of financial difficulties experienced by
one 
or more financial institutions due to nature risks
spreading to the entire financial system.
6.8.1.2.2 Social and societal  risks
La Banque Postale is also exposed to risks arising from social
and societal issues.
The EBA defines social factors  as all  social issues that may
positively or negatively affect the financial performance or
solvency 
of an entity, a sovereign or an individual. There
are many social factors. They may concern the  rights, well-
being and interests of individuals and communities, or
inequality,  health,  inclusion, labour relations, occupational
health and safety, human  capital and community issues.
Social risk  is the  risk  of a negative financial  impact on
La  Banque  Postale stemming from the current or
prospective impacts of social factors on its counterparties
or assets. In relation to La  Banque  Postale’s businesses,
social  risk may refer to the failure  of the Group’s practices
in terms of employment, employee health and safety or
the protection of  personal data.
Societal risk is the risk of financial losses arising from more
or less rapid regulatory changes introduced in response to
social injustice, changes in consumer behaviour or market
developments.

6.8.1.2.3
Governance  risks
The 
EBA defines governance factors as all issues relating to
measures,  rules,  decision-making bodies, information and
supervisory processes that may have a positive or negative
impact  on the financial performance or solvency of an
entity,  sovereign or individual.  Governance factors cover
governance  practices (leadership and executive
remuneration,  audits,  internal controls,  tax avoidance,
board independence, shareholder  rights,  corruption and
other compliance issues), as well as how  companies or
entities incorporate  environmental  and social  factors  into
their  policies and procedures. Governance risk is the risk  of
any negative financial impact on La  Banque  Postale
stemming 
from the current or prospective impacts of
governance  factors on its counterparties or assets. Within
the framework of  La  Banque   Postale ’s businesses, it
concerns the risk of financial losses and/or reputationaldamage resulting from the failure of the rules and
procedures to manage, administer and control the Group
in accordance  with  sound governance principles.
La Banque Postale makes a distinction between:
•the risk of financial loss due to failure to take into account
environmental and social risks in the Group’s strategy
and  organisation;
•image and reputational risks related to the failure of
La  Banque  Postale to  meet its  commitments resulting
from poor implementation of the strategy decided by
the Group and its subsidiaries, and deficiencies in the
control processes ensuring  its correct implementation;
•the risk of damage to La  Banque Postale’s reputation as
a result of its involvement in social conflicts or
environmental controversies.
6.8.2
ESG risk governance
ESG organisational  structure  & risk 
management
Following  its designation as a mission-led company in
February 2022, La  Banque  Postale has embedded ESG
principles
 more deeply in its governance. Its Articles of

The Sustainability Department, which reports directly to the

ESG aspects. The head of the department sits on the
Executive 
Committee and is a member of
La Banque Postale’s existing bodies. The department helps
to ensure that ESG factors are fully taken into  account by
La Banque  Postale’s various  entities.
Since  2020, ESG risks have been incorporated into
La  Banque  Postale’s risk  governance, in particular by

and  coordination of all ESG-based initiatives. In order to
encourage 
their inclusion in all of the Group’s risk control

La  Banque  Postale Group’s Risk Appetite Framework are

ESG  risks are identified in the same way as other risks in
the bank’s  risk  mapping and  their management  is

Validation Committee, etc.).
The Group Risk Department, in particular its ESG Risk unit,
verifies the proper implementation of the level 2 ESG risk

the risk management framework with the subsidiaries and

The Group Compliance Department (GCD) helps to monitor

management 
frameworks, producing Compliance

The GCD is also in charge of La  Banque   Postale Group’s
compliance system, the target of which is to guarantee
compliance with the regulations covering in particular:
money 
laundering and financing  of terrorism; fraud,
bribery and corruption; customer protection; provision of
investment services
 and mandatory regulatory training.

6.8.3 Risk  identification and assessment
ESG  risks raise unprecedented challenges and issues  for
all participants in the financial system. La Banque Postale
is very committed to the just  transition and places the
control of these risks at the top of its priorities. The first
step  in developing and deploying an effective risk
management  framework  consists  of identifying  the risks.
The identification of ESG risks is the result of
comprehensive  monitoring of La  Banque  Postale’s
external environment (regulatory, legislative, economic, etc.),
its business portfolio and internal functioning (financing,
investments, internal processes,  etc.), as well as its  strategic
guidelines. The latter take into account the guidelines of
civil society, in particular  those of non-governmental
organisations specialising in the subject.
In particular, the climate risk factor must be identified
before  lending decisions are made, in order to anticipate
the possible  effects of  climate change  on the  future  of the
business, customer solvency or mortgages or other forms
of loan collateral. La  Banque  Postale’s lending
commitments are designed to steer financing towards
sectors  and activities that are less exposed to ESG risks.
For example, in order to increase the asset portfolio’sresilience  to transition risk,  La Banque Postale is helping to
finance 
the energy transition, focusing exclusively on
renewable energy projects and imposing an outright ban
on the financing of  new  fossil fuel projects.

6.8.4 Measuring and monitoring the balance sheet  impact of ESG risks
6.8.4.1 Measuring exposure to ESG risks
In order to manage ESG risks, La  Banque  Postale has
defined 
several metrics at different levels of the organisation,
covering both its operational scope and its banking businesses.
The non-financial rating indicator  has been incorporated
into  the risk appetite framework since 2021. As
La Banque Postale’s target is to remain the leader in terms
of non-financial performance, it is expected that its
ratings  in this area will reflect  this  ambition  and that,  on
average, La  Banque Postale  will  be in  the top percentile  in
the various  agency  rankings.
The impacts of climate change and any failure to manage
the related risks  may generate  a reputational  risk for
La Banque  Postale . This risk is addressed at  Group  level as
part of the  strategic and  business risk-mapping process. It
includes the risks associated with all actions that may
have a direct or indirect impact on the Group’s reputation
among 
the public, its shareholders, supervisors or the
market.
In addition to these global indicators for measuring ESG
risks, La  Banque  Postale has developed specific indicators
for monitoring climate risks on the one hand, and social
and  societal risks on the other. The calculation of these
indicators is based on methodologies defined by
La Banque Postale, based in  particular on the regulations
in force, best market practice and the data available to
date. Estimates  have  been  calibrated  to optimise the
coverage  of certain banking books  when data is lacking or
is of poor quality. The methodologies, data and
assumptions 
used are  subject to  a process of continuous
improvement,  with the aim of achieving the most
accurate  calculations and assessments  possible.
These  indicators  are presented  below.

These may take the form of sector-specific policies, reviews
and  adjustments of La  Banque Postale’s internal processes,
or stronger control and monitoring arrangements. In this
respect, 
La Banque Postale has defined its sectoral policies
to phase out coal,  oil and gas by 2030. Added to this are

the 
aviation sector, adopted in 2022, enabling it to define

sector. In 2023, La  Banque  Postale adopted a policy to
govern 
the financing of companies whose activities give
rise to a deforestation risk.
Provisions:
In 2024, La  Banque  Postale includes provisions relating to
climate risks. These provisions were defined in  addition to
the sectoral provisions  already in place by addressing two
main  portfolios:
•transition risk on  the corporate  portfolio, in  particular by
assessing the impact of an increase in carbon prices on
the solvency  of counterparties;
•physical risk of flooding on the retail customers real estate
loan portfolio and the impact that it may have on
expected recoveries in the event of litigation.
These assessments will be refined and supplemented at
each  closing of financial statements and as  the system
matures.
Scenario analyses and stress tests:
La  Banque  Postale participated in the  two climate stress
test exercises conducted respectively by the French
Prudential 
Supervision and Resolution Authority (ACPR) in
2020,  and by the ECB in the first half of 2022. These
exercises highlighted the impacts of the risks concerned
over different  time horizons (short and long term).
The pilot climate stress test exercise conducted by the
ACPR between July 2020 and April 2021 provided
La  Banque  Postale with its first opportunity to measure
the Group’s transition risk and physical risk by economic
sector  and over a long period (30 years). The target was to
raise awareness of climate risk among financial
institutions  and  – for the  first  time  – to measure their
vulnerability to this risk (impact on credit risk, market risk
and sovereign  risk).This exercise was subsequently followed and
supplemented by an exercise carried out by the ECB for
the year 2022. The  aim of this exercise was to assess the level
of preparedness of European banks in the face of climate
risks through a qualitative questionnaire, quantitative
reporting and a  scenario analysis  exercise.
La  Banque  Postale was assessed on its internal stress-
testing system,  its exposure to carbon-intensive sectors
(measured in terms  of revenue) and  its ability to cope with
climate shocks according to several scenarios (NGFS
transition scenarios
(1), severe drought and flooding).
Based on the results of these exercises, La Banque Postale’s
overall  performance is in  line with the average for euro
zone 
banks. Its portfolio’s exposure to the most carbon-
intensive  sectors is  limited and its concentration on the
most carbon-intensive firms is low. This exercise collected
and structured additional data on the climate risk
exposure across different time horizons and scenarios, as
well  as raised awareness and structured the processes in
place.
An 
internal stress test framework has been developed by
La  Banque  Postale, capitalising  on the experience
acquired during these exercises, in order to measure the
impacts  of the climate risk on  its business model and
study its resilience. By projecting over a  horizon of one  to
three years on a constant balance sheet basis, the analysis
covers both Retail and Non-Retail credit portfolios
and  results in a sensitivity impact on provisions.
La  Banque  Postale aims  to roll  out this exercise  over a
period of more than 10 years in 2025.
Ad hoc sensitivity scenarios were also developed to assess
the materiality  of the  climate risk  in terms of  market risk
and  operational risk.
The analysis of the market exposures applies the short-
term  (three years) NGFS disorderly transition scenario and
covers outstanding bonds, cash and non-consolidated
equity investments. The assumption  of this disorderly
short-term  transition  aims to reflect market  risk and
capture potential shocks.
The operational risk scenarios examine the climate risk in
terms  of business continuity, reputational risk  and liability
risk. Their target is to estimate the impact of a probable
and  significant crisis on La  Banque  Postale’s activities,
making 
it possible to cover the different  types of impact:
physical  risks with the 100-year Seine flood scenario and
transition 
risk with the green laundering scenarios. The
assumptions of these  scenarios deliberately target  a
strong  shock over a limited time horizon (one year) and
are used to calibrate the bank’s insurance coverage needs
(Seine flood).
The 
data, combined with the ESG risk management work,
provided a basis  for incorporating climate issues in the
Bank’s Internal Capital Adequacy Assessment Process
(ICAAP)  and led to an increase in the coverage of climate
risks by capital. They are also used in the context of risk
management: in the mapping of climate risks and the
work to produce the materiality matrix. These exercises
are part of La  Banque   Postale’s overall approach to
identify strategic levers for the decarbonisation of  its loan
portfolios in order to ensure compliance with its trajectories.

Internal  control and monitoring  of ESG risks within
La Banque  Postale  is based on  the three lines of  defence

First line of defence
Primary  responsibility for ESG risk management lies with
the Group entities, whose managers are responsible for
implementing  a risk  management framework that
complies  with  internal and external  requirements. In
addition,  each employee provides assurance that risks are
properly 
managed at their level through their  knowledge,
experience, 
judgement  and  compliance with their entity’s
rules. The Sustainability Department, supported by the Group
Risk  Department,  is also responsible for steering the
operational  implementation of the ESG aspects of the
strategic  plan. As a result, the business lines’ operational
departments and the ESG experts constitute the first line of
defence.
Second line of defence
The Group Risk Department, in particular its ESG Risk unit,
verifies  the proper implementation of the level 2 ESG risk
management  framework, performs studies and analyses
to obtain  assurance  that  the level of exposure  to ESG risks
is acceptable and complies with the commitments given
by La  Banque  Postale, and reports on this  work to
La  Banque  Postale’s Executive Board and Supervisory
Board. 
It also oversees the coordination and harmonisation
of work on  the risk  management framework with the
subsidiaries and  within the  Group.  The  Group  Compliance
Department  (GCD)  supports the monitoring of Social and
Governance risks (please refer to Chapter 3 on governance
for more  details).
Third  line of defence
The Internal Audit Department acts as the  last line of defence
by performing periodic controls on all of the Group’s
entities.  The system is described in La  Banque  Postale
Group’s Periodic Controls Charter.  ESG risks are an
integral part of the Internal Audit Department’s audit
programme.6.8.6.2

physical  and transition risks based on the indicators put in

of the Bank’s  portfolios may be carried  out  from time to

In addition, external publications are communicated by

(excluded from the Paris-Aligned Benchmark). This  exclusion
is based  on data  relating to the  share of sectoral revenues
of non-financial sector companies as specified in points
(d) to (g) of Article 12.1 and Article 12.2 of the Climate
Benchmark Standards Regulation  (Delegated Regulation
(EU)  2020/1818) (1).Due  to the absence of a reference list or precise data that
would allow these companies to be clearly identified,
La  Banque   Postale has developed a methodology that
comes 
close to meeting this target and is identifying these
companies in two stages:
•the first stage consists of identifying the companies whose
business is  mentioned in the delegated regulation, based
on its sector identifier (NACE code) and on the
companies 
listed in the “Global Oil  & Gas Exit List”
(GOGEL)
(2) or the “Global Coal Exit List” (GCEL)(3)
published 
by the Urgewald NGO. The sectors identified
are: extraction, distribution and refining of hard coal and
lignite; extraction, distribution and refining of oil fuels;
extraction, 
manufacturing and distribution of gaseous
fuels; and electricity generation;
•the second stage consists of excluding from the
pre‑selected companies those companies with a low-
carbon  pathway  approved by the Science Based Targets
(SBTi)  initiative, or whose main activity is the production
of electricity from renewable energy sources.
Thus, this methodology makes it possible to identify a
total exposure to companies excluded from the Paris-
Aligned Benchmark of €411 million. On the other hand,
the amount of  sustainable exposures, i.e. aligned with the
European Green Taxonomy, amounts to €498 million.

Taxonomy-related  information 
In accordance with the regulations, La   Banque  Postale
calculates and publishes the results of its eligibility
analysis 
and alignment with the targets of the European
Green  Taxonomy.
The Taxonomy-based analysis  of a financed asset is carried
out in four  stages :
(i) ide ntification  of assets eligible for one of the targets of
the taxonomy; 
(ii) identification  of assets contributing to one of the
eligible assets  (“CCS”);  
(iii) identification  of assets not harmful to one of the other
five target s (“DN SH”); and  
(iv) identific ation  of assets meeting the minimum social
guarantee  criteria  (“MSS”).
These  four steps make it possible to calculate  the Bank’s
Green Asset  Ratio  (GAR),  the  target of which  is to quantify
a proportion of “sustainable” assets by comparing the
amount  of aligned assets to the amount of the Bank’s
hedged assets. At  31 December  2024, La Banque Postale’s
GAR  was 5.7% in terms of turnover and 6.0% in terms of
CapEx.  It mainly  consists of real estate financing to
households.
The 
mandatory GAR calculation is based on a detailed analysis
of each asset, without the use of estimates. To provide
further  information, a voluntary GAR is also calculated,
using  estimates  and  a slightly  broader  analysis scope. 
At 31 December  2024, La   Banque  Postale’s voluntary
green  assets  ratio  was 2.3%, i.e. 8.0% in terms of turnover
and 8.3%  in total  CapEx.  La  Banque  Postale’s off-balance sheet alignment ratio is
3.2% in terms of turnover and 5.7% in terms of CapEx for
the share of assets under management. It mainly consists
of 
assets under management held by the Group’s asset
management subsidiary, LBP  AM. It is 0% for  financial
guarantees.
La  Banque  Postale’s alignment ratio includes the results
of 
CNP  Assurances’ taxonomy analysis using the equity
method. The latter amounted respectively to 3.3% in
turnover (4.5% in CapEx) and 0.7% for investment and
underwriting activities. 
Very little data is currently available concerning the
alignment with the  European Green Taxonomy of
counterparties’ 
assets and the projects financed by the
Bank. Data availability  should improve with each
successive  calculation exercise and as all economic
players become more proficient in applying the
Taxonomy.  Work is also underway to establish  systems for
the collection of  customer data. 
In addition, the remaining uncertainty with regard to the
interpretation of certain  regulatory provisions should
gradually be resolved, allowing La  Banque  Postale to
further clarify  its disclosures  in future publications.  
These disclosures will systematically take into account
changes in the applicable standards and the interpretations
adopted  by the market,  the Group and its  subsidiaries.
For more information, please refer to Section 2.2.6 of this
document .

Other  climate  change mitigation measures not covered 
by the European  Green  Taxonomy
The purpose of this table is to present the initiatives
launched by La  Banque  Postale in response to climate
change that are  not covered by the European Green
Taxonomy. These initiatives concern the bond portfolios
and the corporate and retail trading books that contribute
to mitigating  transitional  and  physical  climate  risk.
This  table covers assets which the Bank has internally
classified as green or sustainable  for other purposes
(green bond framework, green  products, Banque de
France  regulatory reporting on the use of regulated
savings,  etc.).  The  first half of the table lists green bonds
acquired from third  parties, while the second half lists
lending 
associated with products such as Eco-PTZ housingloans and energy renovation loans. In addition, in this table
La  Banque  Postale also includes financing for  real estate
assets that comply with Thermal Regulation 2012 (RT 2012) or
Environmental 
Regulation 2020 (RE 2020) but are not
included in the GAR calculation. The green or sustainable
products offered by the Bank to its customers are
described in  Chapter 2 of this document dedicated to non-
financial information.
Overall, at 31 December 2024, €11 billion of La Banque Postale
assets were identified as having a green target, excluding
those 
present within the mandatory ratio of the European
Green Taxonomy.
